statement: Every distinct subject an organization tracks is represented by its own table, and the table's fields represent the characteristics that describe that subject.
Tables are the foundation of a database; a sound database depends on tables being properly designed.
Data are the raw values stored in the database, whereas information is data processed so it is meaningful and useful; the designer must keep the two distinct.
Build a preliminary field list capturing the organization's fundamental data requirements as the core set of fields the database must define.
Derive the table list partly by reviewing the field list objectively (letting the fields suggest subjects), not solely from the interview-derived subjects list, to avoid missing tables.
A given characteristic should appear only once on the field list; remove all but one occurrence of duplicate characteristics.
Rename generic characteristics (e.g. Name, Address, City, Phone) with a subject prefix so each field reflects its true relationship to a specific subject.
Choose the field/characteristic name that conveys its intended meaning clearly, completely, and unambiguously.
Each item on the field list must have a unique name.

Distinguish a characteristic from a subject: if an item represents a collection of things or can be broken into smaller pieces with its own characteristics, it is a subject and belongs on the subjects list, not the field list.
A calculated field stores the result of a string concatenation or a mathematical expression as its value.
Remove calculated fields from the preliminary field list onto a separate calculated-field list, because they are used in a specific way later in the design process.
Field names containing words such as amount, total, sum, average, minimum, maximum, or count are likely calculated fields.
Record each characteristic that carries a value list (enumerated list) along with its acceptable values, since such lists often enforce a business rule.
Do not bother recording value lists for obvious sets such as yes/no or true/false; record only distinct, specific value sets.
Analyze the organization's current database before designing the new one, to identify aspects of the current system useful to the new design.
The analysis process has three steps: reviewing how data is collected, reviewing how information is presented, and conducting interviews with staff.
Conduct interviews only after gathering the data-collection and information-presentation samples, so the interviews can probe specific samples.
Interview users before management, because users see the daily operational detail and their answers help you interpret management's responses.
Alternate open-ended and closed questions in interviews: open-ended questions surface subjects, closed questions elicit the details of a chosen subject.
Identify subjects by finding nouns that name a person, place, thing, or event; these become tables.
Identify characteristics by finding nouns (usually singular) that describe an aspect of a subject; these become fields.
Keep the list of subjects and the list of characteristics on separate sheets.
Review the preliminary field list and calculated-field list with users and management to catch any omitted fields before proceeding.
Do not treat the field and table lists as absolutely final; expect to revisit them because new requirements commonly surface as the design unfolds.
Attach a succinct, clear description to every data-collection and report sample, recording its purpose and how it is used, for reuse later in the design.
A sample that represents more than one subject is complex; use the subject-identification technique to decompose it.
The level of structural and data integrity achieved is in direct proportion to how thoroughly the design process is followed.
Designing a database without a sound design method leads to poor design whose typical symptoms are inconsistent data and inaccurate information.

Do not adopt the current database structure as the basis for the new structure, because copying it transfers every hidden problem (awkward tables, poor relationships, inconsistent field specifications) into the new database.
Begin the design process by defining the end result: a mission statement declaring the database's purpose and mission objectives declaring the tasks performed against its data.
The mission statement declares the specific purpose of the database in general terms and is defined at the very start to keep the design focused and prevent unnecessary size or complexity.
A good mission statement is succinct, general, unambiguous, and free of phrases describing specific tasks.
The mission statement is complete only when it states the database's specific purpose and is understood and agreed upon by everyone concerned.
A well-written mission objective is a declarative sentence defining a single general task, free of unnecessary detail and unambiguous.
Decompose any mission objective that represents more than one general task into two or more separate mission objectives.
A mission objective should state what task the data supports, not how it is implemented, because implementation belongs to the application-development process.
Mission objectives drive later definition of table structures, field specifications, relationship characteristics, views, data integrity, and business rules.
Derive mission objectives from both the explicit and the implicit information in interview responses; failing to capture implicit information yields an incomplete set of objectives.

The database design process has seven phases: define mission statement and objectives; analyze the current database; create the data structures; determine and establish table relationships; determine and define business rules; determine and establish views; review data integrity.

Creating data structures means establishing tables from the identified subjects, associating each table with fields representing the subject's characteristics, designating a primary key, and then defining field specifications for every field.
Establish each table relationship's logical connection using primary and foreign keys or a linking table, then set the relationship's characteristics.
Business rules are constraints imposed on data, data structures, or relationships, identified through interviews and documented; they establish levels of data integrity.
Use validation tables to support business rules when a field has a finite range of values, ensuring the consistency and validity of stored values.
Determining and establishing business rules is an ongoing, iterative process, because as the organization grows its perspective on the data changes and its rules must change with it.
Define views from interviews about how users work with data (some need detail, some summary) and set retrieval criteria for any view that must return a limited or specific set of records.

The review-data-integrity phase has four steps: review each table against proper-design criteria (table-level integrity), review and check field specifications (field-level integrity), test the validity of each relationship (relationship integrity), and review and confirm the business rules.
Implement the logical database structure in an RDBMS only after completing the entire design process.
The design process is never truly finished, because the database structure will always need refinement as the organization evolves.

Conduct every interview prescribed by the design process regardless of database type or organization size (using self-interviews when designing for yourself), because omitting an interview risks missing information that adversely affects the final structure.
Establish interview guidelines before conducting interviews so they are run consistently and successfully.
Limit each interview to about ten participants, because larger groups raise participant intimidation and reduce participation.
Conduct separate interviews for users and management, because the two groups hold different perspectives and separating them avoids conflicts that diffuse results.
condition: when an organization has distinct user and management groups

statement: Use open-ended questions as the default in interviews and reserve closed questions for intentional, sparing use, because closed questions supply their own responses and prevent elaboration.
Maintaining control of the interview is the single most important interview guideline.
Prepare interview questions in advance to give the interview focus, direction, and continuity of thought.
Establish a detailed record of every interview, via notes, an assigned transcriber, or a tape recorder used only with the participants' permission.

Analyze the current database by reviewing how data is collected (paper, data-entry screens, web forms) and how information is presented (reports, screen presentations, web pages), gathering a sample of each.

The goal of analyzing the current database is to determine whether it supports current information requirements, uncover structural deficiencies, and determine how it must evolve to support future requirements.
Paper-based databases typically contain inconsistent, erroneous, duplicate, redundant, incomplete, and stale data, so analyze them only to identify items worth incorporating into the new database.
A legacy database (in use five or more years) is not guaranteed sound even when relational; duplicate fields and redundant data, common in older nonrelational systems, cause data-integrity problems.
Each table must represent only one subject and contain no duplicate fields.
Refine fields so each stores only a single value (no multipart or multivalued fields), and move or delete any field that is not a distinct characteristic of the table's subject.
Every table must have a properly defined primary key that uniquely identifies each record in the table.
Complete the entire design process regardless of the database's type, size, or purpose, because partially following it is nearly as bad as not following it and an incomplete design is a poor design.

A field specification (traditionally called a domain) defines all the elements of a field across three categories: general elements (e.g. field name, description, parent table), physical elements (e.g. data type, length, display format), and logical elements (e.g. required value, range of values, default value).

There are four types of data integrity: table-level, field-level, and relationship-level integrity (all structure-based) plus business rules (based on how the organization interprets and uses its data).

A table relationship is characterized by three things: the relationship type (one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many), the participation type (optional or mandatory), and the degree of participation (the minimum and maximum number of related records).
The core structures of every relational database are fields, records, and tables; a view is a virtual table used to work with data drawn from two or more tables simultaneously.

A key field uniquely identifies records within a table and establishes relationships between tables, whereas an index is strictly a software device used to optimize data processing; a key and an index are not the same thing.
A relationship both helps ensure data integrity and is the mechanism by which a view draws data from multiple tables.
Determine each relationship's participation characteristics either from the nature of the data stored in the tables or from specific business rules.
Data integrity refers to the validity, consistency, and accuracy of the data in a database, and the accuracy of retrieved information is in direct proportion to the level of data integrity imposed.
Table-level integrity (traditionally entity integrity) ensures there are no duplicate records and that the field identifying each record is unique and never null.

Field-level integrity (traditionally domain integrity) ensures every field's structure is sound, its values are valid/consistent/accurate, and fields of the same type (e.g. all CITY fields) are defined consistently throughout the database.

Relationship-level integrity (traditionally referential integrity) ensures the relationship between a pair of tables is sound and that records stay synchronized whenever data is inserted, updated, or deleted in either table.

Business rules impose restrictions based on how the organization uses its data (such as a field's range and types of values, a table's participation type and degree, and the synchronization used for a relationship) and must be considered alongside the three structural integrity types.

A relationship exists between two tables when records of one can be associated with records of the other, and is established either through primary and foreign keys or through a linking (associative) table depending on the relationship type.
A relationship enables multitable views and is crucial to data integrity because it helps reduce redundant data and eliminate duplicate data.
There are exactly three relationship types (cardinalities) between a pair of tables: one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many.

A one-to-one relationship relates each record in one table to exactly one record in the other and is established by copying the parent table's primary key into the child as a foreign key; it is the only relationship in which both tables may share the same primary key.

A one-to-many relationship relates one record in the parent (the 'one' side) to many records in the child (the 'many' side), is established by copying the parent's primary key into the child as a foreign key, and is the most common relationship because it eliminates duplicate data and minimizes redundant data.

Resolve a many-to-many relationship with a linking table whose structure is built from copies of both tables' primary keys, which together form the linking table's composite primary key and separately each act as a foreign key.
Do not resolve a many-to-many relationship by inserting fields of one table into the other, because that leaves the relationship 'unresolved' and harms data integrity; use a linking table instead.

A table's participation in a relationship is mandatory when at least one record must exist in that table before related records can be entered in the other, and optional when no such record is required.
The degree of participation specifies the minimum and maximum number of records a table may have associated with a single record in the related table, notated as min,max.
Determine each table's participation type and degree from how the tables' data is related and how the data is used.

Tables are the chief structures of the database; each table represents a single specific subject, the logical order of its records and fields is irrelevant, and it always has a primary key that uniquely identifies each record.
The subject a table represents is either an object (a tangible person, place, or thing) or an event (something occurring at a point in time) whose characteristics you wish to record.

A data table stores dynamic data used to supply information and is the most common table type, whereas a validation (lookup) table stores largely static data used specifically to implement data integrity.
A field (attribute) is the smallest structure in the database, represents one characteristic of the table's subject, and is the structure that actually stores data.
Every field in a properly designed database holds one and only one value, and the field's name identifies the type of value it holds.

Three field types appear in poorly designed databases: multipart (composite) fields holding two or more distinct items, multivalued fields holding multiple instances of the same value type, and calculated fields holding a concatenation or the result of a mathematical expression.
A record (tuple) is a unique instance of the table's subject, comprises the entire set of the table's fields, and is identified throughout the database by a unique value in its primary key.
A view is a virtual table composed of fields from one or more base tables; it stores only its structure and draws its data from the base tables rather than storing data itself.

Views matter for three reasons: they let you work with data from multiple related tables at once, they can prevent specific users from seeing or manipulating particular fields (security), and they can implement data integrity (a validation view).
The two most significant key types are the primary key and the foreign key, and a key's type determines its role within the table.

A primary key is a field or group of fields (a composite primary key when two or more) that uniquely identifies each record, identifies the record and the table throughout the database, and enforces table-level integrity.
Every table in the database should have a primary key.

A foreign key is a copy of another table's primary key placed in a second table; it establishes the relationship and enforces relationship-level integrity because its values must match existing primary-key values, preventing orphaned records.
A null represents a missing or unknown value and is not the same as a zero or a string of blank spaces, both of which are valid, meaningful values to a query language such as SQL.
Represent a value that does not apply to a record with an explicit value such as 'N/A' rather than a null, to keep the information clear.
condition: when a field's value is not applicable to a particular record

statement: Nulls adversely affect mathematical and aggregate operations because any operation involving a null evaluates to null, producing undetected inaccurate results; prevent this by disallowing nulls in fields used in such expressions.
Whether to allow nulls in a table depends on how the data is used.
The most detrimental result of improper database design is inaccurate information, which can adversely affect the organization's operations and bottom line.
Use an RDBMS program's design tools and sample databases only after creating the logical database structure, because those tools help implement the physical tables, not design the database.
Treat the logical database design as the architectural blueprint and the physical RDBMS implementation as the finished building: complete the logical design first, then implement it physically.

The relational database model rests on set theory and first-order predicate logic, and this mathematical foundation is what lets it guarantee accurate information and makes it predictable, reliable, and sound.

The objectives of good design are: support both required and ad hoc retrieval; build tables properly and efficiently (one subject, distinct fields, minimal redundancy, a unique-value identifier); impose field-, table-, and relationship-level integrity; support the organization's business rules; and lend itself to future growth.
Good design yields a structure and data that are easy to modify and maintain, information that is easy to retrieve, and end-user applications that are easy to build.
Choose a database-design methodology, learn it well, and apply it faithfully, because a trial-and-error approach wastes time and forces repeated repairs.
A design methodology yields a fully normalized, sound structure only if followed completely; you cannot shortcut, circumvent, de-emphasize, or omit any part and still expect a sound structure.

Normalization is the process of decomposing large tables into smaller ones to eliminate redundant and duplicate data and to avoid insert, update, and delete problems, testing table structures against normal forms (rule sets) and modifying them until sound.

A sound table has a field that uniquely identifies each of its records, and every field in the table describes the subject the table represents (the plain-English equivalent of passing Third Normal Form).
Redundant data opens the possibility of a value being entered inconsistently, which in turn produces inaccurate information; minimizing redundancy is therefore central to data integrity.

In a relational database the physical order of records and fields is immaterial and each record is identified by a unique-value field, which together give the data logical and physical independence so a user need not know a record's physical location to retrieve it.
A relationship between a pair of tables is established implicitly through matching values of a shared field.

SQL is the standard language for creating, modifying, maintaining, and querying relational databases; a basic query uses SELECT…FROM to choose fields and tables, WHERE to filter records, and ORDER BY to sort results.

The relational database provides built-in multilevel integrity (field, table, relationship, and business levels), logical and physical data independence from applications, guaranteed data consistency and accuracy, and easy retrieval across related tables.
An RDBMS is software to create, maintain, modify, and manipulate a relational database, and its quality is a direct function of how fully it supports the relational model.
A database is an organized collection of data used to model an organization or an organizational process, whether stored on paper or in software.

There are two types of databases: operational databases (used for OLTP, storing dynamic constantly-changing data) and analytical databases (used for OLAP, storing static historical, time-dependent data); the two require radically different design methodologies.

Decompose any field whose value contains two or more distinct data items (such as a single ADDRESS field holding street, city, state, and zip) into separate single-item fields, so the data can be retrieved and sorted independently.

The overall database-development process has three phases: logical design (tables, fields, primary and foreign keys, relationships, data integrity), physical implementation (creating tables, keys, relationships, and integrity in software), and application development.

Always complete the logical design as fully as possible before physical implementation, so that structural decisions are made consciously and methodically and the number of later structural modifications is minimized.
Perform the logical-design and physical-implementation phases separately to ensure maximum focus, effectiveness, and efficiency.

Most database problems fall into two categories — application problems and data problems — and poor database design is typically the root cause of data problems such as missing, incorrect, mismatched data and inaccurate information.
Do not base a new database on a vendor's sample database structure, because doing so risks creating an improper, inefficient, and incomplete design.
Database design is more an art than an exact science, drawing on intuition and communication skills as much as on theoretical and technical knowledge.
Classify every table by the role it plays into one of four table types: data table, linking table, subset table, or validation table.
Give each table a unique, descriptive, self-explanatory name that is meaningful to the entire organization.
A table name must clearly and unambiguously identify a single subject; a vague or ambiguous name usually means the table represents more than one subject and should be split.
Use the minimum number of words needed to convey a table's subject, avoiding both cryptic abbreviations and overly long names.
Do not use words conveying physical characteristics (such as file, record, or table) in a table name, because they add confusion and a name containing them often represents more than one subject.
Do not use acronyms or abbreviations in a table name, because they are hard to decipher and often mean different things to different parts of the organization.

Do not use proper names or other words that unduly restrict the data a table can hold (e.g. 'Southwest Region Employees'), because doing so forces problematic duplicate table structures as the organization grows.

Do not give a table a name that implicitly or explicitly identifies more than one subject (such as names containing 'and', 'or', a slash, an ampersand, or 'Miscellaneous'), because each table must represent only one subject.
Use the plural form for table names (a table represents a collection) and the singular form for field names, so the two are easy to distinguish in documentation.

Every table description must both explicitly define the table's subject and state why that subject is important to the organization; if you cannot explain why a table matters, reconsider whether it is needed.
Compose each table description to be clear and succinct: do not merely restate the table name, and avoid being either too brief or too verbose.
Do not include implementation-specific information (such as how or where a table is used or accessed) in a table description, because that belongs to implementation, not design.
Make each table description self-explanatory and independent; do not make one table's description depend on or cross-reference another's.
Do not use examples in a table description, because a well-defined description is clear, succinct, and self-explanatory without them.
Assign each field to the table whose subject it best describes, assigning a field to more than one table when appropriate, and verify the assignments later when refining table structures.
Do not use an RDBMS or computer during the logical-design process until the design is complete (unless using design-specific CASE software); work on paper to avoid premature-implementation traps.
An ambiguous, vague, or unclear field name is a sign that the field's purpose has not been thoroughly identified.
Each field name must appear only once in the entire database; the only exception is a field that establishes a relationship between two tables.
exception: a field used to establish a relationship between two tables may appear in more than one table

statement: A field name must accurately and unambiguously identify the single characteristic the field represents (e.g. split a vague 'Phone Number' into 'Home Phone', 'Work Phone', and 'Cellular Phone').
Prefix generic field names (such as Address, City, State) with the table name or an abbreviation of it, and apply the chosen prefixing convention consistently throughout the database.
Do not use acronyms in field names and use abbreviations only judiciously — an abbreviation must enhance, not obscure, the field name's meaning.
Do not put words that identify more than one characteristic in a field name (names containing 'and', 'or', a slash, or an ampersand); split each implied characteristic into its own field.
Use the singular form for a field name, because a plural name implies the field holds more than one value (a multivalued field).

The Elements of the Ideal Field: it represents a distinct characteristic of the table's subject; contains a single value; cannot be decomposed into smaller components; contains no calculated or concatenated value; is unique within the database (except relationship fields); and retains most of its properties when it appears in more than one table.
Resolve a multipart (composite) field by identifying the distinct items in its value and making each item its own separate field.

Resolve a multivalued field by removing it to a new table and relating that new table back to the original via a field from the original table; decomposing a multipart field yields new fields, whereas decomposing a multivalued field yields a new table.
When another field has a one-to-one dependency on a multivalued field, include that dependent field in the new table built to resolve the multivalued field.
Do not resolve a multivalued field by flattening it into several numbered single-value fields, because that structure cannot be searched or sorted reliably and arbitrarily caps the number of values.
A relational database will always contain some redundant data; the designer's goal is to keep redundant data to an absolute minimum.

Redundant data is acceptable only when it results from a field that relates two tables; redundancy arising from any other field or table anomaly is unacceptable because it threatens data consistency and integrity.
condition: when the repeated value results from a field used to relate two tables

statement: The only necessary duplicate field is one that establishes a relationship between two tables; remove all other duplicate fields (reference fields and multiple-occurrence fields).
exception: a duplicate field that establishes a relationship between two tables is necessary and is kept

statement: Reference fields — duplicate fields added so a table holds all the data a report needs — are poor design because they force users or applications to keep every occurrence consistent at high risk of error; assemble report data with a view instead.

The Elements of the Ideal Table: it represents a single subject; has a primary key; contains no multipart or multivalued fields; contains no calculated fields; contains no unnecessary duplicate fields; and contains only an absolute minimum of redundant data.
Confirm whether a field or table complies with the ideal-element checklists by loading it with representative sample data (on paper), which is the best way to reveal anomalies.

A subset table represents a subordinate subject of a data table; it holds the fields germane to that subordinate subject plus a field relating it to the data table, but not the characteristics common to both, which stay in the data table.
A table with many blank field values usually represents more than one subject; resolve it by extracting each subordinate subject into a subset table.
Tables with almost identical structures are commonly unidentified subset tables; refine them by moving the common fields into a new data table and relating the subset tables to it.
Keys are crucial because they precisely identify each record, help establish and enforce table-level and relationship-level integrity, and establish table relationships.
There are four main key types — candidate, primary, foreign, and non-keys — and a key's type determines its function within the table.
A candidate key is a field or set of fields that uniquely identifies a single instance of the table's subject, and every table must have at least one candidate key.

The Elements of a Candidate Key: it is not a multipart field; contains unique, non-null values; does not breach security or privacy rules; is not optional in whole or part; comprises the minimum number of fields needed for uniqueness; uniquely and exclusively identifies each record and each field value within a record; and its value changes only in rare or extreme cases.
Do not use Social Security Number (or values such as passwords) as a candidate or primary key, because it can be null and breaches the organization's privacy rules.
A candidate key composed of two or more fields is a composite candidate key; use the minimum number of fields necessary to define uniqueness, because overly complex keys are hard to work with.
When a table has no natural field or field-set that qualifies as a candidate key, create an artificial (surrogate) candidate key: a new field built to conform to all the Elements of a Candidate Key.

Create an artificial candidate key not only when a table has no natural one but also when it would be a stronger or more convenient key than the available ones; a single-field ID is a common artificial key that conforms to the Elements of a Candidate Key, makes a good primary key, and simplifies establishing relationships.

A primary key exclusively identifies its table throughout the database, uniquely identifies and represents each record, and guards against duplicate records; it is the most important key in the table.
Select each table's primary key from its pool of candidate keys, and enforce that it meets the Elements of a Primary Key, which are identical to the Elements of a Candidate Key.

When choosing among candidate keys for the primary key, prefer a simple single-field key over a composite one, prefer a key whose name incorporates the table name, and otherwise choose the key most meaningful to the organization.

A primary key's value must exclusively identify the value of every other field in a record; test this by loading sample data and asking for each field whether the primary-key value exclusively identifies it, and remove any field it does not exclusively identify because that field is unnecessary to the table.

Each table must have exactly one primary key, and each primary key in the database must be unique — no two tables share the same primary key, except a subset table, which must share the primary key of its parent data table.
exception: a subset table shares the primary key of its parent data table

statement: After the primary key is chosen, designate the remaining candidate keys as alternate keys; they provide an alternative means of uniquely identifying a record in the RDBMS.
A non-key is a field that serves as no kind of key (candidate, primary, alternate, or foreign); it represents a characteristic of the subject and its value is determined by the primary key.

Table-level integrity ensures there are no duplicate records, that the primary key exclusively identifies each record, that every primary-key value is unique, and that primary-key values are never null; it is established by defining a primary key that fully complies with the Elements of a Primary Key.

After defining table structures and keys, review them with users and management to confirm the appropriate subjects are represented, the table and field names and descriptions are meaningful to everyone, and every appropriate field is assigned to its table.

Defining a field specification for every field establishes and enforces field-level integrity and enhances overall data integrity; teams that skip it typically spend up to three times as long fixing the resulting database as proper design would have taken.

Defining field specifications forces a complete understanding of the data's nature and purpose, and the full set of specifications forms the database's data dictionary — a blueprint for implementing fields in an RDBMS.
The consistency, quality, and accuracy of the data and of information retrieved from it are in direct proportion to how completely the field specifications are defined.

A field attains field-level integrity when it has a complete set of specifications: its identity and purpose are clear, its definitions are consistent across the database, its values are consistent and valid, and the modifications, comparisons, and operations allowed on its values are clearly identified.

A field specification organizes a field's attributes into three categories: general elements (e.g. field name, parent table, label, specification type, description), physical elements (data type, length, decimal places, character support, input mask, display format), and logical elements (key type, uniqueness, null support, required value, default value, range of values, edit rule, comparisons allowed, operations allowed).
A field's parent table is the only table in which the field appears, unless the field participates in establishing a relationship.
exception: a field that participates in a relationship also appears in the related table

statement: A label is an alternate, usually shorter display name for a field; never use the label as the official field name — keep the precise field name as official and use the label only in the end-user interface.

There are three field-specification types: Unique (the default, for a field that appears once or serves as a primary key), Generic (a template ensuring consistent definitions for fields of the same general meaning, such as a generic STATE field), and Replica (the default for a field based on a generic field or serving as a foreign key, drawing most settings from a source specification).

Use a field alias only in rare cases, such as when the same field must occur twice in one table (e.g. PRESIDENT ID and VICE PRESIDENT ID for two EMPLOYEE ID NUMBER occurrences), and use aliases judiciously because they can obscure a field's true meaning.

A field description must accurately identify the field and state its purpose, be clear and succinct, not merely restate the field name, avoid jargon/acronyms/abbreviations, exclude implementation-specific information, be independent of other field descriptions, and contain no examples.
Difficulty composing a suitable field description is a sign that the field needs further refinement.

Prefer general data types (Alphanumeric, Numeric, DateTime) over specific SQL data types when setting a field's Data Type, because SQL data types are implemented inconsistently across RDBMS programs and the general types are easier for users and management to understand.

Set the Character Support element to restrict which character classes (letters, numbers, keyboard characters, special characters) a user may enter, which prevents meaningless data and enhances field-level integrity.
Set Input Mask (to enforce a consistent data-entry format) and Display Format (to govern how a value is presented) using generic settings, because RDBMS programs implement both differently.

Set Null Support to 'No Nulls' for primary keys, alternate keys, and required fields, and allow nulls only when there is a valid reason; never use a blank to represent a meaningful value such as 'None' or 'N/A' — put such values in the Range of Values instead.
exception: a field may allow nulls when there is a valid reason for a missing or unknown value

statement: Set a field's Required Value to 'Yes' whenever the field serves as the primary key.
condition: when the field serves as the primary key

statement: Use a default value only when it is genuinely meaningful (e.g. 'WA' when most customers are in Washington); do not set an arbitrary default value that has no real meaning.

The Range of Values element specifies every valid value for a field across three categories (general, integrity-specific, business-specific); never use 'Other' or 'Miscellaneous' as a value, since they are nonspecific and signal that the field needs refinement.

The Edit Rule element sets when a value may be entered and whether it may later be edited (Enter Now/Later combined with Edits Allowed/Not Allowed); use a default value with the 'Enter Later' options so the field is not null until a value is supplied.

Set Comparisons Allowed and Operations Allowed to limit which comparison operators, arithmetic/concatenation operations, and operands a user may apply to a field's values, which prevents meaningless comparisons and operations.

Define field specifications by first defining as many as you can yourself and then completing the rest with a representative group of users and management familiar with the data, and do not rush this phase.

A table relationship connects logically related tables, further refines table structures and minimizes redundant data, and is the mechanism that lets a view draw data from multiple tables; a properly defined relationship ensures relationship-level integrity.
A given pair of tables participates in only one type of relationship at a time, and the relationship type rarely needs to change — only a major change to one of the table structures would force it.

A one-to-one relationship usually involves a subset table but not always; it can also be used to deliberately separate a subject's fields by access or security (e.g. public EMPLOYEES data versus restricted COMPENSATION data).

Do not establish a many-to-many relationship by embedding repeated copies of one table's key field in the other (which creates a flattened multivalued field) or by embedding single copies of the other table's fields (which creates unnecessary duplicate fields and redundant data).

An improperly established relationship causes insertion anomalies (you cannot add a record without supplying a non-null primary key) and deletion anomalies (deleting one record loses other data stored only in that record).
A self-referencing (recursive) relationship exists between records within a single table rather than between two tables, and it can itself be one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many.

Identify existing relationships by building a table matrix (every table listed across the top and down the side) and examining each table pair, considering only direct relationships and ignoring indirect ones.

Determine the relationship for a table pair by asking, from both tables' perspectives, associative or contextual (ownership-oriented or action-oriented) questions about how a single record relates to one or more records in the other table; the pair of answers reveals the relationship type.
Determine the official relationship between a table pair by combining the answers from both perspectives with the formulas 1:1 + 1:1 = 1:1, 1:N + 1:1 = 1:N, and 1:N + 1:N = M:N.
Establish a one-to-one or one-to-many relationship by copying the parent table's primary key (the 'one' side) into the child table (the 'many' side), where it becomes a foreign key.

In a one-to-one relationship a parent record must exist before a related child record; when one table is a subset table, it usually takes the child role, and the foreign key often also serves as the child table's primary key.

Establish a many-to-many relationship by creating a linking table from copies of both tables' primary keys (which together form its composite primary key and each act as a foreign key), naming it for the relationship's nature, and adding it to the final table list; this dissolves the many-to-many into two one-to-many relationships.

A linking table almost always has a composite primary key in the logical design; occasionally add another field (such as TERM) to keep the key unique, and move fields into the linking table when doing so reduces redundancy.

An inherent one-to-many relationship exists between a multivalued field's set of values and the record they reside in, and resolving the multivalued field into a new table inherits that one-to-many relationship.

Establish a self-referencing one-to-one or one-to-many relationship with a foreign key residing in the same table as the primary key it refers to, and establish a self-referencing many-to-many relationship with a linking table built from two fields of the same parent table.

Be vigilant with self-referencing relationships, because their presence can indicate a need for new field or table structures (e.g. tracking which staff are managers may imply a need to track departments); ensure each self-referencing relationship serves a useful purpose.

The Elements of a Foreign Key: it has the same name as the primary key it was copied from (except in a self-referencing relationship), it uses a replica of that primary key's field specifications (with Key Type set to Foreign, Uniqueness Non-unique for one-to-many or Unique for one-to-one, Values Entered By User, and Range limited to existing primary-key values), and it draws its values from the primary key it refers to.
A foreign key value must already exist as a value of the primary key it refers to, which ensures consistency between the two fields and establishes relationship-level integrity.

Define a deletion rule for every relationship to determine what the RDBMS does when a parent record is deleted, guarding against orphaned records; the five rules are Deny (keep and mark inactive), Restrict (block deletion while related child records exist), Cascade (delete the parent and its related child records), Nullify (delete the parent and set related foreign keys to null), and Set Default (delete the parent and set related foreign keys to their default value).
Use the Restrict deletion rule as the default and the other rules as the organization's use of the data warrants.
Always set the deletion rule from the parent table's perspective, because deleting a parent record affects related child records whereas deleting a child record does not affect the parent.
Using a Nullify deletion rule requires the foreign key's Null Support to be set to 'Nulls Allowed', and using a Set Default deletion rule requires the foreign key to have a Default Value set.
condition: when using a Nullify or Set Default deletion rule

statement: Determine each table's type and degree of participation from obvious circumstances, common sense, or standards, often deferring the rest to the business-rules phase; degree is written as (min,max) and an unlimited maximum is written with N.

A relationship attains relationship-level integrity when it is properly established (primary/foreign keys or a linking table), supports meaningful inserts (participation type), supports safe deletes (deletion rule), and meaningfully limits related records (degree of participation); verify every relationship against a checklist before incorporating it into views.

A business rule is a constraint based on how an organization perceives and uses its data, so every organization must have its own specific set of business rules — two organizations may share an identical rule for entirely different reasons.

There are two types of business rules: database-oriented rules, whose constraints can be established in the logical design by modifying field-specification elements and/or relationship characteristics, and application-oriented rules, whose constraints must be established in the physical design or in the database application; the logical-design stage handles only database-oriented rules.

Business rules fall into two categories: field-specific rules, which constrain elements of a field specification, and relationship-specific rules, which constrain a relationship's characteristics such as its type or degree of participation.
Define and establish field-specific business rules before relationship-specific ones, to stay focused on one rule type at a time.
Define and establish business rules working with the representative group of users and management, so each constraint is meaningful and its necessity is agreed.

Define and establish each field-specific business rule with a six-step procedure: select a table; review each field for needed constraints; define the rules; establish them by modifying the appropriate field-specification elements; determine the actions that test the rule; and record the rule on a Business Rule Specifications sheet.
A business rule makes a field's value contextually meaningful (for example, requiring a SHIP DATE to fall on or after the ORDER DATE); without the rule the value could be entered meaninglessly.

Establish a field-specific business rule by modifying the field-specification elements it affects; a single rule may affect several elements (e.g. 'a county must be associated with each customer' sets Required Value to Yes, Null Support to No Nulls, and Edit Rule to Enter Now/Edits Allowed).
Every business-rule constraint is tested by one of three actions — inserting, deleting, or updating a record or field value — so determine which of these actions tests each rule.

Document every business rule (database- and application-oriented) on a Business Rule Specifications sheet recording its statement, constraint, type, category, test-on actions, structures affected, field elements or relationship characteristics affected, and action taken, to give a standard, trackable record.

Establish relationship-specific business rules with a six-step procedure parallel to the field-specific one, modifying the relationship's characteristics (type and degree of participation) rather than field-specification elements.

When a business rule would be violated by deleting a record in the child table, add or change a Restrict deletion rule on the child table — amending the general rule that deleting a child record has no adverse effect.
exception: when deleting a child record would violate a required business rule

statement: Use a validation table to enforce a business rule that limits a field's range of values (especially when the value set is large and fixed) by relating the field's parent table to the validation table so the field becomes a foreign key drawing its values from the validation table.
condition: when a business rule restricts a field to a relatively fixed set of valid values

statement: Defining and establishing business rules is an ongoing task; expect to revisit, add, and modify rules as the organization changes the way it functions.

A view is a virtual table that draws its data from base tables and stores only its own structure; the RDBMS rebuilds and repopulates it on every access, so a view always reflects the most current data.

Define and use views to work with multiple related tables at once, reflect current information, customize data to specific user needs, enforce data integrity (via a validation view), and provide security or confidentiality by exposing only selected fields.
Three types of views are defined during logical design — data, aggregate, and validation — while materialized and partitioned views are RDBMS-specific physical-implementation concerns.
The only requirement for a multitable view is that its base tables bear a relationship to one another, which keeps the information the view presents valid and meaningful.

Modifications made through a data view flow back into the base tables subject to field specifications and business rules, but you cannot modify primary keys and you cannot modify any data in an aggregate view because all its fields are grouping or calculated fields.

A data view has no primary key of its own because it is not a table, and any redundancy it displays is acceptable because the data is not stored in the view but drawn from properly designed base tables.
An aggregate view displays aggregated data using calculated fields (Sum, Average, Minimum, Maximum, Count) together with grouping fields, and its data cannot be modified.
A validation view enforces a range-of-values constraint like a validation table but draws its data from base tables instead of storing its own and can incorporate data from multiple tables.

Identify a database's view requirements together with users and management by reviewing your design notes, the data-entry/report/presentation samples, the table subjects, the table relationships, and the business rules.

A view may contain calculated fields (concatenations, expressions, or aggregate functions) even though tables may not; include a calculated field when it provides pertinent, meaningful information or enhances how the view presents its data.

Filter a view's records by imposing criteria (expressions tested against field values), include every field a criterion tests in the view's structure, and use the minimum number of criteria needed to return the required records.

Document every view with both a view diagram and a View Specifications sheet (name, type, base tables, calculated-field expressions, filters); view names follow the table-name guidelines except that a view name may identify more than one subject.
Perform a final review of overall data integrity modularly, sequentially reviewing each component: table-level integrity, field-level integrity, relationship-level integrity, and business rules.

Table-level integrity review checklist: the table has no duplicate fields, no calculated fields, no multivalued fields, no multipart fields, and no duplicate records, every record is identified by a primary-key value, and each primary key conforms to the Elements of a Primary Key.
Field-level integrity review: confirm each field conforms to the Elements of the Ideal Field and has a complete set of field specifications.
Relationship-level integrity review: confirm each relationship is properly established, has appropriate deletion rules, and has the correct type and degree of participation for each table.

Business-rule review: confirm each rule imposes a meaningful constraint, is correctly categorized, is properly established by modifying the right field-specification elements or relationship characteristics, is backed by validation tables where needed, and is documented on a Business Rule Specifications sheet.

Assemble the complete logical-design documentation — final table list, relationship diagrams, field-specification sheets, business-rule sheets, calculated-field list, view diagrams, table-structure diagrams, and view-specification sheets — into a central repository.

The design documentation is vital because it records the complete database structure, serves as RDBMS-independent blueprints and instructions for implementation, and lets you assess the effects of any later structural modification before making it.

Avoid flat-file ('throw everything into one big table') design, because it causes redundant and inconsistent data and lacks integrity, typically exhibiting multipart fields, calculated fields, unnecessary duplicate fields, no true primary key, and multiple subjects in one table.

Do not use a spreadsheet as a relational database; when an organization needs to collect, store, maintain, and manipulate data, design and implement a real database, because spreadsheet 'databases' exhibit duplicate, multipart, and multivalued fields and are tedious to query.

When moving to a true database, abandon the spreadsheet-view mindset: a database stores data in separate fields rather than as laid out on a report, trading fixed spreadsheet layouts for far greater data integrity and far more flexible retrieval.

Do not design a database around the RDBMS software, because an RDBMS provides only implementation tools (not design principles), and designing around it constrains the design to your perception, knowledge, and skill with that product and commonly yields poor structure, weak data integrity, and inconsistent data.

Always design the logical structure without regard to any RDBMS, driven by the organization's information requirements, and choose the implementation approach and the RDBMS only after the design is complete.
People who understand the fundamentals of proper database design comprehend and use their RDBMS and its tools better than those who do not.

There are only two circumstances under which it is permissible to bend or break the rules of proper design — designing an analytical database, or improving processing performance — and even then you should design properly first and break a rule only as a deliberate, justified decision.
exception: designing an analytical database, or improving processing performance after exhausting other options

statement: An analytical database legitimately contains calculated fields (to record point-in-time state or aggregate results), which violates operational-design rules, and it requires a radically different design methodology from an operational database.
condition: when designing an analytical (OLAP) database rather than an operational one

statement: Breaking the rules for performance is really a trade-off against data integrity: it introduces inconsistent data, redundant data, impaired integrity, and inaccurate information, so weigh whether the perceived performance gain is worth the weakened integrity.

Before breaking the rules to improve performance, try other means first — upgrade hardware, tune the operating system, review the database design, review its implementation, and review the application program — and break the rules only as a last resort.

If you must break a rule, document the reason, the design principle violated, the database aspect modified, the specific modifications, and the anticipated effects on the database and application, and add this record to the design documentation.
Data consistency means that every occurrence of a given field value throughout the entire database is exactly the same.

Duplicate data is a non-primary-key value that appears in more than one table, which is distinct from a duplicate field (a field that appears in two or more tables) and should be minimized except where it results from relating tables.
PostgreSQL 10 adds SCRAM-SHA-256 password authentication; md5 is no longer considered safe, and migrating from md5 to SCRAM-SHA-256 is strongly recommended.

Logical replication (in core as of PostgreSQL 10) publishes a set of tables that other servers subscribe to; one server can publish some tables while subscribing to others, so there is no fixed master/slave role.
Quorum COMMIT (PostgreSQL 10) lets you require any N of M listed synchronous standbys to confirm before COMMIT returns, via synchronous_standby_names = ANY n (...).
PostgreSQL 10 brought declarative table partitioning into core: it auto-creates child constraints and routes parent-table changes to the matching child.
exception: In PostgreSQL 10 it does not auto-create child tables for unmatched rows, has no hash partitioning, does not move an updated row to a different partition, and does not process partitions in parallel.

statement: By default the optimizer assumes columns are independent and multiplies per-column selectivities, giving wrong row estimates when columns are correlated; CREATE STATISTICS stores multivariate statistics so the optimizer captures cross-column functional dependencies.
condition: Columns referenced together are functionally dependent or correlated.

statement: Prefer ICU collations over operating-system collations for long-lived data: an OS collation change silently corrupts b-tree ordering (a b-tree is a sorted list), and ICU gives stronger ordering-stability guarantees.
PostgreSQL 10 supports parallel b-tree index scans and parallel bitmap scans.
exception: Among index types, only b-tree benefits from parallelism in this version.

statement: In PostgreSQL every statement runs inside a transaction; a standalone query is itself a transaction.
now() returns the transaction start time, so it is constant for every call within the same transaction; wrap multiple statements in BEGIN ... COMMIT to make them one transaction.

PostgreSQL commits only error-free transactions: after any statement error the transaction is aborted and further commands are rejected until it ends, and a COMMIT then performs a ROLLBACK (unlike MySQL, which is less strict).
Use SAVEPOINT inside a long transaction as a recovery point: ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT returns to that point and lets the transaction continue instead of failing entirely.
condition: Within a single transaction; a savepoint's life ends when the transaction ends.

statement: PostgreSQL runs DDL transactionally — DDL can execute inside a transaction block and be rolled back.
exception: DROP DATABASE and CREATE/DROP TABLESPACE are not transactional.

statement: Deploy a schema or software upgrade inside a single transaction so the change applies atomically and you never run a mixture of old and new structures.
Under MVCC a transaction sees only data committed before its read began and cannot see another active transaction's uncommitted changes; readers and writers do not block each other.
PostgreSQL locks only the rows affected by an UPDATE (row-level locking), so many concurrent transactions can modify different rows of the same table without blocking each other.
Reading max(id) and then inserting max+1 from concurrent transactions causes a race that yields duplicate keys or duplicate rows; avoid this pattern.

To generate gapless, unique numbers without a heavy table lock, increment a single-row watermark table inside a CTE (WITH ... UPDATE ... RETURNING) and use the returned value: only a row lock is held, reads are not blocked, and it scales better than LOCK TABLE.
Avoid ACCESS EXCLUSIVE table locks: they block all concurrent reads and writes and are the most restrictive of the eight table lock modes.
Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE to lock selected rows for a read-modify-write so concurrent transactions cannot overwrite each other's changes; the locks release on COMMIT/ROLLBACK.
When a FOR UPDATE row lock may be held a long time, use SELECT FOR UPDATE NOWAIT (error instead of wait) or set lock_timeout to bound the wait.
condition: A selected row may already be locked by another transaction.

statement: Use SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for queue/worker workloads so each worker grabs disjoint unlocked rows instead of all workers serializing on the first locked row.
SELECT FOR UPDATE on a child row also blocks UPDATE of the referenced parent row (to protect the foreign key), which can create unexpected lock contention on shared lookup tables.
condition: A foreign key references the locked row.

statement: Row-level lock strength orders as FOR UPDATE (strongest) > FOR NO KEY UPDATE > FOR SHARE (multiple holders allowed) > FOR KEY SHARE (weakest).
PostgreSQL's default isolation level is READ COMMITTED, where each statement takes a fresh snapshot, so a transaction can observe another transaction's committed changes between its own statements.

Use REPEATABLE READ when a transaction needs one consistent snapshot for its whole duration (e.g., multi-page reports); it freezes the snapshot at transaction start and is not more expensive than READ COMMITTED.
condition: Consistent multi-statement reads are required.

statement: Use SERIALIZABLE (SSI) only with a solid understanding of the engine: it makes single-user-correct logic correct under concurrency, but transactions may fail by design and incur a performance penalty.
condition: The team understands the engine and can retry failed transactions.

statement: READ UNCOMMITTED is not supported in PostgreSQL; requesting it is silently mapped to READ COMMITTED.
Under REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE, a write that conflicts with a concurrently committed change fails with 'could not serialize access', so applications must catch this and retry the transaction.
A deadlock occurs when two transactions wait on each other; PostgreSQL detects it after deadlock_timeout (default ~1s) and aborts one transaction, reporting the conflicting row's ctid.

Advisory locks lock an arbitrary application-chosen number rather than rows and, unlike normal locks, do NOT release on COMMIT, so they must be released explicitly (pg_advisory_unlock / pg_advisory_unlock_all).
UPDATE and DELETE never overwrite existing row versions (so ROLLBACK works and concurrent readers still see the old version), so dead rows must be cleaned up asynchronously rather than at COMMIT.
VACUUM records dead space in the relation's Free Space Map for reuse; in most cases it does NOT shrink the table or return space to the OS.
exception: Space is returned to the OS only when the dead rows are at the physical end of the table.

statement: autovacuum runs in the background (waking every autovacuum_naptime, default 1 min, forking up to autovacuum_max_workers) and vacuums a table once changed rows exceed autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor (0.2) of the table AND at least autovacuum_vacuum_threshold (50) rows.
Running VACUUM (or autovacuum) advances the frozen-XID watermark to prevent transaction-ID and multixact wraparound; autovacuum_freeze_max_age forces a vacuum before a table's age reaches the limit.

Avoid VACUUM FULL on large tables: it takes an exclusive lock and rewrites the entire relation, blocking writes for the duration; to rebuild a bloated table without blocking writes, use an online tool such as pg_squeeze.
condition: The table is large.

statement: Long-running transactions postpone cleanup — a dead row can be reclaimed only once no active transaction can see it — which causes table bloat; old_snapshot_threshold can abort over-old snapshots to bound this.
A transaction that is only reading is given a virtual transaction ID and does not consume a real transaction ID, so transaction IDs are not exhausted too quickly.
Disabling autovacuum per table (autovacuum_enabled = off) is justified only for very short-lived or staging tables that will be dropped soon; for most tables it is a bad idea.
condition: The table is short-lived/staging and will be dropped soon.

statement: Bad indexing is the leading cause of bad PostgreSQL performance, and memory tuning cannot compensate for a missing index.
Use EXPLAIN to inspect the planner's chosen execution plan when a query is slow; PostgreSQL processes a statement in four stages — parser, rewrite, optimizer, executor.

The optimizer picks the plan with the lowest estimated cost; costs are abstract penalty points combining I/O (seq_page_cost=1 per 8 KB block) and CPU (cpu_tuple_cost=0.01, cpu_operator_cost=0.0025) and cannot be converted to milliseconds.
On SSDs, set random_page_cost close to 1 (default 4) because SSDs have no meaningful gap between random and sequential read speed; the default value suits spinning disks.
condition: Storage is SSD/flash.

statement: The number of parallel workers scales with table size (tiny tables run serially to avoid overhead); a table must roughly triple in size to justify each additional worker, gated by min_parallel_relation_size (8 MB).
psql \timing reports client-measured time including network latency, not server execution time, which matters for very short queries.
A b-tree index turns a full-table scan into a sub-millisecond lookup; PostgreSQL uses Lehman-Yao high-concurrency b-trees that allow many concurrent reads and writes on the same index.

Indexes are not free: each one consumes significant disk space and slows every INSERT/UPDATE because all indexes must be kept in sync, so over-indexing (e.g. many never-used indexes) badly hurts write throughput.
condition: Write-heavy tables or many redundant/unused indexes.

statement: A b-tree returns rows already in sorted order, so it can satisfy ORDER BY, min()/max(), and top-N (LIMIT) queries without sorting the whole set, and it can be read forward or backward.

PostgreSQL can combine several indexes (or use one index twice) in a single query via a bitmap scan: it builds a block list from each index, unions (OR) or intersects (AND) them, fetches those blocks, then rechecks rows; a bitmap scan is a scan method and is unrelated to an Oracle bitmap index.

A bitmap scan is most beneficial when it avoids re-reading the same block repeatedly or when combining several low-selectivity conditions whose intersection is small; PostgreSQL 10 adds parallel bitmap heap scans.
condition: Conditions are individually weak but jointly selective, or matches cluster in shared blocks.

statement: PostgreSQL does not use an index just because one exists; it chooses an index only when the cost model says it is cheaper than a sequential scan, and seq-scans when the predicate matches most of the table.
Execution plans depend on the actual input values and data distribution, not only the query text, so the same query can switch plans and produce unpredictable runtimes.
Physical row ordering (on-disk correlation) strongly affects speed: highly correlated data needs few blocks while shuffled data touches many more blocks for the same rows, degrading performance.
ANALYZE populates pg_stats (row counts, value distribution, and on-disk correlation) that the planner depends on; it normally runs automatically via the autovacuum daemon.

CLUSTER rewrites a table into one index's physical order to restore correlation, but it locks the table (no concurrent insert/modify), supports only a single ordering, and the clustered order is not maintained afterward — correlation decays over time.
exception: Acceptable only when the table can be locked and one search criterion dominates.

statement: Use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) to actually run a query and compare planner estimates against real rows/time and the count of 8 KB blocks touched (a shared hit means it came from shared-buffer cache); it is the best way to tell whether the planner's estimate was right.

An index-only scan answers a query entirely from the index without touching the table when all selected columns are present in the index, giving significantly better performance; adding extra columns to an index (a covering index) can enable this.
condition: Every selected column is contained in the index.

statement: For a multi-column (combined) index, PostgreSQL can use a leading-column prefix (e.g. (postal_code,last_name,first_name) serves postal_code, postal_code+last_name, and the full key) but cannot use the sorted property for a non-leading column alone; one tailored combined index beats separate per-column indexes, which fall back to bitmap scans.
A functional index stores the output of a function rather than the column value, so the function must be IMMUTABLE (same input always yields the same output); cos() is indexable but age() is not.
condition: The indexed function is IMMUTABLE.

statement: Use a partial index (CREATE INDEX ... WHERE) to exclude very frequent values and keep the index small and efficient; it pays off only when the excluded value covers a large fraction of the table (roughly 25% or more), e.g. gender or nationality.
condition: The excluded value(s) make up a large share (~25%+) of the rows.

statement: CREATE INDEX takes a SHARE lock that blocks writes to the table; on large production tables use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY to build without blocking writes — it takes at least about twice as long and can leave the index INVALID if a conflicting operation occurs.
exception: CONCURRENTLY is not guaranteed to succeed; a conflict can mark the index invalid.

statement: An operator class tells an index how to compare and order a type; a b-tree operator class requires the five strategy operators (<, <=, =, >=, >) plus one support ('same'/compare) function.

Operator-class support functions must be IMMUTABLE and written in a procedural or compiled language rather than plain SQL (SQL functions can be inlined, defeating the custom ordering), and should follow the community _lt/_le/_ge/_gt naming convention.
PostgreSQL 10 provides six built-in index access methods — btree, hash, gist, gin, spgist, and brin — and additional types (e.g. rum) can be added as extensions.

Use hash indexes only on PostgreSQL 10 or later: before version 10 they had no WAL logging and were not crash-safe or replication-ready; hash indexes are also larger than b-trees (about 125 MB vs 90 MB for 4 million integers).
exception: Before PostgreSQL 10, hash indexes lacked WAL logging and crash safety.

statement: GiST indexes are hierarchical bounding-box trees suited to geometric, range-type, and fuzzy search and to KNN distance ordering; a GiST index can emulate a b-tree, but doing so is not recommended.
GIN indexes invert text or multi-value data — each distinct key is stored once with a posting list of matching rows — making them compact for full-text search, but they do not provide sorted output.
SP-GiST is designed mainly for in-memory use (on disk it needs many page hits) and implements space-partitioned structures such as quadtrees, k-d trees, and radix trees.

BRIN indexes store only the min/max per range of blocks (128 blocks / 1 MB by default), so they are extremely small but lossy (the scan rechecks extra rows); they are efficient only on highly correlated data such as time-series or data-warehouse loads and are nearly useless on shuffled data.
condition: Indexed data is highly correlated with physical row order.

statement: A bloom-filter index (contrib bloom) lets you index many columns at once for arbitrary equality combinations not known at design time; it is probabilistic — it may return too many rows but never too few — and the entire filter must be read.
condition: Many candidate filter columns with unknown query combinations.

statement: Use the pg_trgm trigram extension (with a GiST or GIN index) for fuzzy/similarity search; its <-> distance ranges from 0 (identical) to 1 (dissimilar) and is computed by splitting strings into 3-character trigrams.

A pg_trgm trigram index can accelerate LIKE patterns with wildcards anywhere (e.g. '%neusi%') and even simple regular-expression matches, unlike a plain b-tree, which only speeds up a trailing wildcard.

Full-text search uses to_tsvector to stem text into lexemes and drop stop words, then matches with to_tsquery via the @@ operator; matching is language-dependent (the text-search configuration) and & / | build AND/OR queries, so 'wanted' matches text containing 'want'.

To index full-text search, either build a functional GIN index on to_tsvector(...) (smaller but recomputed) or store a materialized tsvector column kept current by a tsvector_update_trigger on INSERT/UPDATE (more space, faster queries); because the trigger runs in the same transaction, the column stays consistent.
condition: Choose by the space-vs-query-speed trade-off.

statement: Use an exclusion constraint (EXCLUDE USING GiST, e.g. with btree_gist) to enforce that no two rows overlap on chosen columns — for example preventing the same room from being double-booked for overlapping time ranges (room WITH =, range WITH &&).

Use GROUP BY ROLLUP to add subtotal and grand-total summary rows (e.g. an overall average) in a single query instead of running separate aggregate queries; the higher-level aggregate rows carry NULL in the rolled-up group-key columns.

CUBE produces every combination of the grouping columns while ROLLUP yields only the hierarchical subtotals; both are shorthand for GROUPING SETS, which lets you list the exact aggregation levels you want.
The output order of grouping-set queries is not guaranteed (PostgreSQL 10 may hash rather than sort), so add an explicit ORDER BY when a stable or sorted result is required.
condition: A deterministic row order is required.

statement: Use the aggregate FILTER (WHERE ...) clause to compute partial aggregates over different row subsets in one query (a simple pivot); FILTER is faster than the CASE WHEN ... ELSE END trick, but push a shared condition into the query's WHERE clause instead when every aggregate needs the same subset.
condition: Different aggregates need different row subsets; otherwise prefer WHERE.

statement: Ordered-set aggregates (WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ...)) sort each group before aggregating: percentile_disc returns an actual value present in the data, percentile_cont interpolates between values, and mode() returns the most frequent value.

A windowing function (an aggregate with an OVER clause) compares each row to its window without collapsing rows, so the row count is unchanged unlike a GROUP BY aggregate; the OVER clause is mandatory because the SQL standard forbids mixing a bare aggregate with non-grouped columns.

A windowing aggregate with OVER (PARTITION BY ...) computes the aggregate within each partition while keeping every row; the partition key can be any expression, not just a column (e.g. PARTITION BY year < 1990).
SQL does not guarantee row order unless the query has an explicit ORDER BY, so windowing and other queries may return rows in an arbitrary order.
Adding ORDER BY inside an OVER clause changes the result: without it the aggregate covers the whole partition, while with it the aggregate is cumulative up to the current row (a running aggregate).

A moving/sliding window frame (ROWS BETWEEN n PRECEDING AND m FOLLOWING) must be paired with ORDER BY or the result is meaningless; UNBOUNDED PRECEDING/FOLLOWING bound the frame, and at the data edges the frame is simply smaller (no NULL padding).
condition: Computing a moving or running aggregate over a frame.

statement: Define a window once with a named WINDOW clause and reuse it across multiple functions instead of repeating the OVER specification, which keeps queries readable and maintainable.
rank() leaves gaps after ties while dense_rank() produces consecutive ranks with no gaps; row_number() assigns a unique sequential number (no duplicates) and can run even without ORDER BY.
ntile(n) splits ordered rows into n groups as evenly as possible; when the rows do not divide evenly, the later groups are the smaller ones.

lag(col,k) and lead(col,k) shift a column k rows down/up within the ordered window (boundary rows yield NULL); lagging an entire row as a composite value lets you detect duplicate or near-duplicate rows even without a primary key, since composite types compare field by field.
When an analytic result cannot be computed in one step, wrap the windowing query in a subselect and compute on top of it (e.g. to backfill nth_value NULLs or post-process ntile groups).

Define a custom aggregate with CREATE AGGREGATE: INITCOND sets the per-group starting state, SFUNC (the state-transition function) runs once per row with the running state plus the row values, STYPE is the state type, and FINALFUNC post-processes the final state (required for results such as averages or a final adjustment).
A custom aggregate can be used directly as a windowing function via OVER with no additional definition.

An aggregate has no parallel-query support by default; declare PARALLEL SAFE/RESTRICTED/UNSAFE, and only SAFE (full parallelism) is valid when the function has no side effects and is order-independent, which makes IMMUTABLE functions good candidates.
condition: The function is side-effect-free and order-independent.

statement: For sliding-window aggregates, supply moving-aggregate functions MSFUNC (add the entering row) and MINVFUNC (remove the leaving row) so PostgreSQL updates the frame incrementally instead of recomputing the whole window per row, which otherwise explodes the number of function calls.
condition: The aggregate runs over a moving window frame.

statement: Prefer running aggregations inside the database: the code is easier to write and the engine is usually more efficient than doing the same work in the application.
You cannot improve performance or reliability without first collecting and understanding system statistics, and there is no point graphing a metric you do not understand.

Inspect pg_stat_activity first to see current activity: it returns one row per connection with database, pid, user, client address, application_name, backend/xact/query start times, state, wait_event, and the current or last query.
Have clients set application_name so an administrator can tell what each of many connections from the same IP is actually doing.

pg_stat_activity shows the active or last-executed query plus state and state_change, so even sub-millisecond OLTP queries can be spotted, and the gap between query_start and state_change is the query's execution time.

Use pg_cancel_backend(pid) to cancel only the running query while keeping the connection, and pg_terminate_backend(pid) to kill the whole connection; note that only psql auto-reconnects — most client libraries do not.

pg_stat_database gives one row per database with commit/rollback counts, block reads vs cache hits (blks_read/blks_hit), tuple counters, temp-file usage, deadlocks, and block read/write times — the basis for database-level monitoring.
first_value(), last_value(), and nth_value() return positional values within the ordered window; nth_value yields NULL for the rows before the nth value is reached.

In pg_stat_database, blks_hit vs blks_read measure shared-buffer cache hits vs misses (the database level cannot distinguish OS cache from real disk), and non-zero temp_files/temp_bytes reveal spilling to disk — often from low work_mem or wasteful queries — which slows operations.

track_io_timing is off by default because per-block timing calls add overhead; measure that overhead with pg_test_timing before enabling it — it is fine on real hardware (~14-23 ns) but can be costly on poorly virtualized systems (four-digit nanoseconds).
condition: Running on virtualized or cloud hardware.

statement: pg_stat_user_tables is the key view for finding missing indexes: look for large tables with high seq_scan / seq_tup_read and low idx_scan; sequential scans are not always bad (backups, analytics), but constant large ones destroy performance.
