A high HOT-update ratio (n_tup_hot_upd) is good for update-heavy workloads because the new row version stays in the same block, avoiding extra index maintenance.
condition: The workload is UPDATE-intensive.

statement: Use pg_stat_user_indexes (idx_scan) to find rarely-used indexes and how much space they waste, but do not blindly drop them.
exception: Usage patterns can change (e.g. new staff), so an unused index may become useful again.

statement: pg_stat_bgwriter exposes checkpoint behaviour: a high checkpoints_req relative to checkpoints_timed signals checkpoints driven by heavy write throughput, and a high buffers_backend (backends writing their own buffers) is generally undesirable.

Watch pg_stat_archiver failed_count / last_failed_wal so WAL-archiving failures do not go unnoticed, and check pg_stat_replication (on the sender) and pg_stat_wal_receiver (on the receiver): no rows in pg_stat_replication means no streaming is happening, and the PostgreSQL 10 *_lag fields show the master-replica time lag.

Enable pg_stat_statements (add it to shared_preload_libraries, restart, then CREATE EXTENSION) and keep it on permanently: its overhead is small and it is the easiest way to find performance problems, aggregating per-normalized-query stats (calls, total/mean/stddev time, cache hits) with parameters replaced by placeholders.

A slow-query log (log_min_duration_statement) only captures individual slow queries and can mislead, because many medium queries (e.g. 1000 x 500 ms) can outweigh a few long ones; pg_stat_statements gives the aggregated picture, so treat the slow log as a source of information, not the source.

pg_stat_statements stddev_time flags queries with unstable runtimes (uncached disk reads, plan changes from different parameters, or concurrency/locking), and it truncates queries at track_activity_query_size (default 1024 bytes) — raise it (e.g. 16384) for Hibernate or long queries.

When reviewing pg_stat_statements, always produce sorted output (e.g. by total_time) and focus on the top few queries, since the first queries usually cause most of the load and working through the top 1000 is not worth it.

Do not rely on stderr for long-term logging; turn on logging_collector to produce real log files and use log_filename with log_truncate_on_rotation (e.g. postgresql_%a.log) to rotate and recycle them.
Configure log_line_prefix to include at least a timestamp (and ideally user, database, and transaction id) so log entries are interpretable; PostgreSQL 10 defaults it to '%m [%p]'.

Avoid log_statement='all' and log_connections/log_disconnections on OLTP systems because extensive logging significantly slows the system (analytical systems are affected less); use targeted settings such as log_min_duration_statement, log_lock_waits, and log_temp_files instead.
condition: OLTP / write-latency-sensitive system.

statement: Set log_temp_files (e.g. to a few megabytes) to identify the specific queries causing temporary-file I/O that pg_stat_statements only aggregates, and set log_timezone consistently when servers span multiple time zones.
A nested-loop join is O(n^2) and efficient only when one side is very small; with two large inputs its runtime explodes.
condition: One join input is very small.

statement: A hash join hashes both inputs and matches on hash keys, which suits equality joins but must materialize all the values into a hash.

A merge join needs both inputs sorted (an O(n log n) sort) and scales to large data; sorted input can come from an index, but an index pays off only when the result is much smaller than the table — otherwise a sequential scan is cheaper than reading index plus table.
condition: The result set is much smaller than the table.

statement: Since PostgreSQL 10, all join methods (nested loop, hash, merge) also have parallel versions that the planner evaluates.

Before costing, the planner rewrites the query: it inlines views into subselects, flattens subselects into a plain join, then propagates equality constraints (if aid=bid and aid=cid then bid=cid; if cid=4 then aid=bid=4) to expose indexes and join orders not visible in the original SQL.
After its transformations, PostgreSQL performs an exhaustive search over plans and join orders and chooses the cheapest by the cost model.

An OFFSET (even OFFSET 0) or a LIMIT inside a view or subquery acts as an optimization fence that blocks inlining/flattening and forces materialization — it can cripple performance, or be used deliberately as an optimization barrier.
Keep an indexed column bare on one side of a predicate: constant folding handles col = 3+1 (index used), but col - 1 = 3 puts an expression on the indexed column and forces a sequential scan.
PostgreSQL inlines IMMUTABLE SQL functions (e.g. ld() becomes log()), cutting call overhead and letting a functional index on the inlined expression match equivalent queries.

Join pruning removes a LEFT JOIN when no columns are selected from the right side and the right join key is unique (so the join cannot add rows); therefore dropping unused selected columns can eliminate joins, which especially helps ORM/middleware-generated queries.
condition: Right-side join key is unique and no right-side columns are selected.

statement: Prefer UNION ALL over UNION unless you actually need duplicate removal: UNION ALL just appends, while UNION adds a Sort/Unique step to deduplicate that is expensive on large datasets; the planner pushes WHERE restrictions into each set-operation branch to enable indexes.

Read execution plans inside-out; each node has a cost block (estimates) and, under EXPLAIN ANALYZE, an actual-time block (real timing) — find where the actual time jumps to locate the bottleneck, and turn on EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, VERBOSE, COSTS, TIMING, BUFFERS).
Verify that planner row estimates are reasonably close to the actual row counts, because bad estimates cause bad plans; stale statistics call for ANALYZE, though autovacuum usually maintains them.

PostgreSQL keeps statistics on columns, not on expressions, so a predicate over an expression (e.g. cos(id)) is badly mis-estimated; creating an index on that expression makes ANALYZE track expression statistics and fixes the estimate even if the index is never used.

Cross-column correlation breaks the default independent-column estimate (which multiplies per-column selectivities) and mis-estimates correlated predicates; PostgreSQL 10 multivariate statistics (CREATE STATISTICS) address this.

Query runtime swings widely with cache state: a fully cached query can be on the order of 100x faster than one fetching random blocks from disk, and randomly distributed data can require roughly one disk block per returned row.

Run a query twice before measuring so the cache is warm, and remember that every server restart clears both the PostgreSQL and filesystem caches, which can cause severe slowdowns immediately after a restart or failover.
To reduce high random-buffer usage, CLUSTER the table into index order — fine for analytical workloads but usually not feasible on OLTP because it takes a table lock and rewrites the whole table.
condition: Analytical workload that can tolerate a table lock.

statement: An outer join with an extra ON condition (e.g. a LEFT JOIN b ON aid=bid AND bid=2) keeps ALL left rows so the row count is unchanged; a reported outer-join performance problem is often actually a semantics bug, so verify the join's correctness before tuning it.

PostgreSQL can freely reorder inner joins but can reorder outer joins only under specific algebraic identities (some requiring the predicate be strict for a column of the nullable side), and long chains of LEFT JOINs often cannot be reordered at all.
condition: The reordering identity's strictness preconditions hold.

statement: When a query has many joins, planning every join order is expensive, so lower join_collapse_limit (or use explicit JOIN syntax) to cut planning time; implicit, explicit, and CROSS-JOIN forms with the same predicates plan identically up to that limit.

The enable_* planner switches (enable_seqscan/indexscan/hashjoin/mergejoin/nestloop/...) do not truly disable a method — they only make it very expensive — so use them to tune individual queries, never globally, since PostgreSQL has no Oracle-style query hints.

GEQO (genetic query optimization) replaces exhaustive search once a query exceeds geqo_threshold (default 12 relations) to keep planning tractable; prefer fixing join order via join_collapse_limit before relying on GEQO.
condition: The query joins more relations than geqo_threshold.

statement: With default 8 KB blocks a single PostgreSQL table holds up to 32 TB (128 TB with 32 KB blocks); very large tables are a reason to partition for easier management and sometimes better speed.

Inheritance-based partitioning uses a parent plus child tables (INHERITS); querying the parent returns all child rows via an Append node, child tables may add extra columns and share the parent's sequence, and the tables are independent, linked only through the system catalog.

Add a CHECK constraint matching each partition's value range so the planner can use constraint exclusion to prune irrelevant partitions; non-overlapping constraints prune best, and PostgreSQL accepts a constraint only if every existing row already satisfies it.
condition: Every existing row satisfies the constraint.

statement: ALTER TABLE on an inheritance parent propagates column changes to all child tables, but indexes do NOT propagate — each child table must be indexed separately.
exception: Indexes are not inherited; they must be created per child table.

statement: Move a partition between parents atomically with ALTER TABLE ... NO INHERIT / INHERIT (e.g. to archive old data), and drop a whole partition's data instantly with DROP TABLE on the child rather than a slow DELETE.

PostgreSQL 10 declarative partitioning (PARTITION BY RANGE/LIST, CREATE TABLE ... PARTITION OF) is built-in but limited: a row cannot move between partitions when its partition key is updated (it errors out), there is no hash partitioning yet, and each partition still needs its own indexes.
exception: In PostgreSQL 10: no cross-partition row moves on key update, no hash partitioning, indexes per partition.

statement: work_mem governs the in-memory size for hash aggregation and sorts: when the groups or sort do not fit, PostgreSQL falls back to a GroupAggregate with on-disk external sort, which is far slower, so raising work_mem lets it use the faster in-memory HashAggregate/quicksort.
work_mem is allocated per sort/hash operation, not globally, and a single query can consume it several times, so size it carefully; a LIMIT query uses a fast top-N heapsort.
Use maintenance_work_mem (not work_mem) to speed up CREATE INDEX, VACUUM, and ALTER TABLE; like work_mem it is per-operation and allocated on demand.

Optimize a query logically and semantically first; memory settings such as work_mem give only a final speedup on top of an already-good query and are not a substitute for proper indexes or better queries.

PostgreSQL lets you write stored procedures in several languages (SQL, PL/pgSQL, PL/Perl(U), PL/Python, PL/Tcl(U)); function code is passed as a string and treated as a black box by the executor, and SQL functions should be preferred when possible because they give the optimizer the most freedom.
Use dollar quoting ($$ ... $$, or a tagged $body$ ... $body$) instead of single-quoting function bodies to avoid escaping embedded quotes; pick a custom tag when the body itself contains $$.

A function executes inside the calling transaction rather than autonomously, so you cannot perform transactional flow control (COMMIT/ROLLBACK) inside it; PostgreSQL 10 has no autonomous transactions.

Function overloading makes mysum(int,int) and mysum(int8,int8) distinct functions, and CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION cannot change a signature, so delete obsolete signatures to avoid accumulating stale functions.

Never build SQL by concatenating user input in PL/pgSQL, because it enables SQL injection (e.g. a parameter containing '; DROP TABLE ...); instead use quote_literal/quote_ident/quote_nullable, or format() with EXECUTE ... USING, to parameterize safely.

Trusted procedural languages (PL/Perl, PL/Tcl) are sandboxed — no loading libraries, opening network sockets, or system calls — whereas untrusted variants (PL/PerlU, PL/Python, PL/TclU) can do anything and so only a superuser may create them; in PostgreSQL, Python is available only as an untrusted language.

Use PL/pgSQL EXCEPTION blocks (WHEN <condition> / WHEN OTHERS) to catch errors; the BEGIN/EXCEPTION block acts like a savepoint, so only that block is rolled back rather than the whole transaction, and sqlerrm holds the error message.

Raise your own errors with RAISE <error_code> USING MESSAGE = ...; PostgreSQL ships a full set of predefined SQLSTATE error codes so you can catch specific conditions (e.g. division_by_zero, unique_violation).
Use GET DIAGNOSTICS for ROW_COUNT, and GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS inside an EXCEPTION block for returned_sqlstate / message_text / pg_exception_context, to obtain a backtrace for debugging.

Use a cursor to process a result set too large for memory: rows are produced only as FETCH is called, lowering memory use; looping over a result set in PL/pgSQL (FOR ... IN SELECT) creates an implicit cursor automatically, and PostgreSQL optimizes to produce the first cursor_tuple_fraction (default 10%) quickly.

A set-returning function (SRF) is always fully materialized in memory so SQL can rescan it, unlike a streaming cursor, so wrapping an SRF in a cursor defeats the streaming benefit — be careful with SRFs over huge result sets.
A trigger function must be declared RETURNS trigger; access the affected row via NEW (INSERT/UPDATE) and OLD (UPDATE/DELETE), and in a BEFORE trigger modify NEW and RETURN NEW to apply the change.

A table may have an unlimited number of triggers, and when several exist they fire in a deterministic order — all BEFORE triggers alphabetically, then the row operation, then AFTER triggers alphabetically.
Trigger functions can read context variables (TG_NAME, TG_TABLE_NAME, TG_WHEN, TG_LEVEL, TG_OP, TG_NARGS, ...), so one generic function can serve many tables and avoid duplicate code.

PostgreSQL 10 statement-level triggers can access the changed rows via transition tables (REFERENCING NEW/OLD TABLE ... FOR EACH STATEMENT), but using transition tables over billions of rows has performance implications.
condition: Large row volumes amplify the cost of transition tables.

statement: Mark each function's volatility correctly: VOLATILE (the default) cannot be optimized away and can block index use; STABLE returns the same result within one transaction (e.g. now()); IMMUTABLE always returns the same output for the same input and permits the most optimization, including functional indexes.
Calling functions too often is the main cause of bad stored-procedure performance, so reducing the number of function calls is the first optimization lever.

PL/pgSQL caches execution plans automatically, while PL/Perl and PL/Python let you choose via SPI prepared queries: prepare short queries to cut parse/plan overhead, but leave long queries unprepared so the planner can re-pick a better plan each time.
condition: Short repeated queries benefit from preparing; long queries may not.

statement: Tell the optimizer a function's relative cost with COST (a multiplier of cpu_operator_cost, default 100, lower for C) and a set-returning function's expected size with ROWS (default assumption 1000), so the planner orders expensive or large functions correctly.

Stored procedures extend the server: CREATE DOMAIN builds a constrained type (e.g. an email domain validated by a CHECK that calls a function), and CREATE CAST (AS IMPLICIT/ASSIGNMENT), custom operators, and collations can all be built from functions.

SPI is the C interface that every procedural language uses to run SQL inside a function (the function already shares the database connection, so do not open a new one); each language wraps it — e.g. PL/Perl spi_exec_query/spi_query/spi_fetchrow with elog, PL/Python plpy.execute/plpy.cursor with plpy.notice.
PL/Python catches errors with try/except on plpy.SPIError (or specific spiexceptions such as DivisionByZero / UniqueViolation), so a caught error does not destroy the transaction.
Shared state across PL/Perl calls uses the $_SHARED hash, but within a complex statement you usually cannot rely on the order in which functions are called.
condition: Function call order within one statement is not guaranteed.

statement: PostgreSQL enforces a layered permission chain — bind address (listen_addresses), host-based auth (pg_hba.conf), instance (roles/login), database (CONNECT/CREATE), schema (USAGE/CREATE), table, column, and row-level security — and every layer must permit access for a read to succeed.
PostgreSQL does not accept remote connections by default; set listen_addresses to the server's own IP addresses (or * for all), not client IPs, and restart, because changing it requires a restart.

PostgreSQL listens on a single TCP port (default 5432) and forks one process per connection; max_connections (default 100, plus superuser_reserved_connections) requires a restart because shared memory is preallocated.
Raising max_connections is cheap (only minor context-switch overhead); what actually loads the server is the number of open snapshots from long-running transactions, not the connection count.

Prefer Unix-socket connections over the loopback device (127.0.0.1) for local-only access: they avoid network exposure and are measurably faster for small queries (benchmarked at roughly 174k vs 107k tps).
condition: The client and server are on the same host.

statement: pg_hba.conf rules (local/host/hostssl/hostnossl with DATABASE USER ADDRESS METHOD) are matched top-down and the FIRST matching rule wins, so order matters — a broad allow placed before a specific reject makes the reject unreachable.

Choose authentication methods deliberately: avoid trust (no password) and md5/password for remote access (md5 is weak and password sends plaintext) and use scram-sha-256 on PostgreSQL 10+; peer/ident map an OS user to a database user for local logins, and cert authenticates via the client certificate's CN.
Enable SSL by setting ssl = on (requires restart) and placing server.crt/server.key in PGDATA (the key must be chmod og-rwx), then verify per-connection encryption through the pg_stat_ssl view.

In PostgreSQL users and roles are the same object (CREATE USER defaults to LOGIN, CREATE ROLE defaults to NOLOGIN) and exist at the instance level, so a role is visible to every database in the instance.

Model permissions with roles: create a NOLOGIN group role (e.g. bookkeeper), grant it the permissions once, and have LOGIN users INHERIT from it (the default), so individuals keep separate identities for auditing while sharing one permission set.
The creator of an object is automatically its owner, and the owner holds all permissions on it including the right to drop it, while a SUPERUSER bypasses all permission checks entirely.

Apply least privilege to role attributes: grant CREATEDB/CREATEROLE/REPLICATION/BYPASSRLS only when needed (run replication as a dedicated non-superuser), bound access with CONNECTION LIMIT and VALID UNTIL, and keep passwords ENCRYPTED (the default).
Set per-user or per-database defaults with ALTER ROLE ... [IN DATABASE] SET <parameter> (e.g. TimeZone, work_mem); the change takes effect on the user's next connection, not immediately.

The PUBLIC pseudo-role grants apply to everyone, and by default PUBLIC can CONNECT to databases and create objects in the public schema, so a secure setup should REVOKE those from PUBLIC (ideally before databases are created) and grant access explicitly.

Database-level GRANT covers CONNECT (connect to the database) and CREATE (create a schema, NOT a table, since tables live inside schemas), while schema-level GRANT covers USAGE (enter/see the schema) and CREATE (place objects in it).
Owning a table is not sufficient to rename it: DDL such as ALTER TABLE ... RENAME requires CREATE on the containing schema, and the permission error names the schema rather than the table.

Table GRANTs are per-action (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/TRUNCATE/REFERENCES/TRIGGER): INSERT does not imply SELECT (you need both to read what you inserted), and TRUNCATE is a separate privilege from DELETE because TRUNCATE locks the table; you can grant on ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA and delegate with WITH GRANT OPTION.

Column-level security via GRANT SELECT (column) ON table restricts access to specific columns; once it is in use, SELECT * fails because it requests every column including forbidden ones, so name columns explicitly instead of using SELECT *.
condition: Column-level privileges are in effect.

statement: Use ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES (FOR ROLE creator, IN SCHEMA s) to auto-grant permissions on future objects, so newly created tables are not accidentally left without the intended grants.

Use row-level security policies (CREATE POLICY with USING for read visibility and WITH CHECK for writes, PERMISSIVE/RESTRICTIVE, scoped per command and role) to restrict which rows a user can see, enabling multi-tenant tables where each user sees only their own rows.

ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY applies a deny-all default, so a user with full table grants sees zero rows until explicit CREATE POLICY rules are added — a safe default that forces permissions to be set explicitly.

Multiple RLS policies are OR-combined by default (PERMISSIVE, so more policies expose more rows); use RESTRICTIVE to AND-combine them in PostgreSQL 10+, and note USING filters existing rows (SELECT/UPDATE) while WITH CHECK filters new or modified rows (INSERT/UPDATE).

An INSERT under RLS needs a FOR INSERT policy with WITH CHECK, and using RETURNING * additionally requires a SELECT (USING) policy that admits the returned row — otherwise the insert succeeds but RETURNING errors out.
condition: RETURNING is used on an RLS-protected table.

statement: Inspect table permissions and policies with psql \z (or aclexplode()); the acl codes are a=INSERT, r=SELECT, w=UPDATE, d=DELETE, D=TRUNCATE, x=REFERENCES, t=TRIGGER.

You cannot DROP a role that still owns objects or is referenced by grants/policies; REASSIGN OWNED BY old TO new transfers ownership, and the practical mitigation is to assign as few permissions as possible directly to real people and abstract them into roles.

PostgreSQL offers logical dumps (pg_dump producing SQL text) and transaction-log shipping (binary); pg_dump runs in one REPEATABLE READ transaction, so the dump is a consistent start-time snapshot with no foreign-key violations, but it excludes changes made while the dump runs.

A textual pg_dump is CPU-architecture-independent and restorable across architectures, unlike a binary copy whose on-disk format is architecture-dependent; there is no separate dump privilege, so anyone who can read the data can back it up.

Do not pass the database password on the command line (it appears in the process table); instead use libpq environment variables such as PGPASSWORD, a ~/.pgpass file (chmod 0600), or a .pg_service.conf service file.
Use pg_dump switches for subset dumps: -a data only, -s schema only, -n/-N include/exclude a schema, -t/-T include/exclude tables — partial dumps can speed backups up considerably.

Prefer the custom (-Fc) or directory (-Fd) dump format over plain text: both are compressed (roughly 90% smaller), carry a table of contents (pg_restore --list) and allow selective restore, and the directory format also supports parallel dump/restore with -j N.

Replay a plain-text dump with psql db < file.sql and a custom/directory dump with pg_restore (-j for parallel restore across multiple tables); pg_restore adds to an existing database and may error-but-continue if the target is not empty.

pg_dump works per database and excludes instance-global objects such as roles, so use pg_dumpall (or pg_dumpall -g for globals only) to capture them; pg_dumpall is single-threaded and plain-text only, so a full-instance backup is pg_dumpall -g plus a per-database custom/directory dump.

Logical dumps suit small to medium data but have two downsides: you lose everything since the last snapshot, and restoring is slow because every index is rebuilt from scratch rather than copied as in a binary backup.

The Write-Ahead Log (WAL/xlog) provides crash safety by writing changes to the log before the data files, so after a crash PostgreSQL repairs the data files from the WAL; writing directly to a data file risks corruption from a partial write.

Never delete WAL files manually (the directory was renamed pg_xlog to pg_wal in PostgreSQL 10 to discourage this): doing so can stop the server from restarting after a crash, and PostgreSQL recycles WAL itself via checkpoints; the number of WAL files is unrelated to transaction size.

A checkpoint flushes all dirty buffers up to a point out to the data files so older WAL can be recycled, and checkpoints are triggered either by time (checkpoint_timeout) or by space (max_wal_size, a soft limit).

In PostgreSQL 9.6+ prefer wider checkpoint distances: they are almost always favorable because blocks are sorted before write (less random I/O) and fewer full-page writes mean LESS total WAL is generated; raise checkpoint_completion_target (default 0.5) to spread checkpoint I/O and flatten spikes.

Configure Point-In-Time Recovery by setting wal_level=replica and max_wal_senders>=2, archive_mode=on, and an archive_command (e.g. cp/rsync/scp of %p to safe storage) that returns 0 on success — a non-zero return makes PostgreSQL retry, since no WAL file may be lost; PostgreSQL 10 already defaults wal_level and max_wal_senders correctly.

PITR loses less data than a dump (you can restore to a chosen point in time, not just the backup instant) and restores faster because indexes are copied rather than rebuilt, and base backups via pg_basebackup run while the database is fully operational.

Use pg_basebackup for the initial base backup: -D an empty target dir, -h the source, --checkpoint=fast (so it does not wait up to an hour for the next checkpoint), and --wal-method=stream (a self-contained backup, the PostgreSQL 10 default); throttle with -r/--max-rate to protect the master's I/O, remap tablespaces with -T, and use -Ft for a single tar file.

Replication requires explicit entries in pg_hba.conf whose DATABASE column is the literal 'replication', and should use a dedicated role with only LOGIN and REPLICATION rights (and a password) rather than the superuser account.

Monitor archiving with pg_stat_archiver (archived_count, last_archived_wal, failed_count/last_failed_wal) to catch stalls; the .backup file emitted during pg_basebackup marks where replay begins, so for the current backup any WAL older than that file can be deleted.

For PITR, set a recovery target (recovery_target_time/_name/_xid) in recovery.conf; replay first reaches a 'consistent recovery state' and then applies WAL toward the target, after which recovery.conf is renamed recovery.done. Use pg_create_restore_point('label') plus recovery_target_name to recover exactly to a known event (e.g. the end of a nightly job) when the timestamp is unknown.

To find the right recovery point, set hot_standby=on and recovery_target_action='pause' (or call pg_wal_replay_pause/pg_wal_replay_resume) so you can inspect the database mid-recovery and continue, because once recovery completes the server is promoted and WAL replay cannot be resumed.

PostgreSQL never cleans the WAL archive itself, so you must remove WAL older than the oldest base backup you still need — e.g. with pg_archivecleanup ARCHIVEDIR OLDESTKEPTWALFILE, or as archive_cleanup_command on a standby.

Set up streaming replication by configuring the master (wal_level=replica, max_wal_senders, hot_standby=on) plus replication rules in pg_hba.conf, then run pg_basebackup -R on the standby (which writes recovery.conf with standby_mode=on and primary_conninfo); confirm a wal sender on the master and a wal receiver on the standby, and note replication can cascade (a standby can stream from another standby).

Halt replay on a standby with pg_wal_replay_pause() — WAL still streams and is persisted, only the apply stops — and resume with pg_wal_replay_resume(); this is useful to shield a replica from a risky master change so you can fail over to the pre-change data, and these functions run only during recovery (on the standby).

Track replication lag via pg_stat_replication on the sender, where sent_lsn/write_lsn/flush_lsn/replay_lsn show how far WAL has been sent, written, flushed, and made visible (PostgreSQL 10 adds *_lag time intervals), and via pg_stat_wal_receiver on the receiver; keeping replication healthy is essential or a master crash loses data.

Promote a standby with pg_ctl promote: existing read-only connections become read/write without reconnecting, and the server advances to a new timeline (encoded in WAL filenames), which lets PITR follow the correct branch after a promotion.

Replication conflicts arise because the master is unaware of reads on the standby: a master DROP TABLE or VACUUM that removes rows still needed by a long standby query forces a choice — max_standby_streaming_delay (default 30s) bounds how long the standby waits before cancelling the query, and hot_standby_feedback=on makes the standby report its oldest xid so the master defers cleanup, at the cost of possible master bloat.
condition: A long-running read on the standby conflicts with row removal on the master.

statement: Prevent a standby from falling so far behind that it needs a full resync (because the WAL it needs was already recycled by checkpoints) by raising wal_keep_segments to cover the worst-case delay (e.g. a large index build flooding WAL over a slow link), or by using replication slots.

Synchronous replication (synchronous_standby_names on the master plus application_name in the standby's primary_conninfo) makes a master commit wait until at least one replica flushes the transaction, sharply reducing data-loss risk; but if no viable synchronous standby exists the master blocks on commit forever, so use at least three nodes (one master, two standbys), and PostgreSQL 10 adds FIRST/ANY num_sync(...) quorum syntax.
condition: Enough viable synchronous standbys are available.

statement: Tune durability per scope with synchronous_commit (settable per transaction, user, or database): off (async, may lose up to 3x wal_writer_delay), local (flush on master only), remote_write (replica OS-acknowledged), on (flushed on master and replica), and remote_apply (also replayed/visible on the replica, enabling safe read load-balancing) — trading latency for safety, e.g. async for a log table but synchronous for a payment.

Use replication slots so the master only recycles WAL once every replica has consumed it, which guarantees a standby cannot fall behind enough to need a resync (better than guessing wal_keep_segments); but a slot for a dead or forgotten consumer makes the master retain WAL forever and can fill its disk, so always monitor and alert on slots.
exception: An inactive/abandoned slot accumulates WAL and can fill the master's disk.

statement: PostgreSQL has two slot types: physical slots protect standard streaming replication (wal_level=replica suffices), and logical slots drive logical decoding/replication and require wal_level=logical plus an output plugin.

Create a physical slot with pg_create_physical_replication_slot (pass true to reserve WAL immediately), reference it via primary_slot_name in recovery.conf, list slots in pg_replication_slots, and remove it with pg_drop_replication_slot.

Logical decoding (pg_create_logical_replication_slot with a plugin such as test_decoding/wal2json/pgoutput) streams committed row changes in a chosen format like tail -f for the database; pg_logical_slot_get_changes consumes data (then it is gone) while pg_logical_slot_peek_changes leaves it, and pg_recvlogical streams it from the CLI — used for audit/debug, multi-master (BDR), and cross-version upgrades (pglogical).
For logical decoding to emit the old row data on UPDATE/DELETE rather than 'no-tuple-data', set the table's REPLICA IDENTITY FULL; otherwise only the post-change row identity is logged.

Use PostgreSQL 10 logical replication (CREATE PUBLICATION on the source, CREATE SUBSCRIPTION on the target, wal_level=logical) to replicate selected tables rather than the whole instance; the target table must already exist (PostgreSQL will not create it), and replicating within one instance requires pre-creating the slot and passing create_slot=false.
condition: Source and target tables share an identical layout.

statement: Extensions add functionality without bloating the core; CREATE EXTENSION loads one into a single database (not the whole instance) and supports SCHEMA placement, a specific VERSION, and CASCADE to auto-install dependencies, while pg_available_extensions / pg_available_extension_versions (driven by .control files) list what is installable.
Always install the contrib modules alongside PostgreSQL: they contain vital extensions (such as pg_stat_statements) that make operations and troubleshooting much easier.

btree_gist / btree_gin add b-tree behaviour to GiST/GIN indexes, enabling features b-trees lack such as KNN nearest-neighbour ordering (the <-> operator) on standard types, which returns the closest N rows quickly — useful for 'around X' queries where exact bounds are hard to state.

Prefer postgres_fdw (built on SQL/MED) over the older dblink for cross-database access, and use file_fdw to expose an on-disk file (CSV/text) as a queryable foreign table — the planner even fetches statistics and costs it like a real table of the same size.

Diagnose table bloat with pgstattuple (dead_tuple_percent and free_percent): some dead rows and free space are normal, but a table that is mostly dead tuples and free space needs action, and pgstatindex similarly reports index bloat (leaf density near the 90% default FILLFACTOR is healthy).

Use pg_buffercache to inspect what is in shared_buffers (join its oid columns to pg_database/pg_class; relkind r=table, i=index) and see which objects or databases dominate the cache, and use pg_prewarm to repopulate the cache (optionally a block range) after a restart clears it.

Restrict the superuser-only filesystem extensions: adminpack (pg_file_read/write/rename/unlink, pg_logdir_ls) and pageinspect (raw block/page/tuple inspection for corruption diagnosis) are powerful and callable only by superusers.
Use pgcrypto for in-database symmetric and asymmetric encryption and decryption of column data.

Set up postgres_fdw as CREATE EXTENSION, then CREATE SERVER (host/dbname/port in OPTIONS), CREATE USER MAPPING, and CREATE FOREIGN TABLE (or IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA to bulk-link a schema); as of PostgreSQL 10 it pushes filters, joins, and aggregates to the remote side (shown as 'Remote SQL' in EXPLAIN) to minimize data transferred.
Troubleshooting starts with data: set up monitoring (e.g. pgwatch2) first, because without data there is no way to diagnose problems.

Check pg_stat_activity first on an unfamiliar system: count active/idle/idle-in-transaction connections per database, hunt long-open transactions (now()-xact_start) and long-running active queries (now()-query_start), and look for ungranted locks or connections from suspicious hosts.

A transaction left open for hours (idle in transaction) is dangerous because it blocks VACUUM cleanup and causes table bloat, so monitor and terminate over-long transactions (or bound them with old_snapshot_threshold / snapshot too old).

Prefer the aggregated pg_stat_statements view over the slow-query log to find performance problems: the slow log captures only individual slow statements and is dominated by expected long jobs (index builds, exports) while missing the many-medium-queries case; note pg_stat_statements does not account for query parse time.

Work a query-inspection checklist: find where time jumps in the plan, check for missing indexes (the main cause of bad performance), use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) to spot excessive buffer use, enable track_io_timing to separate I/O from CPU, fix bad row estimates, and mark over-called functions STABLE or IMMUTABLE where possible.

Use perf top to see which C functions dominate CPU; spinlock contention (much time in s_lock, very high CPU with collapsed throughput and low I/O) can sometimes be relieved by setting huge_pages=off at the OS level.
condition: Symptoms point to spinlock contention (time in s_lock).

statement: PostgreSQL log levels escalate DEBUG -> ... -> ERROR -> FATAL -> PANIC: watch the frequency of ERROR (syntax/permission issues), treat FATAL (e.g. shared-memory allocation failures) as serious, and note PANIC (e.g. corruption) forces a shutdown.

Diagnose I/O by enabling track_io_timing and reading pg_stat_database blk_read_time/blk_write_time (often high alongside temp_files/temp_bytes caused by low work_mem/maintenance_work_mem) and per-query pg_stat_statements (a query with over ~30% disk wait is I/O-bound), then confirm with vmstat where high wa with low bi/bo indicates a random-I/O disk bottleneck.

A 'checkpoints are occurring too frequently' log message is only a performance issue, not a data-integrity danger, and is fixed by raising max_wal_size (formerly checkpoint_segments) to widen the checkpoint distance.

For storage corruption, zero_damaged_pages=on replaces unreadable blocks with zeros (causing data loss, so use with care), whereas clog corruption ('could not access status of transaction') is effectively unrecoverable — back up immediately, rebuild the instance, and treat rescued data as suspect.
condition: Hardware/storage corruption has occurred.

statement: Each PostgreSQL connection is a separate process sharing memory, so if one backend crashes (or is killed with kill -9) the postmaster terminates all connections and runs roll-forward recovery to prevent shared-memory corruption from spreading — which looks like a crash/restart but is a deliberate data-protection measure.

Detect table bloat via pg_stat_user_tables (n_live_tup vs n_dead_tup) or pgstattuple, and fix it with VACUUM FULL (which takes a table lock and blocks writes, so it is bad on large tables) or, on PostgreSQL 9.6+, with pg_squeeze, which reorganizes a table online without blocking writes.

When migrating to PostgreSQL, moving the data and schema is usually easy but rewriting SQL is the hard part; PostgreSQL supports many advanced SQL features that MySQL/MariaDB/SQLite lack (lateral joins, CUBE/GROUPING SETS, recursive CTEs, the FILTER clause, window functions, WITHIN GROUP ordered sets, TABLESAMPLE), so check each engine's feature support before porting.
In PostgreSQL a CTE (WITH clause) can itself contain data-modifying statements (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), which most other databases cannot do.

SQL result-limiting syntax is non-portable: PostgreSQL uses LIMIT/OFFSET (and supports the standard FETCH FIRST ... ROWS ONLY), while Oracle (row_num, 12c), SQL Server (TOP-N, 2012) and others differ, so expect to rewrite it when porting a query.

PostgreSQL has no out-of-the-box temporal/versioning tables and no SQL:2016 time-series pattern matching (only Oracle implements the latter), so those features must be reimplemented with triggers and with window functions/subselects.

Migrate Oracle data either with oracle_fdw (expose Oracle tables as PostgreSQL foreign tables via IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA; it needs the Oracle OCI client) or with ora2pg (a Perl tool that migrates schema, data, privileges, and partitions and does basic PL/SQL-to-PL/pgSQL conversion); neither fully migrates stored procedures, which need manual work.

Fix common Oracle-to-PostgreSQL syntax gaps: DELETE requires a FROM (DELETE FROM t), there is no dual (create a one-row view) and sysdate maps to clock_timestamp(), and Oracle's (+) outer-join operator must be rewritten as a proper OUTER JOIN; the orafce extension supplies many Oracle types/functions, and a study found roughly 73% of Oracle SQL runs unmodified when orafce is installed.

MySQL/MariaDB without strict mode silently corrupts data, which complicates migration: it coerces values into NOT NULL columns (inserting 0 or an empty string for NULL), truncates over-precision numerics, and treats NULL as 0, whereas PostgreSQL rejects such violations — so expect to clean broken data when porting, because broken rows cannot simply be inserted.

PostgreSQL's ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE ... USING lets you supply an explicit conversion expression rather than silently mangling data, so a narrowing type change fails unless you provide a rule (e.g. USING (data / 10)).

Migrate MySQL/MariaDB to PostgreSQL with pg_chameleon (converts the schema and replicates data, diverting bad rows to a discard table) or mysql_fdw (IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA with WHERE/column push-down); a good pattern is to import the foreign schema into a throwaway schema, CREATE TABLE ... (LIKE foreign_table), INSERT ... SELECT to load and clean the data, then add constraints and indexes afterward — and port stored procedures/triggers manually.
For a first-time PostgreSQL install with no existing database to migrate, install the latest stable release for the target OS.
condition: installing for the first time with no existing database to upgrade

statement: Upgrade off any end-of-life PostgreSQL major version (e.g. 8.4 and earlier): once EOL, no further security updates or serious bug fixes are issued.
Keep current with the latest micro (patch) release; a micro upgrade within the same major version needs only binary replacement plus a restart and only patches bugs, so nothing stops working.
condition: micro upgrade within the same major version

statement: Each extension must be enabled separately in every database that uses it; enabling it in one database does not make it available in others.
Install extensions into a dedicated schema (added to search_path) rather than letting them litter the public schema.
exception: some extensions dictate their install schema and cannot be moved (e.g. plv8 must live in pg_catalog)

statement: For data-change logic prefer triggers over rules; rules are legacy for action-based queries — harder to debug and writable only in SQL, not other procedural languages.
Organize tables into multiple schemas rather than leaving everything in public once a database grows large.
condition: the database has very many (e.g. thousands of) tables; for a few tables public is fine

statement: To allow a materialized view (9.4+) to be refreshed concurrently without locking it for reads, the view must have a unique index.
condition: using non-locking concurrent refresh on 9.4+

statement: Use unlogged tables to make writes faster when crash-durability/logging is unnecessary.
condition: data loss on crash is acceptable for that table

statement: PostgreSQL is a poor fit as an embeddable single-user database (unlike SQLite or Firebird) because it performs its own role management, security, and journaling rather than leaving that to the application.
A setting whose context is 'postmaster' requires a full service restart to change, whereas a 'user'-context setting needs only a reload; a restart terminates active connections, a reload does not.
After editing postgresql.conf, confirm that pg_settings.setting equals reset_val; if they differ, the change has not taken effect and the server still needs a restart or reload.
On 9.4+, settings written to postgresql.auto.conf (via ALTER SYSTEM) override the same-named settings in postgresql.conf.
Set shared_buffers fairly high — on the order of 25% of system RAM — but expect diminishing returns beyond about 8 GB; changing it requires a restart.
condition: up to roughly 8 GB; gains diminish past that

statement: On a dedicated server set effective_cache_size to half or more of onboard memory; it affects only query planning (not allocation), and setting it too low can make the planner forgo indexes; a change needs at least a reload.
condition: dedicated PostgreSQL server

statement: Keep work_mem (per sort / hash-join / table-scan operation) relatively low when many users run simple queries, since it is allocated per operation; a change needs at least a reload.
condition: many concurrent users running simple queries

statement: Do not set maintenance_work_mem (vacuum/housekeeping memory) higher than about 1 GB; reload after changing it.
Setting shared_buffers too high is a common cause of a PostgreSQL server failing to start after a postgresql.conf edit.
A stale postmaster.pid left by a failed shutdown can block a restart and may be safely deleted from the data cluster folder.
Memory settings such as work_mem can also be set at database, user, session, and function scope — e.g. raise work_mem only for one sort-intensive function or power user.
When a server breaks after a config edit, read the last line of the most recent log file (data-folder root or the pg_log subfolder); the raised error is usually self-explanatory.
Changes to pg_hba.conf take effect only after a reload or restart.
PostgreSQL evaluates pg_hba.conf top-down: the first rule that matches (whether it grants or rejects) stops processing, and if no rule matches the connection is denied.
Order pg_hba.conf rules carefully — a broad reject rule (e.g. 0.0.0.0/0 reject) placed before a specific allow rule (e.g. 127.0.0.1/32 trust) will lock out the users the later rule meant to admit.
The ident and peer authentication methods are available only on Linux, Unix, BSD, and macOS, not on Windows.
condition: server OS is Windows

statement: Adding an IPv6 rule to pg_hba.conf on a server without IPv6 networking can prevent the file from loading.
condition: server lacks IPv6 support

statement: If postgres cannot parse pg_hba.conf it blocks all access or refuses to start; back up the file before editing it.

The trust authentication method asks for no password and lets anyone meeting the IP/user/database criteria connect; restrict it to local or private-network connections, and prefer avoiding it since IPs can be spoofed.
condition: restricted to local/private single-user access where security is low-concern

statement: pg_hba.conf authentication only gatekeeps the connection; a connected user must still satisfy role and database access privileges.
Terminating connections is not a graceful operation and should be used sparingly; the client application should be the first line of defense against runaway queries.
Use pg_cancel_backend(pid) to cancel running queries without dropping the connection, and pg_terminate_backend(pid) to kill the connection itself; obtain the pid from pg_stat_activity.
Before a backup or restore of an in-use database, terminate the affected connections (pg_terminate_backend) so an eager user cannot immediately restart a canceled query.
For maintainability and security, do not grant login rights to group roles; keep group roles as pure containers for other roles.
Use CREATE ROLE rather than the deprecated CREATE USER / CREATE GROUP (which survive only for backward compatibility).
PostgreSQL never passes superuser rights through inheritance; a member of a superuser group role must run SET ROLE to assume them, and only for that session.
Always specify INHERIT or NOINHERIT explicitly when creating a role instead of relying on the default, so member-rights behavior is unambiguous.
Only superusers can run SET SESSION AUTHORIZATION (impersonate any user regardless of membership), and it changes both current_user and session_user, whereas SET ROLE changes only current_user.
Never alter template0 — it is the pristine model to recover from; make customizations to template1 or to a new template database instead.
A database created from template1 (or any custom template) cannot have its encoding or collation changed; create the database from template0 when you need a different encoding or collation.
condition: needing an encoding/collation different from the template's

statement: To edit or drop a template database, first set its pg_database.datistemplate to FALSE, then set it back afterward.
Isolate multi-tenant data by giving each tenant its own schema (with the same table set), so one tenant cannot see another tenant's rows.
Name each tenant schema to match its login role and rely on search_path = "$user", public, so identical SQL serves every tenant without modification even as tenant count grows.
A SET search_path change does not affect already-open connections; reconnect for it to take effect.
Owning a PostgreSQL database does not grant access to all objects in it: another role can create objects the owner cannot read, though the owner can still drop the whole database.
Granting privileges on tables or functions is useless unless the role also has USAGE on the containing schema (GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA).
DROP and ALTER privileges always remain with an object's owner and can never be granted away.
Some privileges are granted to PUBLIC by default — CONNECT and CREATE TEMP TABLE on databases, EXECUTE on functions, USAGE on languages — so consider REVOKEing these defaults for safety.
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES (9.0+) sets privileges on objects created in the future within a schema/database, but does not change privileges on existing objects.
Install extensions per-database on an as-needed basis rather than into every database; to give a set of databases the same extensions, build a template database with them preinstalled.
Periodically prune extensions you no longer need, since some take significant space and add bloat.
C-based extensions (which most extensions are) must be installed by a superuser.
condition: extension is C-based

statement: Use pg_dump to back up specific databases and pg_dumpall to back up all databases plus server globals; pg_dumpall must run under a superuser account.
Prefer pg_dump for day-to-day backups because it can selectively back up tables/schemas/databases and supports plain-SQL, compressed, TAR, and directory formats.

Compressed, TAR, and directory backups support parallel restore, and parallel backup (pg_dump --jobs, 9.3+) works only with the directory format because each parallel writer needs a separate file; plain-text backups support neither.
condition: for parallel backup, directory format is required

statement: The directory backup format (9.1+) writes one file per table to avoid filesystem file-size limits and exits with an error if the target directory already exists.
pg_dump and pg_dumpall have no password option; supply credentials via a ~/.pgpass file or the PGPASSWORD environment variable.
Back up server globals (roles and tablespace definitions) daily with pg_dumpall --globals-only.

A plain-text SQL backup is the most portable format (loadable into older PostgreSQL or non-PostgreSQL databases) but the least convenient, since you must run the whole script and cannot cherry-pick objects.
Restore plain-text backups with psql and restore compressed/TAR/directory backups with pg_restore.
Run psql restores with --set ON_ERROR_STOP=on to abort on the first error; by default psql continues past errors.

pg_restore (9.2+) with --section=pre-data restores structure without data, useful for using an existing database as a template; pg_restore also supports parallel restore (-j), selective restore, and is mostly backward-compatible (restore an older dump into a newer server).
When creating a tablespace, ensure the postgres service account has full access to the physical folder, and on Unix create the folder (or define an fstab location) before running CREATE TABLESPACE.
ALTER TABLESPACE ... MOVE ALL (9.4+) moves all objects if run by a superuser but only the caller's own objects otherwise, and the database or table is locked during the move.

Never delete files from the data cluster folder to reclaim space: pg_log may be safely purged, but deleting files in pg_xlog's root or pg_clog destroys data, while deleting archived WAL only breaks point-in-time recovery and slave catch-up.

Do not give the postgres OS account full administrative rights — the server may fail to start and it widens the blast radius of an SQL-injection attack; create it as a regular user with rights only to the data cluster and tablespace folders (least privilege).
Do not set shared_buffers near physical RAM: the server may crash or refuse to start; 32-bit Windows is often unstable above 512 MB, and some Linux systems cap it at the compiled SHMMAX.

When PostgreSQL won't start because the port is in use, suspect an already-running service, another service on the port, an orphan postmaster/postgresql.pid (delete it), or an orphaned process (kill all PostgreSQL processes, then restart).
Use noninteractive psql (-f script_file, or -c "statements") for automated and scheduled tasks; for many or repeated commands, write a script first and run it with psql.
Set PGHOST/PGPORT/PGUSER (and PGPASSWORD or a password file) so command-line tools need not be given connection parameters each invocation.

psql AUTOCOMMIT is on by default, so each data-changing statement commits immediately and irreversibly; turn it off (\set AUTOCOMMIT off) to gain ROLLBACK/COMMIT control on risky batch updates, but then remember to COMMIT since uncommitted work rolls back when psql exits.
condition: running a large batch of risky updates

statement: Before importing with psql \copy you must first create a table whose column count and data types match the file; psql does not infer types and will not create the table for you.
psql \copy imports the entire file as a single transaction, so any data error aborts the whole import.

When unsure of incoming data, load it into a staging schema using the most accommodating types (e.g. character varying), inspect it, recast as needed, then distribute into normalized production tables and drop the staging schema.
psql \copy defaults to a tab delimiter; add CSV for comma-separated input, DELIMITER for other separators, NULL AS to map null markers, and note that HEADER works only with the CSV format.

psql \copy is client-side (paths are relative to the client and run with the client user's access), whereas the SQL COPY statement is server-side and runs under the postgres service OS account, so its file must reside where that account can read it.
psql \watch N (9.3+) reruns a statement every N seconds for interactive monitoring, e.g. watching active or not-yet-completed queries in pg_stat_activity.
Editing postgresql.conf or pg_hba.conf from within pgAdmin requires the adminpack extension installed on the server and a superuser login; otherwise the menu is disabled.
condition: editing config files from pgAdmin

statement: For remote servers or very large databases, prefer the command-line backup/restore tools over pgAdmin to avoid adding complexity to an already lengthy process.
condition: remote server or very large databases

statement: A compressed, TAR, or directory backup made with a given pg_dump version must be restored with a pg_restore of the same or a later version.
condition: restoring a compressed/TAR/directory dump

statement: pgScript commits each statement as it runs (unlike a PostgreSQL function, which holds all work in memory and commits in one batch), so it suits memory-hungry batch jobs that need not complete as a single transaction; it works only inside pgAdmin.

pgAgent jobs always run under the pgAgent service/daemon's OS account, so a job that works from the command line can fail under pgAgent purely because that account lacks the needed privileges or network path mappings.

A pgAgent job can report success even when it failed, because pgAgent cannot always tell whether an OS shell script succeeded; inspect the job step log's jsloutput (shell output) to find what went wrong.

When several pgAgent agents share one pgAgent database they all run every job by default; set the job's host agent field to pin it to one machine, give each step batch syntax matching its agent's OS (DOS on Windows, shell/Bash on Linux), and note steps execute in alphabetical order.
Use serial/bigserial (an autoincrementing integer backed by an automatically created sequence) as a surrogate primary key when a table has no obvious natural key.
Dropping a serial column also drops its companion sequence, but renaming the table does not rename the sequence — rename the sequence manually if naming symmetry matters.
To share one sequence across multiple tables, declare the columns as integer/bigint and default them to nextval(sequence_name) rather than using serial.
varchar (no size modifier) and text are stored identically and perform equivalently in PostgreSQL, so choose between them on intent/compatibility grounds, not performance.
Use char only for genuinely fixed-length values (e.g. zip, phone, SSN): char is right-padded with spaces, costing more storage, and offers no performance advantage over varchar.
varchar and text are both capped at about 1 GB, and any value too large for a record page is pushed out to TOAST storage.
PostgreSQL array indexes start at 1, and accessing an element beyond the array's upper bound returns NULL rather than raising an error.
Use generate_series (with an integer or temporal type and an optional interval step) to mimic a for-loop in SQL instead of writing a procedural loop or building a filtered Cartesian product.

timestamp (without time zone) display is unaffected by the server's time zone, whereas timestamptz is stored internally in UTC and displayed in the time zone of the session, user, database, or server (in that precedence).
timestamptz does not store a time-zone marker: PostgreSQL converts the input to UTC on storage and discards the original zone, so the zone exists only as display context.
Restoring or moving a database to a server in a different time zone shifts the displayed values of all timestamptz columns; plan for this behavior before a cross-time-zone server move.
Prefer time-zone-aware temporal types (timestamptz) to get automatic DST handling and avoid manual offset arithmetic; timetz is rarely useful since it assumes the current DST and stores no date.
Enter dates in ISO Y-M-D format, because date interpretation varies by culture, server, and database configuration.
The OVERLAPS operator treats periods as half-open (start included, end excluded), unlike BETWEEN which includes both bounds; the difference shows up when a range is a single fixed point in time.
Model intervals with range types rather than two separate start/end columns: ranges add overlap/contains operators, range functions, and range indexing.
condition: where the data can be expressed as a range

statement: In range notation a square bracket is a closed bound and a parenthesis is an open bound; PostgreSQL canonicalizes discrete ranges (integer, date) to the [) form for both storage and display, while numeric and timestamp ranges are continuous and not enumerable.
Add a GiST index on a range column to speed up queries that filter on the range.
Always pass the explicit bound argument to a range constructor function, since the default [) bound is not obvious from the call.
A json column input is validated by PostgreSQL to ensure it is well-formed JSON on insert.
jsonb (9.4+) stores JSON in a binary form that supports indexing, whereas the json type stores the text representation.

Prefer jsonb over json for data you will query or index: jsonb is stored binary and need not be reparsed (much faster), is directly GIN-indexable, and deduplicates keys; choose json only when you must preserve the exact text, whitespace, key order, or duplicate keys.
condition: when exact text/whitespace/key order/duplicate keys must be preserved, use json

statement: jsonb adds containment and key-existence operators (@>, <@, ?, ?|, ?&); pair the @> containment operator with a GIN index on the jsonb column for fast containment queries.
JSON arrays are zero-indexed, whereas native PostgreSQL arrays are one-indexed — a common source of off-by-one errors when mixing them.

An xml column validates that values are well-formed XML on insert but does not validate them against any DTD or XSD; enforce structural rules with a CHECK constraint using xpath_exists, and write custom functions for DTD/XSD validation.
The xml type has no direct index support, so index subparts with functional indexes, as you would for the plain json type.
Dropping a table that another table's column type depends on requires CASCADE (or dropping the dependent column first), and CASCADE silently removes that dependent column.

For a table created with CREATE TABLE ... OF a composite type (9.0+), you cannot ALTER its columns directly; instead alter the underlying composite type (ALTER TYPE ... CASCADE) and the change propagates to every table of that type.
A wrong or misapplied index is worse than useless, so index choice must be deliberate and verified.
An inherited child table receives the parent's columns and inherits later structural changes and CHECK constraints, but does NOT inherit primary-key, unique, or index definitions.
Partition data with parent-child table inheritance plus a per-child CHECK constraint, so the planner uses constraint exclusion to skip child tables that cannot satisfy a query's condition.

Unlogged tables write far faster (roughly 15x in the authors' experience) but are truncated on crash, are not written to the WAL, and cannot use GiST indexes (B-Tree and GIN are fine); use them only for rebuildable or ephemeral data.
condition: data is rebuildable/ephemeral and need not survive a crash

statement: PostgreSQL does not automatically create an index for a foreign key constraint (unlike primary-key and unique constraints); add one yourself to speed up joins and cascading actions.
Foreign-key referential actions (ON UPDATE / ON DELETE CASCADE, RESTRICT, etc.) prevent orphaned rows; RESTRICT is the default, but state it explicitly for clarity.
Adding a UNIQUE constraint automatically creates a unique index, disallows NULLs, and can serve as a foreign-key target; a bare unique index with no constraint does allow NULLs.
PostgreSQL has no conditional unique constraint; enforce uniqueness over only a subset of rows with a partial UNIQUE index (CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... WHERE ...).

CHECK constraints may use functions and boolean expressions, let the planner skip rows that cannot satisfy them, and — unlike primary-key, foreign-key, and unique constraints — are inherited by child tables.

Use an exclusion constraint (9.0+) to enforce uniqueness via a non-equality operator such as the overlap operator (&&) — for example to prevent double-booking a room/time; exclusion constraints generally use GiST (install btree_gist for compound B-Tree parts) and auto-create the index.
condition: uniqueness must be enforced with a non-equality operator, e.g. scheduling/overlap

statement: Give primary-key and unique constraints names that are unique within the schema, conventionally embedding the table and column names.
Choose the index method deliberately — B-Tree, GiST, GIN, SP-GiST, and hash each suit different data types and operators.
B-Tree is the general-purpose default index (chosen automatically and the only method available for primary and unique keys) and is usually sufficient.

GiST suits full-text, spatial, scientific, unstructured, and hierarchical data and is lossy — it stores an approximation, so retrieving or finely checking values needs an extra recheck lookup; it cannot enforce uniqueness except inside an exclusion constraint.

GIN suits full-text search and the jsonb type (and hstore, pg_trgm); it copies indexed values (non-lossy), so reads limited to covered columns are faster than GiST but updates are slower, and it cannot index very large values due to a per-row size limit.
Avoid hash indexes in PostgreSQL: they are legacy, rate below GiST and GIN, and are not tracked by the WAL, so they cannot be used in streaming-replication setups.
You can mix different index types on one table and build multiple indexes on the same column; the planner will consider them all.

The default operator class is usually fine, but B-Tree text_ops/varchar_ops do not support LIKE (~~), so for frequent wildcard/LIKE searches on text or varchar build the index with the text_pattern_ops / varchar_pattern_ops opclass.
condition: doing many LIKE/wildcard searches on text or varchar

statement: Each index works against a single operator class, so create separate indexes to cover multiple opclasses on the same column (e.g. one for equality and one for LIKE).

Use a functional index (e.g. on upper(col)) for case-insensitive or expression-based searches, and always query with the same function so the index is used; PostgreSQL 9.3+ also supports indexes on materialized views.
condition: case-insensitive or expression-based searches

statement: Use partial (filtered) indexes to cover only the rows matching a WHERE predicate: they are smaller, more likely to fit in RAM, save disk space, and can enforce subset uniqueness.
condition: only a known subset of rows is queried

statement: A partial index's WHERE function must be IMMUTABLE (no CURRENT_DATE or data from other tables/rows), and the planner uses the partial index only when the query's WHERE is a superset of the index's condition — querying through a view that embeds the condition avoids this pitfall.

The planner combines single-column indexes on the fly via a bitmap index scan, so when future query patterns on compound fields are unpredictable, prefer single-column indexes and let the planner combine them.
condition: query patterns over the compound columns are unpredictable

statement: A compound B-Tree index on (a, b, ...) also serves queries that filter only on the leading column a, so a separate index on a alone is redundant.
Index-only scans (9.2+) let the planner satisfy a query from the index without touching the table, so a compound index covering both the filtered and the output columns speeds those queries.
Each additional column makes a compound index fatter and less able to fit in RAM, so do not overload compound indexes with columns.
When the same query recurs, store it as a view; routing access through views adds an indirection layer useful for permission control and logic abstraction.
Prefer INSTEAD OF triggers over rules to make complex or multi-table views updatable, since the trigger approach is standards-compliant.
A single-table view that outputs the primary key is automatically updatable (9.3+), whereas a multi-table join view is not simply updatable (the change is ambiguous) and requires INSTEAD OF triggers.
Add WITH CHECK OPTION (9.4+) to a view to block inserts or updates that would move rows outside the view's WHERE condition.
Use a materialized view when the underlying query is slow and slightly stale data is acceptable, as in OLAP reporting.
Unlike a plain view, a materialized view can be indexed to speed up reads.
Materialized views never refresh automatically; schedule REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW via cron, a pgAgent job, or a trigger.
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY (9.4+) keeps the view readable during refresh but requires a unique index on the view and takes longer to complete.
condition: a unique index exists on the materialized view

statement: A materialized view cannot be changed with CREATE OR REPLACE — you must DROP and recreate it, losing its indexes; for a maintained physical sort prefer an ORDER BY in the view definition over CLUSTER, since ORDER BY persists across each REFRESH while CLUSTER must be re-run.
PostgreSQL-only SQL shortcuts are often not ANSI-compliant, so avoid them when the SQL must port to other database products.
DISTINCT ON (cols) returns the first row per distinct set after sorting; the query's ORDER BY must begin with the DISTINCT ON columns.
Use the ONLY keyword to restrict SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE to the named table and exclude its child (inherited) tables.
Use RETURNING on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE to return the affected rows; for inserts into tables with serial keys it is invaluable because it returns the newly generated key values.

Prefer the FILTER clause (9.4+) over CASE WHEN for conditional aggregation: it is clearer, faster on large datasets, and avoids the spurious NULLs that CASE injects into NULL-sensitive aggregates like array_agg; FILTER works with any aggregate.
A query's WHERE clause is evaluated before its window functions.

Window functions add aggregate values to each row without GROUP BY or self-joins; PARTITION BY scopes the window to rows sharing values, and an ORDER BY inside OVER turns the window into a running aggregate over the partition start through the current row (independent of the query-level ORDER BY).
LEAD and LAG return NULL when they reach beyond the partition boundary, so always handle the out-of-partition case.
Use a CTE (WITH) to name a reusable subquery scoped to the statement, improving readability or forcing the planner to materialize a costly intermediate result.
Writable CTEs (9.1+) embed UPDATE/INSERT/DELETE ... RETURNING inside WITH, e.g. to atomically move rows from one table to another.
Recursive CTEs (WITH RECURSIVE, combining tables with UNION ALL) handle tree-like and hierarchical structures; among multiple CTEs, later ones may reference earlier ones but not vice versa.
LATERAL (9.3+) lets the right side of a FROM/join reference columns from the left side, but only in that one direction.
Use a LATERAL join to limit rows returned from the joined side per left-hand row (e.g. the last five logins per user); it is faster and more succinct than the equivalent window-function query.
Always write the LATERAL keyword explicitly for clarity, even when the parser could infer it, so the statement also fails clearly on pre-LATERAL PostgreSQL versions.
Place optional (defaulted) function arguments after the non-optional ones, and note that unnamed arguments cannot be supplied with the name := value call syntax.

Mark a function's volatility correctly so the planner can optimize: IMMUTABLE (same output for the same input, fully cacheable), STABLE (constant within a single query), or VOLATILE (the default; may differ per call and required for data-changing or environment-dependent functions).
condition: IMMUTABLE only when output depends solely on the arguments

statement: A STRICT function returns NULL whenever any input is NULL and the planner skips evaluating it, but STRICT on SQL functions can prevent the planner from using indexes, so apply it carefully.
condition: on SQL-language functions, weigh the index-use cost

statement: Use SECURITY DEFINER to execute a function in its owner's security context, which lets users perform an action (e.g. update a table) through the function without holding the direct privilege themselves.
Statement-level triggers fire once per SQL statement, whereas row-level triggers fire once for each affected row.

BEFORE triggers fire before the statement (to cancel or adjust data), AFTER triggers fire after it (for logging or replication), and INSTEAD OF triggers run in its place; BEFORE/AFTER attach only to tables and INSTEAD OF only to views.
A trigger that modifies the NEW row must be a BEFORE trigger, because in the AFTER event all changes to NEW are ignored.
A PostgreSQL trigger function returns the trigger type, takes no arguments, and can be reused across multiple triggers — unlike the per-trigger handler code required by most other databases.

Each trigger has exactly one function; multiple triggers on the same event fire in alphabetical order of trigger name, each seeing the previous trigger's changes, and a ROLLBACK in any one rolls back all earlier triggers' changes for that event (triggers are not separate transactions).
Write trigger functions in any language except SQL (PL/pgSQL is most common), and use a WHEN condition or UPDATE OF column_list (9.0+) to fire a trigger only when relevant columns change.
Trusted languages (SQL, PL/pgSQL, PL/Perl, PL/V8) cannot reach the OS or filesystem beyond the data cluster, so any user may create functions in them.

Untrusted languages (suffixed with U, e.g. PL/PythonU, PL/PerlU) can run OS commands and call web services, so only superusers may author functions in them, and such functions execute under the postgres OS account.
The planner can inline SQL functions — peeking inside to use indexes and collapse repeated computations — whereas functions in other languages are treated as opaque black boxes.
Use SQL for simple scalar/set-returning functions, but switch to PL/pgSQL when you need local variables, control flow, or dynamically assembled SQL (which SQL functions cannot do).
Build a custom aggregate via CREATE AGGREGATE with a state transition function (SFUNC/STYPE) plus optional FINALFUNC/INITCOND; any user-defined aggregate can also be used as a window function.
PL/V8 (trusted JavaScript) runs math-heavy functions far faster than SQL/PL-pgSQL (often 10-20x) and can create window functions, which SQL, PL/pgSQL, and PL/Python cannot.
Tune a slow query in this order: first perfect the underlying SQL, then add indexes, then update planner statistics.

EXPLAIN shows the planner's intended plan without running the query, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) runs it and reports estimated versus actual, and EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) reports shared-buffer hits (a higher count means more rows were served from memory).
To run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) on a data-changing statement (UPDATE/INSERT) without persisting the change, wrap it in a transaction you abort: BEGIN before and ROLLBACK after.
EXPLAIN cost is reported in arbitrary units that vary by hardware, so use it only to compare plans on the same server; the planner picks the plan with the lowest estimated total cost.
A large gap between a plan's estimated and actual row counts usually stems from out-of-date table statistics, so run ANALYZE on the tables before a long query to refresh the statistics.
PostgreSQL caches query plans, so re-running the same or a similar query incurs much lower planning time on subsequent executions.

Begin optimization by finding the bottleneck queries with the pg_stat_statements extension (most frequently run and most costly queries); it must be added to shared_preload_libraries and the server restarted before it collects data.

PostgreSQL has no index hints, but you can disable planner strategy settings (e.g. enable_nestloop, enable_seqscan) per query or globally to discourage a plan; this is only a request, and the planner may still use a disabled strategy when it has no viable alternative.
Nested-loop and sequential-scan strategies tend to be the slowest, so when the planner uses them verify it is out of necessity rather than ignorance — a quick check is to disable them.
The planner chooses a sequential scan when no index can satisfy the query condition or when it judges using the index costlier than scanning the table.
Two common indexing mistakes are leaving out useful indexes and adding indexes that queries cannot use; choose indexes deliberately and write queries to match them.
A query's form must match the index: an index built for the overlap operator (&&) will not serve a value = ANY(array) query, which then falls back to a sequential scan regardless of enable_seqscan.
Check whether your indexes are actually being used by querying the pg_stat_user_indexes and pg_stat_user_tables views.
The planner plans from aggregated statistics (pg_stats), not by scanning all rows, so statistics that diverge from reality cause bad plans — most damagingly, unnecessary sequential scans.
After a large data load or major deletion, manually refresh statistics with VACUUM ANALYZE (VACUUM permanently removes deleted rows; ANALYZE updates the stats).

Only about 20% of a table is sampled to build statistics (less for very large tables); raise the per-column target with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET STATISTICS for columns used heavily in joins and WHERE clauses.

random_page_cost (default 4, suited to today's mechanical drives) is the cost ratio of random versus sequential disk reads; lower it for faster storage (roughly 2.0-2.5 for SSDs), and set it per database, server, or tablespace.
Caching makes repeated queries much faster when the underlying data is unchanged; using common table expressions and IMMUTABLE functions in queries encourages caching.
Do not raise shared_buffers too high for caching, because an oversized cache wastes time being scanned.
The best and easiest way to improve performance is to start with well-written SQL — most queries are not written as efficiently as they could be.
Avoid two SQL anti-patterns: blindly reusing a query pattern (e.g. always using LEFT JOIN where INNER JOIN is more appropriate) and failing to adopt newer dialect features.
Do not overuse correlated subqueries in the SELECT list; consolidating them into a join with aggregation is both shorter and faster.

Avoid SELECT *: it adds network traffic and forces TOAST to reassemble large fields; inside a view definition it is harmless, because unreferenced columns and their computations are not executed unless a query actually requests them.
Use CASE (or the FILTER clause in 9.4+) instead of subqueries for conditional aggregation so the table is scanned only once — generally faster and clearer, and shorter plans usually perform better.
Replicate for two reasons: availability (fail over when restoring a large database would take too long) and scalability (offload reads to read-only slaves).
PostgreSQL built-in replication supports a single master and read-only slaves, and works by making the WAL available for slaves to pull and replay.

Synchronous replication holds a master transaction incomplete until at least one slave is updated, whereas asynchronous replication lets the master commit without waiting — lower latency, but the slave can lag and may miss transactions on a transmission failure.

Streaming replication (9.0+) ships the WAL over the PostgreSQL connection protocol without direct file access, and cascading replication (9.2+) lets a slave feed other slaves (a cascading standby) to reduce latency.
Built-in streaming replication requires every server to run the same PostgreSQL version (and, before 9.3, the same CPU architecture), and unlogged tables do not participate in replication.

Third-party tools (Slony, Bucardo) can replicate individual tables or databases across mixed PostgreSQL versions and OSes and support multimaster, but they rely on triggers and often do not replicate DDL, making them more invasive than plain log shipping.
Start the postgres service on all slaves before starting it on the master, so the master does not change data before the slaves can capture and replicate it.
Use pg_basebackup to clone a master's data cluster while the postgres service is running, avoiding a shutdown when the cluster is too large to copy offline.

Promote a slave by creating its configured trigger_file (e.g. failover.now): PostgreSQL finishes WAL playback and renames recovery.conf to recovery.done, after which the slave is independent and cannot rejoin without re-cloning from scratch.

Foreign data wrappers (9.1+) let PostgreSQL query external sources as foreign tables; queries were SELECT-only in 9.1/9.2 and became updatable in 9.3, with postgres_fdw the only built-in wrapper supporting updates.
PostgreSQL installs two foreign data wrappers by default: file_fdw (local files accessible to the server) and postgres_fdw (other PostgreSQL servers, read and write).
