Changes to a postgres_fdw foreign server's connection options (host, port, dbname) take effect only in a new session, because the connection is opened on first use and kept open.

A PostgreSQL foreign table can expose a subset or all of the remote columns and is updatable by default; add OPTIONS(updatable 'false') to make it read-only, and a table-level updatable setting overrides the foreign-server setting.

A user mapping grants no privileges by itself: you must still GRANT on the foreign table, the mapped role must exist on the foreign server with login rights, and anyone who can connect to your database can reach the foreign server.
SQLite is an embedded, in-process relational database engine: it runs inside the host application's process space rather than as a separate server process.
Because SQLite's engine runs in the same process as the application, it needs no network configuration or separate server administration and avoids the overhead of network calls to a database server.
Multiple independent processes can open and operate on the same SQLite database file; SQLite delegates the required synchronization and locking to the operating system.
condition: multiple processes share one database file

statement: SQLite implements a large subset of ANSI SQL92 (transactions, views, CHECK constraints, correlated subqueries, compound queries) plus triggers, indexes, autoincrement columns, and the LIMIT/OFFSET clause.

SQLite's architecture cleanly separates a front-end SQL compiler (tokenizer, parser, code generator) from a back-end storage engine (B-tree, pager, OS interface), with a virtual machine executing between them.
Every SQL statement in SQLite is first compiled into a bytecode program of VDBE opcodes, which the virtual database engine then executes one instruction at a time.
In SQLite's back-end the pager handles transaction management, database locking, crash recovery, and caching of frequently used pages to minimize disk I/O.
SQLite uses B+-trees to store tables and B-trees to store indexes.
SQLite's OS-interface module abstracts platform-specific operations such as file locking, isolating the other modules from per-operating-system differences and making the engine easier to port.
SQLite requires zero configuration: there is no server to set up, no configuration files, and no database administrator needed to install or run it.

The SQLite database file format is binary-compatible across all supported operating systems, CPU architectures, and byte orders, so a database file created on one platform can be copied to and used on another without conversion.
An entire SQLite database — including its tables, indexes, triggers, views, and schema — is stored in a single ordinary operating-system file.
A SQLite database can hold up to about 2 terabytes of data, bounded in practice by the host operating system's maximum file size.
condition: bounded by the operating system's maximum file size

statement: SQLite natively supports both UTF-8 and UTF-16 text encodings.
SQLite stores variable-length records, allocating only the minimum space needed for each field's value plus one byte of type information rather than padding to the column's declared width.

All of SQLite's core source code is in the public domain with no license or copyright claim, so it may be freely modified, incorporated, distributed, sold, and used for any purpose without royalties or restrictions.
More than half of the SQLite project's code is regression-test code (roughly 30,000 lines of tests against 30,000 lines of core), and the test suite covers over 97% of the core code.

SQLite uses dynamic (manifest) typing: a value's storage type is determined by the value itself, not by the column's declared type, so a field may hold a value whose type differs from its column's declared type.

SQLite's conflict-resolution feature lets an INSERT replace an existing row when it collides on a key (for example INSERT ... ON CONFLICT REPLACE), and the resolution policy can be declared once in the table definition so it applies to later statements.
The ATTACH command attaches an external database file to the current connection so its tables are accessible as if they were local, and DETACH removes it.
SQLite uses coarse-grained locking that permits multiple concurrent readers but only one writer at a time; a writer takes an exclusive lock on the entire database for the duration of the write.

An application with high write concurrency that is also time-critical probably needs a different database than SQLite; the acceptable level of concurrency can only be determined empirically by testing the real application.
condition: high write concurrency and a time-critical workload

statement: Simple single-table SELECT, INSERT, and UPDATE statements are very fast in SQLite — near the speed of RAM or disk — because it avoids network calls and has low transaction-startup and query-planning overhead.
condition: simple single-table statements

statement: SQLite has no sophisticated query optimizer and keeps no elaborate table statistics, so for complex queries over large data sets it is typically slower than databases with advanced query planners such as Oracle or PostgreSQL.
condition: complex queries over large data sets

statement: SQLite is designed for small-to-medium-sized applications and is not a universal drop-in replacement for large-scale relational databases.

At the start of each transaction SQLite allocates a dirty-page bitmap for its rollback journal requiring roughly 256 bytes of RAM per 1 MB of database, so transaction-startup overhead grows linearly with database size and the practical size limit is in the tens of gigabytes despite the multi-terabyte ceiling.

Use SQLite on a network file system only when no more than one connection accesses a given database at a time, because unreliable network-file-system locking can let two clients modify the same file simultaneously and corrupt the database.
condition: database stored on a network file system
exception: safe when no more than one connection accesses the database at a time

statement: SQLite performs file locking through standard operating-system mechanisms — POSIX advisory locks on Unix and the equivalent system calls on Windows.
SQLite views are read-only — DELETE, INSERT, and UPDATE cannot be run directly on a view; to make a view updatable, define an INSTEAD OF trigger that performs the change in its body.
SQLite allows only one active transaction at a time and, in the version documented by the book, does not support nested transactions.
condition: the SQLite version documented by the book

statement: SQLite implements LEFT OUTER JOIN but not RIGHT or FULL OUTER JOIN; a right outer join can be expressed by reversing the table order in a LEFT OUTER JOIN, and a full outer join by combining supported operations.
In the version documented by the book, SQLite's ALTER TABLE supports only the RENAME TABLE and ADD COLUMN operations; DROP COLUMN, ALTER COLUMN, and ADD CONSTRAINT are not supported.
condition: the SQLite version documented by the book

statement: SQLite has no GRANT/REVOKE or user-level access control; the only access controls are the underlying operating system's file permissions, and the application has full access to the entire database file.
In the SQLite version documented by the book, foreign-key constraints are parsed but not enforced by the engine.
condition: the SQLite version documented by the book

statement: For command-line use, prefer the statically linked SQLite command-line program (CLP), which has the database engine compiled in and is self-contained, avoiding any dependency on a separately installed shared library.
For applications that dynamically link to SQLite, use the shared-library (DLL) build so SQLite can be upgraded without recompiling the dependent software.
condition: the application dynamically links to SQLite

statement: To use SQLite safely from multiple threads, build it with thread support enabled (for example ./configure --enable-threads, defining the THREADSAFE flag); the precompiled Unix/Linux shared libraries are not thread-safe.
condition: the program uses SQLite from multiple threads

statement: The SQLite command-line program is one tool with two modes: a command-line/batch mode for scripted administration and an interactive shell mode that acts as a query processor.
Invoking sqlite3 without a database filename opens an in-memory database whose contents are lost when the program exits.
condition: no database filename is supplied

statement: In the SQLite shell, every input line is treated as a SQL statement except lines beginning with a period, which are reserved dot-commands for shell operations.

SQLite defers physically creating a named database file until the first object (such as a table or view) is created, leaving an interval in which permanent database settings can be set before the structure is written to disk.
Set permanent settings such as page size and text encoding (UTF-8 or UTF-16) before creating the first database object, because they cannot be changed once the database has been created.
condition: must be applied before the first database object is created

statement: Declaring a column as INTEGER PRIMARY KEY makes SQLite automatically generate the next integer value for that column when an INSERT statement omits it.
The SQL function last_insert_rowid() returns the most recently inserted autoincrement/rowid value.
sqlite_master is SQLite's system catalog view; each row describes one database object through the columns type, name, tbl_name, rootpage, and sql (the object's DDL definition).

For portable, long-term backups, dump the database to SQL text with the .dump command rather than copying the binary file, because the SQL form is portable across SQLite versions and platforms and compresses well.
condition: long-term or cross-version backups

statement: A binary backup of a SQLite database is just a copy of its single file; running VACUUM beforehand reclaims space freed by deleted objects and yields a more compact copy.
Dropping a SQLite database is simply deleting its database file.

The shell command .read executes a SQL file (used to restore a .dump), while .import loads delimited text into a table by parsing each line with the current separator (default the pipe character), requiring the field count to match the table's columns.
The sqlite3_analyzer tool reports a database's on-disk physical structure — page size, page counts, payload, and space utilization for individual objects and in aggregate.

Under the relational model's Information Principle, the logical representation of data (tables, rows, values) is independent of physical storage, so changing how the database stores data on disk must not affect the logical view that applications see.
A view is a virtual table defined by a relational expression rather than stored data; it appears and behaves like a base table but produces its rows by evaluating that expression.

Use a view to preserve an existing table's logical structure when its base tables change — for example, after decomposing a table for normalization, define a view that joins the new tables so it still looks like the original to applications.
condition: base tables are restructured but applications expect the original logical shape

statement: A relational database's system catalog is itself represented as ordinary queryable relations, so metadata about database objects can be interrogated with the same query language used for regular data.
The relational model requires every relation to have a primary key that uniquely identifies each tuple, with the corollary that a relation may not contain duplicate tuples.

A candidate key is a minimal attribute set whose values are unique for every tuple and all of whose attributes are necessary for uniqueness; a unique-but-not-minimal set is a superkey, and when several candidate keys exist the choice of which is the primary key is arbitrary.
A foreign key is a column (or set of columns) in one table whose values reference the primary key of another table, relating the rows of the two tables to model a real-world relationship.

Referential integrity preserves foreign-key relationships so a referencing row always points to an existing referenced row; without enforcement, deleting referenced rows leaves dangling references and inconsistent data.

The relational model defines four classes of integrity constraint: domain integrity (attribute values within their domain), entity integrity (each tuple uniquely identifiable), referential integrity (foreign-key relationships between tables), and user-defined integrity (such as triggers).

A domain constraint requires each attribute value to fall within its declared domain (for example an integer column rejects non-integers), and CHECK constraints can express arbitrarily complex rules for what values an attribute may hold.
Define integrity constraints in the database schema/catalog itself rather than in application programs, so the rules are enforced uniformly regardless of which application accesses the data.
A null value denotes the absence of a value and is distinct from zero, an empty string, and blank characters; it can mean unknown, missing, or not-applicable.
Normalization organizes attributes within relations to minimize data duplication, because duplication wastes space and, more importantly, increases the opportunity for database inconsistencies.

Normal forms are cumulative: each higher normal form requires all conditions of the lower forms (2NF requires 1NF, 3NF requires 2NF), and a higher normal form has less duplication and more resistance to inconsistency.
First normal form requires every attribute to use a domain of atomic values, meaning a single attribute cannot hold more than one value.

A functional dependency exists when the value of one attribute (or set of attributes) determines the value of another for every tuple (written A maps to B); functional dependencies often signal that duplication lurks in a table.

Second normal form requires the relation to be in 1NF and every non-key attribute to depend on the whole primary key, not just part of a composite key; an attribute dependent on only part of the key signals duplication and should be moved into its own table.

Third normal form requires the relation to be in 2NF and to have no transitive dependencies (a non-key attribute depending on another non-key attribute); transitively dependent attributes should be relegated to their own table.

Normalization cannot guarantee that data is factually correct, but it ensures the data stays internally consistent; the more important the data, the more attention its design and normalization deserve.
Decomposing a table for normalization turns a previously implicit relationship into an explicit, enforceable one backed by a foreign-key constraint.

SQL is a relationally complete query language that combines declarative features (from relational calculus) and procedural features (from relational algebra) and includes almost all relational-algebra operators.
SQL has a structural part, Data Definition Language (DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP), and a functional part, Data Manipulation Language (DML), which retrieves and modifies data.
SQLite supports all of the relational operations in ANSI SQL except right and full outer joins, which can still be achieved by indirect means.
SQL is largely a declarative language: you describe what data you want rather than the step-by-step procedure to obtain it, unlike imperative languages such as C or Perl.

In SQLite, SQL commands are terminated by a semicolon in both the command-line program and the C API, and each command is composed of whitespace-separated tokens (literals, keywords, identifiers, expressions, special characters).
SQL is case-insensitive for keywords and identifiers, but SQLite is by default case-sensitive for string values, so the value Mike is not equal to the value mike.
In SQL, string literals are delimited by single quotes, and a literal single quote inside such a string must be written as two consecutive single quotes.
SQLite has five native storage types (domains): INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB, and NULL.

A CREATE TABLE statement requires at minimum a unique table name and one column; each column has a name, an optional domain/type, and a list of column constraints, with optional table-level constraints following.
The TEMP or TEMPORARY keyword in CREATE TABLE creates a temporary table that exists only for the current session and is destroyed when the connection closes.
Constraints such as UNIQUE, NOT NULL, DEFAULT, and COLLATE can be declared per-column, and a constraint like UNIQUE can also be declared at table level across multiple columns together.
A table can be created directly from a SELECT statement (CREATE TABLE AS SELECT), defining both its structure and its data in one step.
SELECT is the sole data-retrieval command in SQL and the largest and most complex command, implementing relational operations through a series of optional clauses.

Relational operations exhibit closure: each takes relations as input and produces a relation as output, which lets operations be nested into relational expressions of arbitrary complexity (for example one SELECT feeding another).

The clauses of a SELECT command execute in a fixed logical order regardless of how they are written: FROM (join) then WHERE (restriction) then GROUP BY then HAVING then SELECT (projection) then DISTINCT then ORDER BY then LIMIT/OFFSET.
Only the SELECT clause is mandatory in a SELECT command; FROM, WHERE, and the other clauses are optional.
WHERE is a restriction that produces a row-wise subset of a relation, while the SELECT clause is a projection that produces a column-wise subset.
In SQLite, the truth value false is represented by the number 0 and true by any non-zero value.
Operator precedence determines the default order of evaluation in an expression with multiple operators, and precedence can be overridden by using parentheses to declare an explicit order.
The LIKE operator matches string values against a pattern in which the percent sign matches any sequence of zero or more characters and the underscore matches any single character.
The rows returned by SELECT are not guaranteed to be in any particular order unless an ORDER BY clause is used; the SQL standard declares the order otherwise undefined.
LIMIT specifies the maximum number of rows to return and OFFSET the number of rows to skip; OFFSET depends on LIMIT, so LIMIT can be used without OFFSET but not the reverse.
LIMIT and OFFSET do not speed up a query by reducing the rows the WHERE clause must collect; they run last in the pipeline, after ORDER BY, which needs the entire result set to sort correctly.
ORDER BY runs after WHERE but before the SELECT projection, which is why a query can order by a column that is not in the projected result.
Aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, MAX) compute over the rows selected by the WHERE clause, not over all rows from FROM; the SELECT command filters first, then aggregates.

GROUP BY sits between WHERE and SELECT and splits the rows into groups sharing a common value for the grouping column(s), after which aggregates are applied to each group separately rather than to the whole result.

HAVING filters the groups produced by GROUP BY using a predicate over aggregate values, in the same way WHERE filters individual rows; WHERE predicates are expressed in row values, HAVING predicates in aggregate values.
DISTINCT is a restriction that removes duplicate rows by comparing all columns listed in the SELECT clause; it applies no grouping or predicate and acts purely as a uniqueness filter.
Joining links tables in the FROM clause into a single composite input relation, which the subsequent SELECT clauses then filter; joins are the first operation of a SELECT command.
An inner join returns only the rows that satisfy the join condition (matching values in the related columns of the two tables) and is the most common join type.
A cross (Cartesian) join combines every row of one table with every row of another when no join condition is given; an inner join is a cross join narrowed by the join condition.

Conceptually a join is a cross product followed by restriction (the join condition) and projection, but real databases optimize this and do not actually materialize the full cross product of the joined tables.

A left outer join returns the inner-join matches plus the unmatched rows of the left table (with NULLs for the right table's columns); a right join is its mirror, and a full outer join includes unmatched rows from both tables.

SQLite does not support right or full outer joins, but a right join can be rewritten as a left join with the tables swapped, and a full outer join can be built from compound queries (UNION of a left join and a reversed left join).

Avoid NATURAL JOIN in applications because it joins on all identically named columns, so adding or removing a column can silently change the query's results; always state join conditions explicitly instead.
condition: production application queries

statement: Prefer the explicit SQL92 JOIN ... ON (or USING) syntax over the older implicit form that lists tables comma-separated in FROM and puts the join condition in WHERE.
When joining tables, qualify column names as table.column to avoid ambiguity, because a column name shared by more than one joined table is ambiguous and raises an error.
condition: the column name exists in more than one joined table

statement: Table and column aliases (the relational rename operation, with AS optional) shorten references and make self-joins possible by letting a table be joined to itself under two different alias names.

A subquery (a SELECT nested within another statement) can appear anywhere a relational expression is valid: in WHERE (often with the IN operator), in the SELECT list, in FROM, in ORDER BY, and in other commands.
A correlated subquery references a variable from its enclosing query and is therefore evaluated once per row of the outer query.
A subquery used in the FROM clause must be given a name (a rename) so it can be referenced as a derived table.

Aggregating before a join — moving the GROUP BY (and even a LIMIT) into a subquery that runs before the join — reduces the number of rows the join must match and makes the query faster; because the join can disrupt the subquery's order, re-apply ORDER BY in the outer query.
condition: an aggregating query joins a large table whose rows are collapsed by the aggregate

statement: A compound query combines the results of multiple SELECTs with UNION, INTERSECT, or EXCEPT; the relations must have the same number of columns, and only one ORDER BY is allowed, placed at the end and applying to the combined result.
UNION eliminates duplicate rows by default, whereas UNION ALL keeps duplicates.
A CASE expression evaluates its WHEN conditions in order and executes only the first match; if no condition matches and there is no ELSE, CASE returns NULL.
NULL is a placeholder denoting the absence of a value; it is not zero, not an empty string, not true, and not false.

Comparing a value to NULL with the equals operator yields NULL (even NULL equals NULL is NULL), so such a WHERE predicate is never true and matches no rows; test for NULL with the IS NULL or IS NOT NULL operators instead.
SQL uses three-valued logic with true, false, and NULL as truth values, and a NULL propagates through arithmetic and logical expressions so that one NULL can make an entire expression NULL.
COUNT with an asterisk counts all rows regardless of NULLs, but COUNT of a specific column counts only rows where that column is non-NULL, ignoring rows where it is NULL.

Rows where a predicate evaluates to NULL are weeded out by WHERE and contribute nothing to aggregates, so a nullable column can silently corrupt aggregate results (for example SUM over an expression involving a NULL column drops those rows).

Use COALESCE, which returns the first non-NULL value in its argument list, to substitute a default for NULL in expressions and aggregates, and make any query that references nullable columns in predicates or aggregates NULL-aware.
condition: a referenced column may contain NULL

statement: The NULLIF function takes two arguments and returns NULL if they are equal, otherwise it returns the first argument.
In an INSERT, the order of values must match the supplied column list; if the column list is omitted, the values must match the column order declared in the CREATE TABLE statement.
Omitting a column from an INSERT uses its default value, and supplying NULL for an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY column is equivalent to omitting it, which triggers automatic key generation.
INSERT can add many rows at once using an INSERT ... SELECT form (as long as the column counts match), and a subquery can also supply individual values within an INSERT.
CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT copies both structure and data, but constraints from the source table — including autoincrement, indexes, and UNIQUE constraints — are not carried into the new table.
UPDATE sets one or more columns on the rows matched by its WHERE predicate (the WHERE clause works as in SELECT), and UNIQUE or other constraints can abort an UPDATE just as they can an INSERT.
DELETE removes the rows matched by its WHERE predicate and is effectively an UPDATE statement without the SET clause.

Every SQLite table has an implicit 64-bit integer primary-key column called ROWID (also reachable through the aliases OID and _ROWID_), whose values are auto-generated in increasing order whether or not a primary key is declared.
Declaring a column INTEGER PRIMARY KEY makes it an alias for ROWID, giving it an auto-generated, unique, monotonically increasing default value.

By default SQLite may recycle ROWIDs after rows are deleted, so generated ROWIDs are not always strictly ascending; adding the AUTOINCREMENT keyword prevents reuse (tracking the maximum in the sqlite_sequence table) and returns a SQLITE_FULL error once the maximum 64-bit value is reached.
Prefer a plain INTEGER PRIMARY KEY over AUTOINCREMENT unless the application specifically needs keys that are never recycled, because AUTOINCREMENT adds extra bookkeeping overhead.
condition: the application does not specifically require non-recycled key values

statement: If you declare a non-integer primary key or a multi-column PRIMARY KEY, SQLite still maintains its internal ROWID and simply adds a UNIQUE constraint over the declared primary-key columns.

A UNIQUE constraint requires all values in a column or group of columns to be distinct and aborts an INSERT or UPDATE that would create a duplicate; at table level it applies to the combination of the named columns rather than to each individually.
In SQLite a column with a UNIQUE constraint may contain any number of NULL values, because SQLite (like Oracle and PostgreSQL) treats NULLs as all distinct from one another.
The DEFAULT keyword supplies a column's value when an INSERT omits it; a column without a DEFAULT that is omitted from an INSERT is set to NULL.
DEFAULT accepts the reserved words CURRENT_TIME, CURRENT_DATE, and CURRENT_TIMESTAMP to automatically populate time and date columns, which is useful for logging or timestamping events.
A NOT NULL constraint forbids NULL in a column on both INSERT and UPDATE; pairing NOT NULL with a DEFAULT lets an INSERT that omits the column still satisfy the constraint via the default value.

A CHECK constraint defines a boolean expression (any expression valid in a WHERE clause) that is tested on INSERT and UPDATE; all of a table's CHECK constraints must evaluate to true before the modification is applied, otherwise a constraint violation is raised.

Triggers can enforce data-integrity rules that a CHECK constraint cannot express, and can do more than CHECK constraints, so use a trigger when a needed rule is beyond what a CHECK expression can state.
condition: the integrity rule cannot be expressed as a CHECK constraint

statement: Collation defines how text values are compared and therefore what counts as a duplicate; SQLite has three built-in collations — BINARY (the default, byte-wise via memcmp), NOCASE (case-insensitive for the ASCII letters), and REVERSE — and the C API can register custom collations.

SQLite has five storage classes (INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB, NULL); INTEGER values use a variable byte width chosen by magnitude, REAL uses 8-byte floats, and TEXT and BLOB sizes are effectively unlimited.

SQLite infers a value's storage class from its literal representation: quoted text is TEXT, an unquoted number without a decimal point or exponent is INTEGER, an unquoted number with a decimal point or exponent is REAL, the X'...' hex form is BLOB, and NULL is NULL; the typeof() function returns the inferred class.
A single SQLite column can hold values of different storage classes in different rows.

When comparing or sorting mixed storage classes, SQLite orders by class first (NULL lowest, then INTEGER and REAL together compared numerically, then TEXT compared by collation, then BLOB compared by memcmp).
SQLite uses manifest typing: a column may declare a type, but the engine can also infer a type from each value, so declared column types are optional.

SQLite does not enforce strict type checking: a value of any storage class can be stored in a column regardless of the column's declared type, unlike databases such as Oracle that reject mismatched types.

Every SQLite column has one of four type affinities — NUMERIC, INTEGER, TEXT, or NONE — derived from its declared type, and the affinity (rather than a strict type) governs how values are stored in the column.

SQLite assigns column affinity by these rules: a declared type containing INT gets INTEGER affinity; one containing CHAR, CLOB, or TEXT (so VARCHAR too) gets TEXT affinity; one containing BLOB or no declared type gets NONE affinity; anything else, including an unrecognized type, defaults to NUMERIC affinity.

To store values exactly as given (each by its own storage class), declare the column with no type so it gets NONE affinity; beware that declaring an unrecognized type yields NUMERIC affinity rather than NONE.
condition: you want values stored exactly as provided without conversion

statement: A NUMERIC-affinity column can hold all five storage classes but biases toward numeric ones: a TEXT value is converted to INTEGER if possible, then to REAL, and only stored as TEXT if neither conversion works.
A NONE-affinity column stores every value in its given storage class without conversion, and no column ever converts NULL or BLOB values regardless of its affinity.

Type affinity never raises a constraint violation for an incompatible type the way strict typing does; SQLite always finds a storage type for any value, and a column's declared type only determines its affinity.
The CAST function manually converts a value or expression to a specified storage class.
To enforce a specific storage type in a column (since SQLite has no strict typing), combine a CHECK constraint with the typeof() function, for example CHECK(typeof(x) = 'integer').
condition: strict per-column type enforcement is required

statement: A transaction groups a set of SQL commands so they either all succeed together or none take effect, keeping the database consistent if a failure interrupts a multi-step operation.
BEGIN starts a transaction, COMMIT commits all work performed since the BEGIN, and ROLLBACK undoes all work performed since the BEGIN.
By default SQLite runs in autocommit mode: any command not wrapped in an explicit BEGIN..COMMIT/ROLLBACK is run in its own implicit transaction, committed on success and rolled back on error.

SQLite conflict resolution offers five policies for constraint violations — REPLACE, IGNORE, FAIL, ABORT, ROLLBACK — spanning a spectrum from most tolerant (REPLACE) to most severe (ROLLBACK); ABORT is the default and matches the SQL-standard behavior.

On a constraint violation: ABORT (default) undoes the command's changes and ends it but keeps the transaction; ROLLBACK aborts the entire transaction; FAIL stops at the violation but preserves changes already made; IGNORE leaves the offending row unchanged and continues; REPLACE deletes the conflicting row and inserts the new one.

Conflict resolution can be set per statement (INSERT OR policy / UPDATE OR policy) or in a table/index definition (ON CONFLICT), and a statement-level (DML) policy overrides an object-level (DDL) one.
The REPLACE conflict-resolution policy does not invoke DELETE triggers on the rows it removes to satisfy the constraint.
Prefer the IGNORE policy over FAIL when you want every processable row modified, because FAIL stops at the first violation and the order in which SQLite processes rows is nondeterministic.
condition: a multi-row operation may hit a constraint violation partway through

statement: SQLite escalates locks through five states — unlocked, shared, reserved, pending, exclusive; many sessions can hold shared (read) locks at once, only one reserved lock (intent to write) may exist, and promotion to an exclusive (write) lock requires all shared locks to be released first.

Under a reserved lock a session caches its changes in memory and only writes them to the database file once it promotes the lock to exclusive at commit time, which can return SQLITE_BUSY if readers are still active.

Two sessions that each begin with a plain deferred transaction and then try to upgrade a shared lock to write can deadlock, and the resulting pending lock blocks all other sessions from acquiring shared locks, locking everyone out of the database.

SQLite has three transaction types set in BEGIN: DEFERRED (the default, acquires no lock until needed), IMMEDIATE (takes a reserved lock immediately, blocking other writers), and EXCLUSIVE (takes an exclusive lock, blocking all other access).

When other connections also write to a database, every writer should start transactions with BEGIN IMMEDIATE or BEGIN EXCLUSIVE to serialize writers and avoid deadlocks; a plain BEGIN suffices only when no other connection writes to the database.
condition: multiple connections write to the same database
exception: a plain BEGIN is sufficient when no other connection writes

statement: A view is a stored relational expression (CREATE VIEW name AS sql) whose contents are generated dynamically each time it is used; use a view to name and reuse a frequently run query.
SQLite does not support true materialized (updatable) views, but an INSTEAD OF trigger on a view can map INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on the view to its underlying base tables to emulate one.

Without a usable index SQLite performs a sequential scan that runs in linear time proportional to the row count, whereas a matching index enables an index scan over a B-tree in logarithmic time, far faster on large tables.

Indexes cost storage (they copy the indexed columns) and slow down INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE because every index on the table must also be maintained, so add an index only when a specific, measured performance gain justifies the overhead.
A UNIQUE index enforces uniqueness over the combined values of all its columns, not over each column individually.

SQLite uses a single-column index for WHERE conditions that compare the column to an expression with one of the operators equals, greater-than, greater-or-equal, less-or-equal, or less-than, or that use the column with IN against a list or subquery.

A multicolumn index is used left-to-right: SQLite consumes leading columns constrained by equality or IN and stops at the first gap, and only the rightmost used index column may use an inequality (up to two, for an upper and lower bound).

A trigger runs SQL commands when an INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE event occurs on a table, firing either BEFORE or AFTER the event; an UPDATE trigger can be restricted to specific columns with UPDATE OF column.

Triggers expose the affected row as OLD (original values) and NEW (updated values) via dot notation, and a BEFORE trigger can call RAISE(resolution, message) to reject the event, which lets triggers implement custom integrity constraints.

Because this version of SQLite does not enforce foreign keys, they can be emulated with BEFORE INSERT and BEFORE UPDATE triggers on the child table that reject a missing referenced key, plus a BEFORE DELETE trigger on the parent table that rejects deletion while child rows still reference it.
condition: the SQLite version does not natively enforce foreign-key constraints

statement: ATTACH DATABASE file AS name makes another database file accessible within the current session (the primary database is named main and temporary objects live in temp); when object names collide across databases they must be qualified as name.object, and DETACH removes the attached database.

VACUUM reclaims unused space by rebuilding the database file but will not run while any transaction is open; the auto_vacuum pragma instead shrinks the file automatically when data is deleted (and VACUUM has no effect on an auto_vacuum database).
REINDEX rebuilds indexes — needed after changing the behavior of a user-defined collation, or to rebuild the indexes of a named table or a named index.
SQLite has no configuration file; all configuration is done through PRAGMA statements, some of which have a temporary (session-only) form and a permanent (stored, all-sessions) form.

The synchronous pragma trades durability for speed: FULL waits for data to reach the disk so a power or OS crash cannot corrupt the database; NORMAL pauses less often with a small corruption risk; OFF hands data to the OS without waiting (much faster) but a power loss or OS crash may corrupt the database, while an application crash alone stays safe.

Page size (512 to 32768 bytes in powers of two, default 1024), text encoding (default UTF-8, or UTF-16 little/big endian), and auto_vacuum must be set before any database object is created, because they cannot be changed afterward.
condition: must be set before the first database object is created

statement: The integrity_check pragma scans a database for corruption such as out-of-order or missing pages, malformed records, and corrupted indexes, returning ok when everything is in order.
Opening a database named :memory: (or an empty string) creates a RAM-only database that is private to the connection that created it and is discarded when that connection closes.

SQLite executes every command via a prepared query in three phases — prepare (compile the SQL into VDBE byte code), execute (step through the byte code, where each step of a SELECT returns one row with SQLITE_ROW until SQLITE_DONE), and finalize (free the statement's resources); wrapper functions bundle the three phases into a single call.

A connection always operates under exactly one transaction at a time, and all statements derived from the same connection share that one transaction context; to run statements in separate transactions you must use separate connections.

Use parameterized statements with positional (question-mark) or named (colon-prefixed) placeholders and bind values to them: SQLite escapes the bound values automatically, helping avoid syntax errors and SQL-injection attacks, and an unbound parameter defaults to NULL.

Reusing a prepared statement by resetting it and binding new values avoids recompiling the SQL (tokenizing, parsing, and code generation), which significantly speeds up repeated queries compared with finalizing and re-preparing.
condition: the same statement is executed many times

statement: The exec() wrapper runs SQL (typically non-SELECT or DDL) in one call and can process a string of several semicolon-delimited statements together, stopping at the first failure; the get_table() wrapper runs a query and returns the entire result set in memory.

Do not use get_table() for large result sets because it holds the whole result in memory; use a prepared query instead, which keeps only one record (its database page) in memory at a time and is better for traversing large results.
condition: the result set is large

statement: Wrapped queries (exec and get_table) cannot use parameterized SQL or access the column data and metadata available through a statement handle, so prepared queries are better for repetitive or metadata-dependent tasks.
Handle errors on nearly every API call; common codes include SQLITE_ERROR, SQLITE_BUSY, and SQLITE_SCHEMA, and the last error can be read with sqlite3_errcode() and described with sqlite3_errmsg().

A SQLITE_SCHEMA error means another connection changed the schema between preparing and executing a statement, invalidating it, so the statement must be recompiled; schema errors can occur only between prepare() and the first step(), after which the connection's lock prevents schema changes.

An application that builds SQL from unfiltered user input is vulnerable to SQL-injection, where crafted input injects extra statements (for example reading sqlite_master or dropping tables); guard against it with parameter binding or by escaping values (such as the %q and %Q substitutions of sqlite3_mprintf).
condition: SQL is constructed from user-supplied input

statement: SQLite exposes runtime hooks registered per connection — a commit hook, a rollback hook, and an update hook (for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE row changes); a non-zero return from the commit hook turns the commit into a rollback.

The authorizer callback (sqlite3_set_authorizer) provides compile-time, fine-grained access control over operations at the database, table, and column level, letting an application limit both access and modification.

User-defined functions, aggregates, and collations are stored in program memory, not in the database (unlike stored procedures), so a program must re-register them on every connection that intends to use them.

A user-defined aggregate is implemented with a step function called for each record (accumulating an intermediate value in a context) and a finalize function called after the last record to compute the final aggregate value and clean up.

User-defined collations (sqlite3_create_collation) let you define custom text comparison and sort methods for locales or data (such as date formats) not well served by the default BINARY, NOCASE, or REVERSE collations.

A lock's duration shadows its transaction's: a lock is not released until the transaction concludes (or the program crashes), and in autocommit mode step() and finalize() act as the transaction and lock boundaries.

A read transaction moves UNLOCKED to SHARED and back, while a write transaction proceeds SHARED to RESERVED to PENDING to EXCLUSIVE; multiple readers and one writer coexist because the writer does its work in RESERVED using an in-memory page cache and enters EXCLUSIVE only to flush at commit.

Only one connection can hold a RESERVED or EXCLUSIVE lock at a time, and PENDING is a gateway lock: while a writer holds it waiting for EXCLUSIVE, no new connection can reach SHARED, so no new readers or writers may enter the database.

Do as much work as possible in the RESERVED state (its capacity set by the cache_size pragma) so the EXCLUSIVE lock is held only long enough to flush pages to disk; a page cache too small to hold the changes forces early entry into EXCLUSIVE and reduces concurrency.
condition: concurrency matters and the transaction modifies many pages

statement: Run interdependent writes inside one explicit BEGIN..COMMIT transaction rather than in autocommit, because autocommit adds rollback-journal overhead per command and lets another connection modify the database between your commands.
condition: multiple writes depend on each other or on specific database values

statement: The rollback journal stores original copies of modified pages so the pager can restore the database on rollback or crash; a hot journal (a journal present without a RESERVED lock) indicates a crashed transaction and triggers recovery by the next connection to open the database.

When SQLite cannot obtain a lock it returns SQLITE_BUSY; you can register a busy handler (returning true to keep retrying or false to surface SQLITE_BUSY) or use sqlite3_busy_timeout() to sleep for a fixed period before giving up.

For a write, do not brute-force retry step() on SQLITE_BUSY in autocommit mode, because the database state is indeterminate and you may deadlock against a connection holding RESERVED; begin the write with BEGIN IMMEDIATE (or BEGIN EXCLUSIVE) so you know your lock state and can retry safely.
condition: a write operation returns SQLITE_BUSY

statement: Do not read and write the same table at the same time, even from a single connection: an open SELECT places a B-tree cursor on the table, so any statement that tries to modify it returns SQLITE_BUSY; instead read the rows fully into memory or a temporary table and then perform the writes.

A SELECT statement's SHARED lock and cursor are released only when the statement reaches the end of its result set (the final step returns SQLITE_DONE) or is finalized, so always finalize a SELECT before writing to the database with another connection.

Temporary tables are maintained outside the main database file, so writing to one needs no RESERVED or EXCLUSIVE lock; staging work in a temporary table lets a reader and writer operate concurrently and minimizes how long write locks are held on the real database.

Rebuilding a table by dropping it and re-creating it with CREATE TABLE AS SELECT from a temporary copy loses the original table's integrity constraints and indexes; preserve them by instead deleting the rows and inserting the staged data back into the original table.

Shared cache mode lets multiple connections within one thread share a page cache (lowering memory use) and allows multiple readers plus one writer on the same database; such connections cannot cross threads, table reads and writes take table locks (returning SQLITE_LOCKED on conflict), and the read_uncommitted pragma lets readers skip read locks at the risk of inconsistent results.

sqlite3_finalize closes a statement, frees its resources, and (in autocommit mode) commits or rolls back the implicit transaction and releases the lock; sqlite3_reset instead keeps the compiled statement and its bound parameters for reuse (avoiding recompilation) while committing the current statement's changes.

Unlike exec(), which runs every statement in a multi-statement string, sqlite3_prepare() compiles only the first statement and returns a tail pointer to the next, so a batch is processed by looping with the tail (optionally testing each with sqlite3_complete).

sqlite3_column_decltype returns a result column's declared schema type, but returns NULL when the column is produced by a literal, expression, function, or aggregate rather than an actual table column.

The sqlite3_column_xxx getters coerce the stored value to the requested type by fixed conversion rules (for example NULL becomes 0 or a null pointer, and TEXT to INTEGER uses atoi); to copy a BLOB or TEXT value, first get its length with sqlite3_column_bytes.
Bound parameters remain bound for the lifetime of a statement handle, persisting across a call to sqlite3_reset, and are freed only when the statement is finalized.

When binding TEXT or BLOB array values, the cleanup argument matters: SQLITE_STATIC tells SQLite the memory is stable and must not be copied or freed, while SQLITE_TRANSIENT tells SQLite to make its own private copy (freed at finalize) because the buffer may change.

SQL parameters can be positional (a bare question mark, numbered sequentially from 1), explicitly numbered (a question mark plus a number in the range 1 to 999, letting one bound value fill several places), or named (a colon-prefixed name resolved to its number via sqlite3_bind_parameter_index).

An INTEGER PRIMARY KEY column is the one column where SQLite enforces the declared type: inserting non-integer data into it yields a SQLITE_MISMATCH error, whereas most columns accept any type of data.

SQLITE_MISUSE indicates the library was used incorrectly, for example calling sqlite3_exec after the database was closed, or using the same database connection pointer simultaneously from two separate threads.

A busy handler must not close the database (doing so can crash the program), and SQLite deliberately will not invoke your busy handler when your SHARED-lock connection is blocking another connection in RESERVED, signalling that you should finalize or reset and restart the write with BEGIN IMMEDIATE.

On a schema change sqlite3_step never returns SQLITE_SCHEMA directly — it returns SQLITE_ERROR; detect the schema change by calling sqlite3_finalize, sqlite3_reset (cheaper, keeps the statement runnable), or sqlite3_expired, then recompile; schema changes are caused by detaching databases, modifying user-defined functions/aggregates/collations or the authorizer, and VACUUM.

The update hook is not invoked for operations on system tables such as sqlite_master and sqlite_sequence, and the rollback hook is not invoked when a transaction is automatically rolled back because the connection is being closed.

The authorizer callback runs at statement compile time and returns SQLITE_OK, SQLITE_DENY, or SQLITE_IGNORE per event: DENY aborts the whole statement with an error, while IGNORE on a column makes reads of it return NULL and updates to it silently fail — letting an application safely run user-supplied SQL with restricted table or column access.

sqlite3_interrupt aborts the current operation on a connection at the earliest opportunity (for a Cancel button or Ctrl+C), and a progress handler installed with sqlite3_progress_handler is called every N VDBE instructions during long queries; returning non-zero from it terminates the query and rolls back its changes, returning SQLITE_ABORT.

For multithreaded use, compile SQLite with thread support; a connection from version 3.3.1 onward may be passed between threads only while it is UNLOCKED (no transaction open), and a connection must never be passed across a fork() call to a child process.
condition: SQLite is used across multiple threads or processes

statement: User-defined functions, aggregates, and collations live in the program, not the database, so a trigger stored in the database that references a user-defined function will error or do nothing when invoked on a connection (such as the shell) that has not registered that function.

An aggregate keeps per-instance state through sqlite3_aggregate_context, which allocates and zeroes a buffer on first use, returns the same buffer on later calls for that instance, and frees it automatically at finalize, whereas a plain function's user-data is shared across all its calls.
A user-defined function signals an error by calling sqlite3_result_error with a message, which aborts the SQL command that called the function and surfaces the message as the error.

sqlite3_result_value returns a function argument unchanged in its original storage class, and because every storage class (even a BLOB) has a text representation, a function argument can always be retrieved in text form regardless of its internal type.

You can enforce strict typing on a column — even for types SQLite does not natively recognize — by writing a validation user-defined function and BEFORE INSERT and UPDATE triggers that call RAISE(ABORT) when the value fails validation.
condition: strict per-column type enforcement is required and a host language or the C API is available

statement: A validating BEFORE INSERT trigger assumes every INSERT supplies the validated column, so give that column a DEFAULT to cover INSERTs that omit it; note that UPDATE triggers (unlike INSERT triggers) can be defined on a specific column and so avoid this issue.
condition: a BEFORE INSERT trigger validates a particular column

statement: A custom collation is a comparison function that returns negative, zero, or positive when the first string is less than, equal to, or greater than the second; collation governs only the comparison and ordering of TEXT values, since SQLite orders other storage classes by class and by numeric or binary value.
A collation is applied by attaching it to a column or index definition with COLLATE, or by specifying it per query (for example ORDER BY column COLLATE NOCASE).
sqlite3_collation_needed defers collation registration: you supply a callback that SQLite invokes with the name of an unrecognized collation so the application can register it on demand.

ISO-format dates sort identically in lexicographic and chronological order, so they work directly with ORDER BY in SQLite, whereas formats like Oracle's DD-MON-YY do not and require a custom collation that parses the date and compares its parts numerically.

When choosing a SQLite language extension, weigh license compatibility, how it maps SQLite storage classes to native types, which of the three query methods it supports, its coverage of API features such as tracing and authorization, and how it links to and lets you upgrade SQLite.
condition: selecting a language binding for SQLite

statement: Language extensions share a common anatomy — a connection object (wrapping a sqlite3 handle) and a cursor or statement object (wrapping a sqlite3_stmt handle) — and the same transaction and locking rules as the C API apply to them.

PySQLite does not run in SQLite's default autocommit mode: it implicitly issues BEGIN before an INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or REPLACE and COMMIT before other commands, so changes are rolled back on close unless you call commit(); it also disallows ON CONFLICT ROLLBACK, and you restore true autocommit by setting isolation_level to None on the connection.
condition: using the PySQLite Python extension

statement: The Tcl extension's transaction method runs a script and automatically commits if it succeeds or rolls back if it errors, and nests safely within an already-open transaction, giving cleaner code than manual BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK with per-command error checks.

Because a SQLite database is an ordinary operating-system file, placing it inside a web server's public directory can let anyone fetch it like a document; keep database files outside public folders and ensure the web-server process running the application has read and write access.
condition: SQLite is used from a web application

statement: SQLite executes a statement as a VDBE bytecode program of opcodes (each with operands P1, P2, P3); the opcode set changes across SQLite versions, so unlike the stable C API you must not generate your own VDBE bytecode and run it across different versions.
Prefixing a SQL command with EXPLAIN lists the VDBE bytecode program SQLite would run for it, which can be used to understand and optimize how a query executes.

SQLite records a schema version (cookie) in the database file and stores in each compiled statement the version it was compiled under; at execution the VerifyCookie step compares them, and a mismatch invalidates the statement and raises a SQLITE_SCHEMA error so the application must recompile it.

SQLite's B-tree gives O(log N) lookup, insert, and delete and O(1) bidirectional record traversal, is self-balancing, and automatically handles defragmentation and space reclamation; it has no notion of disk I/O and delegates all reading and writing of pages to the pager.

A value too large for one page (such as a large BLOB) spills onto a linked list of overflow pages, which becomes inefficient for very large BLOBs; for such data consider storing the BLOB in an external file and keeping only the filename in the row.
condition: storing very large BLOB values

statement: The ANALYZE command gathers statistics about indexes and stores them in the sqlite_stat1 table so the query optimizer can make better index choices.

ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN appends a new column and runs in constant time regardless of table size, but the new column may not have a PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint nor a CURRENT_TIME/CURRENT_DATE/CURRENT_TIMESTAMP default, and a NOT NULL column must be given a non-NULL default value.

A transaction spanning multiple attached databases is atomic only when the main database is not an in-memory (:memory:) database; with an in-memory main database, a host crash mid-COMMIT can leave some attached database files updated and others not.
condition: a transaction updates multiple attached database files

statement: DELETE without a WHERE clause removes every row of the table, and SQLite implements a bare DELETE FROM table by dropping and recreating the table for speed, so the reported change count is 0; use DELETE FROM table WHERE 1 to get the actual deleted-row count.
DROP TABLE, DROP INDEX, and DELETE do not shrink the database file in the default mode — the freed space is retained for later inserts; reclaim it with the VACUUM command or by enabling auto_vacuum.

The LIKE operator is case-insensitive only for 7-bit ASCII letters, so accented or other 8-bit characters are matched case-sensitively; GLOB uses Unix file-globbing wildcards and is case-sensitive, and the case_sensitive_like pragma makes LIKE case-sensitive.

A SELECT used as a scalar expression yields the first row's first column (any later rows are ignored) or NULL if it returns no rows, while EXISTS(subquery) is true if and only if the subquery returns at least one row.
An uncorrelated subquery (one that does not reference the outer query) is evaluated once and its result reused, whereas a correlated subquery is re-evaluated every time it is needed.
An unknown PRAGMA produces no error and is silently ignored, so a misspelled pragma name fails silently with no warning; the set of available pragmas may also change between SQLite releases.

By default INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE return no rows; sqlite3_changes() (or the count_changes pragma) reports the rows affected by the most recent such statement excluding any changes made by triggers, while sqlite3_total_changes() includes trigger-caused changes.

In a compound SELECT each ORDER BY term must exactly match one of the result columns, and a single ORDER BY and LIMIT at the end apply to the whole combined result; in a simple SELECT, by contrast, an ORDER BY term may be any expression and need not appear in the result.
In an UPDATE statement all right-hand-side assignment expressions are evaluated before any column is assigned, so each expression sees the row's pre-update values.

sum() over no non-NULL rows returns NULL (as the SQL standard requires) whereas the nonstandard total() returns 0.0 and always returns a floating-point value; an aggregate's single argument may be prefixed with DISTINCT to aggregate only distinct values (for example count(distinct X)).
sqlite3_open returns a database handle even when opening fails, and the handle must be released by passing it to sqlite3_close() whether or not the open succeeded, to avoid leaking resources.
All prepared statements must be finalized before calling sqlite3_close(); otherwise sqlite3_close() fails and returns SQLITE_BUSY.

sqlite3_step returns SQLITE_ROW when a row is ready, SQLITE_DONE when finished (after which the statement must be reset before being stepped again), SQLITE_BUSY when it should be retried, SQLITE_ERROR on a run-time error (do not step again), and SQLITE_MISUSE when called on a finalized statement or when one connection is used by two threads at once.

When embedding a text value into a SQL string literal with sqlite3_mprintf, use the %q substitution rather than %s, because %q doubles every single quote to escape it and so avoids syntax errors and SQL-injection.
condition: building a SQL string literal from a text value

statement: Shared-cache mode must be enabled or disabled only when no database connections are active in the thread (doing otherwise causes memory corruption), and because it uses thread-local storage a shared-cache connection's open, prepare, step, reset, finalize, and close must all run in the same thread.
condition: using shared-cache mode

statement: Database choice is a long-term decision whose later reversal can require an expensive migration and substantial application-code changes; validate fit before committing.
Comparing databases only by their components, popularity rank, or implementation language yields invalid or premature conclusions and is useful only for coarse high-level screening.
Every database comparison should begin by clearly defining the goal, because even slight bias can invalidate the whole investigation.
To select a database, simulate your own anticipated workloads against the candidates and measure the performance metrics that matter to you.
Run long-running tests in an environment that mirrors production, because performance and scalability problems often surface only over time or as capacity grows.
condition: detecting performance/scalability problems that appear only at scale or over time

statement: When choosing a database, durability outranks raw speed: prefer a system that saves data slowly over one that loses it quickly.
Before benchmarking a database, enumerate the workload variables — schema and record sizes, number of clients, query types and access patterns, read/write rates, and expected growth.
The absence of a standard stress/benchmark tool in a database's ecosystem may be a red flag.
Use generic benchmarks such as YCSB with caution and tailor them to real-world conditions, or risk drawing wrong conclusions.
TPC-C is an OLTP benchmark whose primary indicator is throughput (transactions per minute) and which requires executed transactions to preserve ACID properties.
Track new database releases, understand exactly what changed and why, and test new versions before rollout, because releases fix bugs but can introduce regressions or new bugs.
A history of complicated database upgrades may signal that future upgrades will also be hard, though smooth past upgrades do not guarantee smooth future ones.
No storage engine is optimal for every use case; choose one based on the target workload because every design embeds trade-offs.
Storage engines are optimized for different goals — low read latency, low write latency, storage density, or operational simplicity — and no single one maximizes all.
A DBMS is composed of transport, query processor, query optimizer, execution engine, and storage engine subsystems.
The query optimizer eliminates impossible and redundant query parts and chooses the most efficient execution plan using internal statistics (e.g., index cardinality) and data placement.
The storage engine's components are the transaction manager, lock manager, access methods, buffer manager, and recovery manager; transaction and lock managers together provide concurrency control.
Memory access is several orders of magnitude faster than disk access.
The main factors limiting in-memory database growth are RAM volatility (lack of durability) and cost.
An in-memory database is not equivalent to a disk-based database with a large page cache, because serialization and on-disk layout overhead prevent the optimizations an in-memory store can make.
Before an operation is considered complete, its result must be written to a sequential write-ahead log to provide durability.
Checkpointing applies batched log records to the on-disk backup so that log entries up to the snapshot can be discarded, which reduces recovery time.
Because disk is accessed block-wise and a row-store block holds all columns, queries that read only a few fields across many records pay to page in unwanted column data.
A column-oriented layout stores each column contiguously, letting column queries read in a single pass and improving cache utilization and compression ratio.

Choose row- versus column-oriented layout by access pattern: records consumed whole with point/range queries favour row-oriented; scans spanning many rows or aggregates over a subset of columns favour column-oriented.
Wide-column stores (e.g., BigTable, HBase) are not column-oriented stores: they group columns into column families stored row-wise and are best for access by a key or sequence of keys.
Most modern storage systems do not delete records in place; they write deletion markers (tombstones) and reclaim the shadowed space later during garbage collection.
Index-organized tables store data records inside the index in key order, saving at least one disk seek per lookup and enabling range scans by sequential traversal.
Primary indexes are most often clustered (data order follows key order), while secondary indexes are nonclustered by definition and may hold several entries per search key.

Referencing data records directly by file offset reduces disk seeks but forces pointer updates whenever a record is moved, whereas primary-key indirection reduces pointer-update cost at the expense of an extra read-path lookup.
Use direct-offset references for read-mostly workloads, but prefer primary-key indirection for write-heavy workloads with multiple indexes to avoid costly pointer updates.
condition: write-heavy workload with multiple secondary indexes

statement: Storage structures differ along three axes — buffering or not, immutable or mutable files, and ordered or unordered storage — and these explain most storage-engine distinctions.
Storing data records in key order enables efficient range scans, whereas storing them out of order (insertion order) enables write-time optimizations.
Binary search trees are impractical as on-disk structures: their low fanout forces frequent balancing, node relocation, and pointer updates, and random insertion order gives poor locality.
An on-disk tree structure should have high fanout (to improve locality of neighbouring keys) and low height (to reduce seeks); fanout and height are inversely correlated.
On spinning disks, seeks dominate the cost of random reads because they require disk rotation and head movement, while reading/writing contiguous bytes (sequential I/O) is relatively cheap.
Because the smallest unit of disk access is a block, reading a single word pages in the whole block; disk-resident data structures must be designed around this block constraint.
On SSDs the smallest readable/writable unit is a page, but the smallest erasable unit is a block (erase block), and pages in an empty block must be written sequentially.
SSD garbage collection can degrade write performance, especially under random and unaligned writes; writing only full blocks and combining writes to the same block reduces required I/O operations.
B-Trees suit disk storage because high fanout plus low height plus infrequent balancing let a lookup make roughly one disk seek per tree level.

In B+-Trees values are stored only in leaf nodes and internal nodes hold only separator keys, so insert/update/delete/retrieve operations touch leaves and propagate upward only during splits and merges.
B-Trees reserve space for future inserts, so storage utilization can fall as low as 50%; higher occupancy does not hurt B-Tree performance.
B-Tree lookup cost is logarithmic from two perspectives: base-N (keys per node) in block transfers, equal to tree height, and base-2 in comparisons via in-node binary search.

A B-Tree node split on overflow allocates a new node, moves half the elements to it, and promotes the split-point key to the parent; splits can propagate to the root, and tree height grows only when the root is split (or two nodes merge into a new root).

On-disk structures should optimize for fewer disk accesses by improving locality, compacting the internal representation, and minimizing out-of-page pointers; keep the number and span of pointers minimal because long dependency chains increase complexity.
When encoding multibyte numeric values, use the same byte order (endianness) for both encoding and decoding.
With a fixed schema, store positional field identifiers instead of repeating field names to reduce data stored on disk.

The slotted-page layout stores cells from one side of the page and their offset pointers from the other, which lets it store variable-size records with minimal overhead, reclaim freed space, and reference records by ID regardless of their exact location.
In a slotted page, cells are kept in insertion order while offset pointers are sorted in key order, enabling binary search over keys without relocating cells on insert/update/delete.

Deleting a record in a page should mark the cell deleted and record its offset and size in an in-memory availability list for reuse, defragmenting the page when contiguous space is insufficient and allocating an overflow page only if defragmentation still does not free enough room.
Free-space fit can use first-fit (faster but may waste the leftover remainder) or best-fit (chooses the segment leaving the smallest remainder).

A storage engine must usually support more than one serialization format for backward compatibility and therefore must record each file's version, e.g., via a filename prefix, a separate version file, or a magic number in the header.
Checksums and CRCs detect accidental data corruption but not tampering; use strong cryptographic hashes when you must verify data has not been intentionally altered.

CRCs detect burst (multibit) errors that weak checksums miss, and computing a checksum per page (stored in the page header) is preferred over per-file so corruption is contained to a single page rather than discarding the whole file.
Verify a page's checksum on read and, on any mismatch, treat the data as corrupt and do not use it.
Placing a magic number in a file or page header provides a cheap validation and sanity check, since a random byte sequence is very unlikely to match it.
Sibling links let a node reach its neighbours without ascending to the parent, but they must be updated during splits and merges and may require additional locking.

Overflow pages let a B-Tree node store up to a fixed max_payload_size (node size divided by fanout) inline and spill the remainder to linked overflow pages, so a fixed-size page never runs out of room for an oversize value.
If data records are consistently oversize, consider specialized blob storage for the large values rather than spilling them across overflow pages.
condition: data records are consistently larger than the node payload limit

statement: Binary search works only on sorted data, so maintaining the sorted-key invariant inside B-Tree nodes is essential for correct lookups.
Breadcrumbs — a stack of the nodes traversed from root to leaf, kept in memory — let an implementation backtrack to propagate splits and merges without persisting parent pointers on disk.
Rebalancing postpones splits and merges by moving elements between sibling nodes, improving node occupancy and potentially reducing tree height at the cost of extra maintenance logic.

Right-only-append optimizations apply when primary keys are monotonically increasing and the update/delete ratio is low: splits concentrate on the rightmost node and the read path can be skipped (PostgreSQL fastpath, SQLite quickbalance).
condition: monotonically increasing primary keys with a low ratio of updates/deletes

statement: Bulk-loading presorted data lets a B-Tree be built bottom-up by appending only at the rightmost position, avoiding splits and merges and keeping only a minimal slice of the tree in memory.
condition: data is presorted before loading

statement: Immutable B-Trees can fill pages completely because no in-place modification space is reserved, giving better occupancy and performance than mutable B-Trees.
Compression trades access speed against compression ratio and RAM/CPU cost: higher ratios fetch more data per access but consume more memory and CPU to compress and decompress.

Prefer page-wise compression over whole-file compression: pages compress and decompress independently and couple with page load/flush, whereas whole-file compression must be recompressed on every update and makes locating a single page hard.
When picking a compression library, evaluate four metrics: memory overhead, compression performance, decompression performance, and compression ratio.
Run space-reclamation maintenance (compaction/vacuum) as an asynchronous background process so cleanup cost is not paid during user-facing inserts, updates, and deletes.
A page can have enough logical free space yet lack a contiguous block large enough for a new cell (fragmentation), in which case the page must be rewritten to defragment it.
On the leaf level a delete only trims the cell offset, leaving the cell bytes in place but unaddressable until overwritten or garbage-collected.
Track freed on-disk page IDs in a persisted free page list (freelist) so free space survives crashes and restarts and is not leaked.
A transaction is an indivisible logical unit of work that must preserve atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability (ACID).
Atomicity means all of a transaction's steps succeed or none do: commit makes all writes visible and is final, while abort rolls back side effects and the transaction may be retried.
Consistency is the only ACID property controlled by the application rather than the database alone, and is the most weakly defined.
Isolation defines when and which of a transaction's changes become visible to concurrent transactions, and many databases deliberately use levels weaker than full isolation for performance.
All changes to database state are applied to cached (page-cache) pages first, and unflushed cached contents are lost on a crash.
A modified cached page is dirty and must be flushed before eviction, whereas an in-sync, unpinned, unreferenced page can be evicted immediately.
Checkpointing coordinates the WAL and page cache: a log record may be discarded only after the page it describes has been flushed, and dirty pages cannot be evicted until the checkpoint completes.
Pin the pages most likely to be reused — especially the upper B-Tree levels near the root — so that part of the tree stays resident and queries only hit disk for the uncached lower levels.

Bélády's anomaly shows that enlarging the page cache can increase the number of evictions when the page-replacement algorithm is not optimal, so the replacement algorithm matters more than raw cache size.

FIFO page replacement is impractical because it evicts the earliest-loaded pages (often the root and topmost levels) that are most likely to be needed again; LRU improves on this but its per-access relinking is costly under concurrency.
CLOCK-sweep is a compact, cache-friendly, concurrency-friendly approximation of LRU whose hand and access bits can be updated with compare-and-swap without extra locking.
Frequency-based eviction (LFU/TinyLFU) orders pages by usage frequency rather than recency and can outperform LRU under heavy load, where recency alone is weakly predictive.
The write-ahead-log rule requires every operation that modifies database state to be logged on disk before the contents of the affected pages are modified.
A transaction cannot be considered committed until the log is forced (durably flushed) up to the LSN of its commit record, and log records must be flushed in LSN order.
Log trimming must stay in lockstep with confirming data reached primary storage, because even slight disagreement between the two can cause data loss.

Most systems use fuzzy checkpoints (asynchronous flush bracketed by begin/end checkpoint records, with recovery resuming from the last completed one) rather than sync checkpoints that pause all operations to flush everything.
Combine physical logging for redo (faster recovery, since changes install quickly) with logical logging for undo (better concurrency, since logical undos apply to pages independently).

Steal vs no-steal governs whether uncommitted pages may be flushed, and force vs no-force governs whether all modified pages must be flushed before commit; these page-cache policies determine which recovery scheme is possible.
A no-steal policy permits redo-only recovery, no-force lets updates be deferred and buffered (needing a larger cache), and force removes redo work at recovery but lengthens commits with extra I/O.
A transaction cannot commit until enough undo or redo information has been written to the log to either roll it back or reapply it after a crash.
ARIES is a steal/no-force algorithm that uses physical redo, logical undo, repeating history, and compensation log records, recovering in three phases: analysis, redo, then undo.

On Linux, fsync clears the dirty flag even from pages that failed to flush and reports errors only to file descriptors open at the time of failure, so a checkpointer that does not hold files open can miss I/O errors and silently lose or corrupt data.
Concurrency control falls into three families: optimistic (OCC), multiversion (MVCC), and pessimistic (PCC).

Optimistic concurrency control assumes conflicts are rare and, instead of locking, validates each transaction's read and write sets for serializability before committing, aborting and retrying on conflict; it is efficient only when validation usually succeeds because retries are costly.
Multiversion concurrency control keeps multiple timestamped record versions so reads can proceed on older committed values with minimal coordination, and is a common basis for snapshot isolation.
A schedule is serializable if it is equivalent to some serial execution of the same transactions, producing the same result as running them one after another in some order.
Concurrent execution can produce read anomalies — dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, and phantom reads — and write anomalies — lost update, dirty write, and write skew.

Isolation levels strengthen in order: read uncommitted (allows dirty reads), read committed (no dirty reads), repeatable read (also no nonrepeatable reads), and serializable (strongest); stronger isolation costs coordination and performance.

Snapshot isolation reads a fixed snapshot of all transactions committed before it started and commits only if its modified values were not changed meanwhile, which precludes lost updates but still permits write skew.
exception: write skew can still occur because independent records each preserving local invariants may jointly violate a cross-record invariant

statement: Under timestamp ordering (Thomas Write Rule), a read of a value with timestamp below max_write_timestamp aborts, a write below max_read_timestamp aborts, but a write below max_write_timestamp is safely ignored, and aborted transactions must restart with a new timestamp.
Two-phase locking has a growing phase that only acquires locks and a shrinking phase that only releases them, so once a transaction releases any lock it can acquire no more.
Two-phase locking (a concurrency-control mechanism for serializability) is entirely different from two-phase commit (a protocol for distributed multipartition transactions) despite the similar name.

Deadlocks (cyclic lock waits) are handled by timeouts, by conservative 2PL that acquires all locks up front, or by a transaction manager that detects them via cycles in a waits-for graph and aborts one transaction (usually the most recent).

Deadlock-avoidance schemes use transaction timestamps as priority: wait-die lets a transaction block only on a higher-timestamp holder, and wound-wait lets it block only on a lower-timestamp holder, aborting otherwise.

Locks and latches are distinct: locks guard logical data integrity, are taken on keys, held for the whole transaction, and managed by the lock manager, whereas latches guard the physical page/tree representation, are taken on pages, and held only briefly.
Hold a latch for the smallest possible duration — only while a page is being read or updated — to maximize concurrency.
