Latch crabbing releases the parent latch as soon as the child is known safe (after the child is latched on reads, when the child is not full on inserts, when the child will not merge on deletes), which is optimistic because structural changes are rare and grow rarer toward the root.
The B-Tree root can always be latched optimistically because it is the last node to split, so the cost of a retry (pointer chasing) is seldom paid.

Blink-Trees add high keys and sibling links so a writer need not hold the parent lock during a split: a new node is reached via its sibling link and the parent pointer is updated lazily, allowing reads concurrent with structural changes and preventing deadlocks from upward-ascending modifications.

Copy-on-write B-Trees modify copied pages into a parallel hierarchy and atomically flip the top pointer, so readers need no latching and never block writers and a crash cannot leave a corrupted page, at the cost of extra space and CPU to copy pages.

LMDB uses copy-on-write over a single-level memory map and therefore needs no page cache, write-ahead log, checkpointing, or compaction, keeping only two root versions and serving lockless readers from an inherently multiversioned structure.

Lazy B-Trees buffer node updates in lightweight in-memory structures and propagate them with a delay, reducing I/O from repeated writes to the same node (e.g., WiredTiger merges a skiplist update buffer on read and reconciles it on flush via a background thread).
Buffering converts many small random writes into one larger write, which matters because random writes are slow on HDDs (head positioning) and on SSDs incur an extra garbage-collection penalty.
FD-Trees confine random write I/O to a small mutable head tree and otherwise use append-only immutable sorted runs that merge from upper to lower levels, avoiding in-place random node updates.

The original in-place-update B-Tree has three weaknesses: write amplification from page rewrites, space amplification from space reserved for future writes, and complexity in latch-based concurrency control.

Fractional cascading speeds search across a cascade of sorted runs by pulling every Nth element up a level and bridging it, so after a full search on the top run each lower run is searched starting from the nearest known match.

A Bw-Tree stores a base node plus an append-only chain of delta nodes addressed through an in-memory mapping table and installs updates with compare-and-swap, making it latch-free and free of reserved space at the cost of traversing and applying the delta chain on every read.
Consolidate a Bw-Tree node's delta chain once it exceeds a configurable length, because reads get more expensive as the chain grows.
Latch-free structures like the Bw-Tree require any thread that encounters an incomplete multi-step structure-modification operation to cooperatively finish it before proceeding.
Cache-oblivious structures give asymptotically optimal transfer counts regardless of cache-line, block, or page sizes, removing the need to tune those parameters per platform.

In-place-update storage is read-optimized (after locating data it can be returned) at the expense of writes, while append-only storage is write-optimized (writes need not locate records) at the expense of reads, which must retrieve and reconcile multiple versions.

Immutable storage gives higher density and prevents fragmentation because no per-record space is reserved and records are laid out sequentially, whereas mutable B-Tree reads, writes, and maintenance are mostly random I/O.

LSM Trees buffer writes in a memory-resident table and append immutable files, converting writes to sequential I/O; the files are merged over time (merge-sort style) during compaction and reconciled during reads.
LSM Trees are particularly well suited to workloads where writes are far more common than reads, because writes never have to locate records on disk.
condition: write-heavy workload (writes far exceed reads)

statement: Because LSM reads and writes do not intersect by design, on-disk data needs no segment locking, which significantly simplifies concurrent access compared with the hierarchical locks/latches of mutable structures.

An LSM memtable is mutable and serves reads and writes in memory, is flushed at a size threshold, and must be backed by a write-ahead log (append and commit in memory before acknowledging the client) to guarantee durability.
Switching the memtable must be atomic: new writes go to the fresh memtable while the flushing memtable stays readable until fully flushed, after which the corresponding WAL segment can be trimmed.
LSM deletes must be recorded explicitly as tombstones, because simply removing a key from the memtable would resurrect an older value still held in a disk-resident table.
Range (predicate) tombstones delete a range of keys at once, but their resolution must account for overlapping ranges and table boundaries.
LSM merge-iteration uses a multiway merge-sort driven by a min-heap priority queue holding one head per iterator, giving O(N) memory in the number of iterators and O(log N) per step.
When the same key appears from multiple LSM sources, reconciliation keeps the record with the highest timestamp and discards the shadowed (older) ones, returning or writing only the winner.
In LSM Trees inserts and updates are indistinguishable upserts, since neither locates the previously associated value before writing.

Compaction must keep the tables being compacted readable until the new table is fully written and swapped in atomically, so enough free disk space for the compacted output must be available during compaction.

Tombstones must be retained through compaction until the engine is certain no older record for the same key exists in any other table (e.g., RocksDB keeps them to the bottommost level, Cassandra to the GC grace period), otherwise deleted data can be resurrected.

Leveled compaction keeps non-overlapping key ranges on level 1 and above with exponentially growing per-level sizes, so the freshest data sits at the lowest index and a read can filter out tables whose key range excludes the searched key.
Size-tiered compaction groups tables by size and can suffer table starvation, where higher levels accumulate untriggered tombstones and raise read cost unless compaction is forced.
Time-window compaction suits time-series workloads with TTLs because it can drop whole files covering an expired time range without compacting their contents.
condition: time-series workload with per-record time-to-live

statement: Immutable on-disk storage faces three amplifications: read (addressing multiple tables), write (continuous compaction rewrites), and space (redundant same-key records).
Compaction strategy is a trade-off: aggressively reclaiming space raises write amplification through continual rewrites, while deferring rewrites raises read and space amplification.

Comparing B-Tree and LSM write amplification directly is misleading unless the source is understood: in B-Trees it comes from write-back and repeated same-node updates, in LSM Trees from migrating data between files during compaction.
The RUM Conjecture holds that Read, Update, and Memory overheads trade off so that reducing any two worsens the third, so a storage engine can be characterized by which two it optimizes.

Under the RUM model B-Trees are read-optimized and LSM Trees are write-optimized; the model is only a first approximation because it ignores latency, access patterns, implementation/maintenance complexity, hardware specifics, and distributed concerns.

An SSTable is a sorted, immutable pair of index and data files written sequentially; even a hashtable index still permits range scans because it only locates the first key and the data file is then read sequentially.
During compaction SSTable data files can be read sequentially without consulting the index, since records are already in key order and merge-iteration preserves order.

A Bloom filter is a space-efficient probabilistic set-membership structure that yields false positives but never false negatives, so an LSM read can skip every table whose filter says the key is definitely absent.

A Bloom filter's false-positive rate is tuned by bit-array size and number of hash functions (larger/more reduce collisions but cost memory and CPU), and because LSM tables are immutable their key count is known up front so the filter can be sized precisely.

A skiplist keeps sorted data using probabilistic balancing with no rotation or relocation and complexity near a search tree, but is less cache-friendly than an in-memory B-Tree because its small nodes are randomly allocated.
Probabilistic data structures (Bloom filter for membership, HyperLogLog for cardinality, Count-Min sketch for frequency) trade exact answers for far smaller space.

In LSM storage, immutable in-memory contents need no locks or latches, and reference counting keeps in-use pages from eviction and ensures in-flight reads finish before compaction removes the underlying files.
Page-wise compression produces pages smaller than and unaligned to disk blocks, so an indirection layer mapping uncompressed offsets to compressed offsets and sizes is needed to address them.

Bitcask is an unordered log-structured engine that appends records directly to logfiles (no memtable) and keeps an in-memory keydir of the latest record per key, giving excellent point-query performance but no range scans and requiring all keys to fit in memory and be rebuilt from logfiles on startup.

WiscKey keeps keys sorted in an LSM Tree and values in unordered append-only value logs so that compacting the small keys is efficient, which suits low update/delete rates; range scans then require random I/O mitigated by SSD parallelism.
condition: low rate of updates and deletes

statement: WAL truncation in an LSM Tree must be coordinated with memtable flushes, because discarding a log segment before its memtable is flushed loses that data if the node crashes.
Continuing to write to an already-switched memtable risks data loss, and failing to keep the old memtable readable until its disk table is ready yields incomplete query results.

SSDs use log-structured storage internally to batch small random writes, improve wear leveling, and extend device life, which makes LSM Trees and SSDs a good match since append-only sequential writes reduce in-place-update amplification.

Stacking multiple log-structured layers (application, filesystem, SSD FTL) can reintroduce the very write amplification, fragmentation, and redundant garbage collection that log-structuring aims to avoid, so the FTL and filesystem must be kept in mind.

On an SSD a page can be written only after being erased, and erase happens only on whole blocks (typically 64–512 pages), so the FTL must relocate a block's live pages before erasing it and performs wear leveling across program-erase cycles.

Interleaved multi-stream writes do not stay sequential at the hardware level and cause fragmentation, so keep the log on a separate device and, more importantly, align partitions and writes to the underlying page/erase size.

Access-method-aware log-structured storage (LLAMA under Bw-Trees) lets garbage collection consolidate delta nodes — even cancelling opposing operations — during relocation, cutting space and read latency; exposing the right cross-layer information makes stacking efficient.

Open-Channel SSDs (e.g., SDF) bypass the filesystem and FTL to give software direct control of wear leveling, garbage collection, and data placement; matching the write unit to the erase (block) size greatly reduces write amplification and exposes channel parallelism.
Bw-Tree garbage collection uses epoch-based reclamation: a node removed from the mapping table during an epoch is freed only after every reader that started in that or an earlier epoch has finished.

SSTable-attached secondary indexes (SASI) couple per-SSTable index files to the SSTable life cycle and maintain a separate in-memory structure for memtable contents, so indexes are built during flush or compaction.

Adding in-memory buffering always reduces write amplification by combining multiple same-page writes; immutability further improves concurrency and space amplification through fully occupied pages but introduces deferred write amplification when data is rewritten between levels.

Vertical scaling is often not viable because bigger machines are more expensive, harder to replace, and need special maintenance, so most modern systems scale horizontally across networked machines acting as one logical entity.
Every concurrent program already has properties of a distributed system, so concurrency is the first hard problem encountered even before crossing a node boundary.
Concurrent and parallel are distinct: concurrent operations overlap in time but execute one at a time, while parallel operations execute simultaneously on multiple processors.

The fallacies of distributed computing — assuming the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the topology is stable, there is a single authority, and transport is free — are dangerous assumptions that make systems fail unpredictably.
Never assume the network is reliable: a successful initial connection does not guarantee a stable link, so handle dropped connections and lost responses gracefully.
Never assume latency is zero or processing is instantaneous; a remote call costs network transport plus local work and may wait in a queue before being processed.
Queue capacity is not infinite, so apply backpressure to slow producers that outpace consumers; merely enlarging a queue hurts latency without raising the processing rate.
Process-local queues exist to decouple receipt from processing, to pipeline stages, and to absorb short bursts, and should be sized from measured processing and wait times against a latency bound.

Do not assume clocks on different machines are in sync; without specialized high-precision time sources, do not rely on timestamps for ordering or synchronization, and know whether the clock source is monotonic.

Distributed algorithms do not always guarantee strict state consistency, so assuming fully consistent state across nodes causes subtle bugs (e.g., reads during schema propagation or a divergent cluster view can corrupt or misplace data).
Local and remote execution are not the same, so hiding a remote call behind a local-looking interface is misleading; expose latency, consistency, and delivery semantics rather than masking them.

A network partition, in which isolated groups keep executing independently and produce conflicting results, is far more dangerous than ordinary packet loss; links can also fail asymmetrically, delivering one direction but not the other.

Design for partial failures so the system keeps operating when part of it is unavailable, and treat testing for failure (injecting partitions, latency, clock drift, bit rot) as the best way to design for it.
Cascading failures spread as an overloaded node pushes load onto others; contain them with circuit breakers that steer away from a failing service and let it recover.
Use exponential backoff so a client waits longer between retries, and add jitter (small random delays) so independent clients do not all retry at the same instant and amplify the load.
Validate and checksum any content exchanged between nodes, because corruption can otherwise be replicated and overwrite good data.

A fair-loss link guarantees that infinitely-retransmitted messages between correct processes are eventually delivered, with only finite duplication and no creation of unsent messages — the basic building block for stronger protocols (like UDP).

Retransmissions can produce duplicate messages, so reprocessing is safe only when the operation is idempotent (yields the same result with no extra side effects); operations like charging a card are not idempotent.

Because not every operation is naturally idempotent, achieve an idempotence-equivalent guarantee through deduplication (tracking processed message IDs) rather than assuming operations are safe to repeat.
A perfect link (TCP-like) provides reliable delivery, no duplication, and no creation, but only within a single session and without guaranteeing the participants stay alive.

Exactly-once delivery is impossible without sometimes transmitting a message more than once; the achievable guarantee is exactly-once processing, by processing a message once and ignoring duplicates, while real systems use at-least-once or at-most-once delivery.
The Two Generals' Problem shows that two parties cannot reach guaranteed agreement over an asynchronous link with possible failures, since each side is always one acknowledgment away from certainty.

FLP Impossibility proves that no fully asynchronous consensus algorithm can tolerate even a single unannounced crash, so consensus cannot always be reached in bounded time without some synchrony assumption.

A correct consensus protocol must satisfy agreement (all processes decide the same value), validity (the value was proposed by a participant), and termination (every correct process eventually decides).

System timing models differ: asynchronous (no bounded delays, failures not reliably detectable, no timeouts), synchronous (bounded delays and comparable rates, enabling timeouts), and partially synchronous (bounds hold only most of the time).

Synchronous-model algorithms that rely on timeouts are more robust in the best case but fail when timing assumptions break (e.g., Raft may transiently have multiple believed leaders), so design for that possibility.

A failure model specifies exactly how processes may fail — crash-stop (stays down; algorithm does not rely on recovery), crash-recovery (recovers, needing durable state and a recovery protocol), omission (skips/loses messages, capturing partitions), and arbitrary/Byzantine (acts contrary to the algorithm).

Byzantine (arbitrary) faults are the hardest to tolerate because a process actively contradicts the algorithm, so safety-critical and trustless systems (avionics, cryptocurrencies) must cross-validate rather than trust responses at face value.
Most practical distributed algorithms assume the crash-failure model and mask failures by forming process groups and adding redundancy, which makes them easier to reason about and implement.

Perfect failure detection is impossible in an asynchronous system because a crashed process cannot be distinguished from a slow one, forcing a trade-off between false positives (suspecting a live process) and false negatives (delaying detection of a dead one).
It is provably impossible to build a failure detector that is both fully accurate and fully efficient, so accuracy and detection speed are a tunable trade-off.
A failure detector must satisfy completeness (every nonfaulty member eventually notices a failure) and is judged on efficiency (how fast) and accuracy (how correct).
Heartbeat- and ping-based failure detection is simple and popular but its precision depends on carefully chosen ping frequency and timeout and ignores how the node is seen by other peers.

Outsourced heartbeats (as in SWIM) ask randomly chosen peers to probe a suspected node, accounting for indirect reachability and yielding more accurate, parallelizable decisions without broadcasting to everyone.
A phi-accrual failure detector outputs a continuous suspicion level from a sliding window of heartbeat arrival times rather than a binary up/down, adapting to changing network conditions.

Gossip-based failure detection aggregates heartbeat counters across many nodes, giving a reliable cluster view even when direct links fail, at a worst-case bandwidth that grows linearly with the number of processes.

Consensus can be solved even with a failure detector that makes an infinite number of mistakes, which is why failure detectors usefully augment the asynchronous model by trading accuracy against completeness.
A leader (coordinator) process reduces synchronization overhead and message round-trips by driving execution from one process, at the risk of becoming a bottleneck.
Leader election should guarantee liveness (a leader eventually emerges) and ideally safety (at most one leader), but many algorithms violate safety under partitions and admit split brain.
To stop a single leader from becoming a bottleneck, partition data into independent replica sets each with its own leader (as Spanner does) rather than electing one system-wide leader.

Leader election differs from distributed locking: the elected leader must be known to all participants and is preferably long-lived, whereas a lock holder's identity is unimportant and any standing preference would starve other processes.

The bully algorithm elects the highest-ranked process as leader; it is simple but violates safety under network partitions (split brain) and its strong preference for high-ranked nodes can cause reelection storms when those nodes are unstable.
Providing each elected leader with a next-in-line failover list lets a detector contact the highest-ranked alternative directly, completing reelection in fewer steps when that alternative is alive.

Storage-engine design is fundamentally a set of trade-offs in which lowering the cost of one operation raises the cost of another, so the three properties buffering, immutability, and ordering should be mixed to match the target workload.

All the classic leader-election algorithms (bully, ring, invitation, candidate/ordinary) are prone to split brain under network partitions, which is avoided only by requiring a cluster-wide majority of votes.
Leader election is equivalent to consensus: if processes can agree on a leader's identity, the same mechanism can reach consensus on anything else.

Combine leader election with failure detection so processes know whether their local knowledge of the leader is still valid, and treat allowing multiple temporary leaders as a liveness optimization whose safety is restored by detecting and resolving leader conflicts.

Replication introduces redundancy via multiple copies, but updating all copies atomically is equivalent to consensus and is costly per operation, so practical systems use cheaper models that look consistent to users while allowing bounded divergence.
Geo-replication serves two purposes at once: increasing availability by surviving the loss of a whole datacenter and reducing latency by placing a copy of the data physically closer to the client.

CAP states that under a network partition a system cannot be both available and linearizably consistent, so it must choose strong consistency with best-effort availability (CP) or availability with best-effort consistency (AP).
CAP concerns network partitions rather than node crashes, so consistency problems can arise even when every node is up but connectivity between them is impaired.
Partition tolerance cannot realistically be traded away like a knob; the genuine choice is between consistency and availability when a partition occurs.

CAP's consistency (atomic/linearizable operations) is not the same as ACID consistency (preserving invariants), and CAP availability is not the same as high availability because CAP puts no bound on latency.
PACELC extends CAP: under a partition choose between consistency and availability, and else (no partition) still choose between latency and consistency.

Harvest (how complete a query result is) and yield (the fraction of requests answered) are tunable relaxations of CAP's strongest forms; trading harvest for yield (returning partial data instead of failing) can build more resilient systems.
A consistency model is a contract between replicas and clients defining visibility and ordering of operations, narrowing the set of permissible histories to make system behavior tractable.
Strict consistency (instant global visibility of every write) is only a theoretical model and is impossible to implement because of physical limits on how fast state can propagate.

Linearizability is the strongest single-object, single-operation model: each write's effect becomes visible exactly once at a point between its start and end, respecting real-time order, prohibiting stale reads, and requiring monotonic reads.

Linearizability is a local, composable property — a system whose objects are all linearizable is linearizable — but operations spanning two independent linearizable objects still require additional synchronization.

Linearizability is expensive (even CPUs do not offer it for main memory by default) and in a distributed system is implemented through consensus, so it should be used only where its guarantees are needed.

Sequential consistency only requires some total order consistent with each process's own program order and imposes no real-time bound, so unlike linearizability it permits stale reads and is not composable.

Causal consistency requires all processes to observe causally related operations in the same order, while concurrent (causally unrelated) writes may be observed in different orders by different processes.
Causal consistency is implemented with logical clocks and per-message context metadata, buffering an operation until all the operations it depends on have been applied.

Vector clocks establish a partial order and detect divergence between event chains, but they only tell you a conflict occurred, not how to resolve it, so resolution is application-specific and some stores instead use last-write-wins.

The session (client-centric) guarantees are read-own-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, and writes-follow-reads; monotonic writes in particular prevents old data from being resurrected and lost.

Under eventual consistency updates propagate asynchronously and, absent further updates, all reads eventually return the latest value, with conflicts resolved by a strategy such as last-write-wins or vector clocks.

Tunable consistency is parameterized by replication factor N, write acknowledgments W, and read responses R, and choosing R + W > N guarantees reads see the most recent write because the read and write sets always overlap.

Increasing read/write consistency levels raises latency and node-availability requirements, while decreasing them improves availability at the cost of consistency (e.g., W=1,R=N favors writes; W=N,R=1 favors reads).
A quorum is ⌊N/2⌋+1 nodes, so a system of 2f+1 nodes tolerates at most f failures and cannot make progress once a majority is unavailable.
Quorum reads and writes do not by themselves guarantee read monotonicity after an incomplete write, so blocking read-repair is needed to make subsequent reads monotonic, at the cost of availability.

Witness replicas reduce storage cost by having witnesses store only a marker that a write occurred and be upgraded to hold the record when copy replicas fail; n copy plus m witness replicas give the availability of n+m copies provided quorums are used and each quorum contains at least one copy replica.
Strong eventual consistency lets updates arrive late or out of order yet converge to the same valid state once all propagate, by carrying enough state to merge diverged replicas.

Conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) are structures whose operations can be applied in any order without changing the result, so replicas can update locally without coordination and reconcile after a partition heals with no lost operations.

An operation-based CRDT (CmRDT) requires its operations to be side-effect free, commutative, and causally ordered (e.g., a grow-only counter whose merge takes the per-slot maximum, or a last-write-wins register keyed on timestamp).
Stacking systems with weaker consistency guarantees on top of stronger ones, or ignoring an underlying system's consistency semantics, can cause unrecoverable inconsistencies and data loss.

Anti-entropy shares delivery responsibility across all nodes by splitting it into best-effort primary delivery plus periodic sync, lowering convergence-time bounds for eventually consistent systems even if the coordinator fails.

Read repair detects replica divergence during a read by comparing replica responses and sending missing updates; blocking read-repair gives read monotonicity for quorum reads but sacrifices availability, while asynchronous read-repair repairs after returning to the client.
Digest reads cut bandwidth by issuing one full read plus hash-only digest requests to the other replicas and comparing hashes; a mismatch then triggers full reads only on the differing replicas.

Hinted handoff is a write-side repair that stores a hint when a target node is down and replays it on recovery; combined with sloppy quorums (writing to healthy non-target nodes) it improves availability at the cost of consistency.

Merkle trees build a hierarchy of hashes so two replicas can compare root hashes and descend only into differing subtrees to locate diverged ranges cheaply, trading tree size against the precision of the ranges, with any data change forcing recomputation of a subtree.

Bitmap version vectors keep per-peer operation logs to reconcile by recency and precisely identify gaps to replicate, but the log cannot be truncated while any node has been down long enough to still need those records.

Gossip protocols propagate updates by cooperative, randomized relay (infective, susceptible, removed states), combining the reach of broadcast with the reliability of anti-entropy and remaining robust under failures and flexible membership.

Register semantics under concurrent access fall into three classes: safe (a concurrent read may return any in-range value), regular (returns the last completed or an overlapping write), and atomic (linearizable).

Fault tolerance is achieved by removing single points of failure and adding redundancy that is usually transparent to the user, but redundancy then requires keeping copies in sync and adding recovery mechanisms.

In gossip, each process periodically relays hot information to f random peers (fanout); some message redundancy is essential to reliability, and a larger cluster requires raising fanout or accepting higher convergence latency.
A gossip process stops relaying a message via loss of interest, computed either probabilistically or by a duplicate-count threshold; counting duplicates can improve latency and reduce redundancy.

Mix a fixed overlay topology (e.g., a spanning tree) for efficient dissemination in the stable state with a fallback to gossip for failover, since a tree distributes in a fixed number of steps but loses a whole subtree on a single broken link.

Use partial views with a peer-sampling service (e.g., HyParView's small active view plus larger passive view) instead of a full cluster view when churn is high, disseminating over the active view and recovering from the passive one.
condition: high churn (frequent node joins/leaves) or large clusters

statement: Anti-entropy mechanisms each optimize one dimension: scope reduction (read-repair and hinted handoff sync only queried or individual missing data), recency (bitmap version vectors log recent diverged writes), or completeness (Merkle trees hash whole datasets to locate differences).

Multipartition transactions require coordination, distributed commit, and rollback protocols, unlike single-partition transactions which can use node-local pessimistic or optimistic concurrency control.

Distributed transactions must be recoverable: if a transaction aborts or times out, its results must be rolled back completely, because a partially executed transaction leaves the database inconsistent.

Atomic commitment will not commit a transaction if even one participant votes against it, requires failed processes to reach the same conclusion as the rest, and therefore does not work under Byzantine failures.
In atomic commitment cohorts can only vote to accept or reject the coordinator's proposed transaction; they cannot change it or propose an alternative.
Two-phase commit runs a prepare phase (distribute the value and collect votes) then a commit/abort phase (make results visible), committing only if all cohorts voted yes and aborting if any voted no.

A cohort failure during 2PC's propose phase forces the coordinator to abort, so a single unavailable node can block transactions, which is why systems like Spanner run 2PC over Paxos groups rather than individual nodes.

2PC is a blocking atomic commitment algorithm: if the coordinator fails after collecting votes but before broadcasting the decision, cohorts are stuck in an uncertain state until the coordinator (or a replacement collecting votes again) recovers.
To recover 2PC, persist each decision to a durable log on the coordinator and keep backup coordinator nodes so a failed coordinator's decisions can be replicated to cohorts.

Three-phase commit adds an extra prepare phase and timeouts on both sides so cohorts can deterministically commit or abort despite coordinator failure, but it assumes a synchronous model with no communication failures.
3PC's worst case is a network partition that splits cohorts so some commit and some abort by the protocol, producing split brain, which is the main reason 3PC is rarely used in practice.

Calvin reaches consensus on a deterministic transaction order up front via a sequencer (batched into epochs), removing execution-time coordination and letting a failed node recover from peers running the same transactions in parallel.

Spanner orders distributed transactions with TrueTime (a wall-clock API exposing an uncertainty bound it waits out) and runs two-phase commit over per-shard Paxos groups so commitment survives the loss of some group members.

Spanner read-write transactions need locks and the Paxos leader while read-only transactions and snapshot reads are lock-free at any replica, and its external consistency gives real-time guarantees equivalent to linearizability (if T1 commits before T2 starts, T1's timestamp is smaller).
Partition (shard) ranges should be sized by load and value distribution, splitting frequently accessed or unusually dense ranges into smaller partitions to spread the load.
When repartitioning after nodes are added or removed, relocate the data before updating cluster metadata and routing requests to the new targets, to keep movement consistent.
Hashing the routing key reduces range hot-spotting because hash values do not sort like the originals, placing lexicographically close keys on different replicas.

Plain modulo placement (hash(v) mod N) forces most data to move when the cluster size changes, whereas consistent hashing maps keys to a ring so a node change affects only its immediate neighbors and on average relocates just K/n keys.

Snapshot isolation reads from a snapshot of values committed before the transaction's start timestamp and aborts one of any two write-write conflicts (first-committer-wins), which prevents read skew and gives efficient lock-free reads but still permits write skew and is not serializable.
exception: write skew remains because two transactions writing disjoint cells can each preserve local invariants yet jointly violate a cross-cell invariant

statement: Percolator builds a transactional, snapshot-isolation API on top of Bigtable using a single-RPC conditional-mutation (read-modify-write), a timestamp oracle consulted at start and commit, and a client-driven two-phase commit with a primary lock used for recovery.

Coordination can be safely avoided for operations that are invariant-confluent (any two invariant-valid diverged states merge into a valid state), which greatly improves performance and scalability but requires defining a merge function for diverged states.

RAMP provides a read-atomic isolation level (all or none of a transaction's updates are visible, precluding fractured reads) with synchronization and partition independence, achieving atomic write visibility without mutual exclusion via a two-phase prepare/commit over metadata.

Consensus algorithms assume an asynchronous model and guarantee safety, while an external failure detector supplies liveness, so a consensus run may wait for a failure to be detected or restart when a live process is wrongly suspected.

A best-effort broadcast makes the sender solely responsible and fails silently if the sender crashes, whereas a reliable broadcast guarantees all correct processes receive the same messages even if the sender crashes (a naive version floods with N² messages via a failure detector and forwarding).

An atomic broadcast (total-order multicast) guarantees both reliable delivery and that all nonfailed processes deliver messages in the same order, and is equivalent to consensus in an asynchronous system with crash failures.

Virtual synchrony delivers totally ordered messages to a dynamic group such that a message sent in one group view can only be delivered in that same view, making view changes a barrier that broadcasts cannot cross.

ZAB (used by ZooKeeper) elects a temporary leader per monotonically increasing epoch and runs discovery, synchronization, and broadcast phases; its broadcast resembles a two-phase commit without aborts, needs only two message rounds, and recovers by streaming missing messages from a single up-to-date follower.
Paxos assigns the roles proposer, acceptor, and learner, requires multiple acceptors for fault tolerance, and needs only a quorum (majority) of acceptor votes for liveness.

Paxos runs a propose/voting phase (Prepare(n) to establish leadership for a proposal number) then a replication phase (Accept!(n,v)), where each proposal carries a unique monotonically increasing number used to total-order operations.

Once a Paxos value has been accepted by at least one acceptor, future proposers must decide on that same value, which is enforced because acceptors return the latest value they have accepted in response to a prepare.

Paxos needs 2f+1 processes to tolerate f failures, and its safety rests on the fact that any two majorities share at least one participant; quorums describe only blocking, so a proposer may message more nodes but proceed as soon as a quorum responds.
Two or more competing Paxos proposers can repeatedly preempt each other and stall progress (livelock), which is resolved by a random backoff that lets one proposer proceed while the others wait.

Multi-Paxos introduces a distinguished proposer (leader) so that, once established, it can skip the propose phase and go straight to replication, significantly improving efficiency over running a full propose round per value.

Multi-Paxos leader leases allow reads from the leader without collecting a quorum, but a lease is a performance optimization rather than a correctness guarantee and relies on bounded clock synchrony — excessive clock drift breaks linearizability.

Multi-Paxos behaves as a replicated log: participants keep a durable log of messages, and once the log is applied to the primary structure as a snapshot the log can be truncated, with snapshot and log kept mutually consistent and truncation applied atomically.

Fast Paxos saves one round-trip by letting any proposer contact acceptors directly, but it needs larger quorums (2f+1) and more acceptors (3f+1), is prone to collisions requiring coordinator recovery, and can end up with higher latency than classic Paxos.
Gossip provides convergent consistency: nodes are more likely to agree on events that occurred further in the past.

Hybrid gossip (Plumtree) eagerly pushes full messages to a small peer subset and lazily forwards only message IDs to the rest, using the lazy-push path both to fetch missed messages and to heal and rebuild the broadcast tree after failures.

A distinguished leader is both a single point of failure and a load bottleneck, so partitioning the value range across independent sub-systems improves availability, performance, and scalability — at the cost of needing atomic commitment for any multi-partition operation.

Egalitarian Paxos (EPaxos) avoids a global leader by making a process the leader for a specific command and ordering commands through dependencies on interfering commands, combining classic Paxos's availability with Multi-Paxos's throughput.
EPaxos commits on the fast path when a fast quorum (⌈3f/4⌉ replicas) agree on dependencies, and falls back to a slow path that updates the dependency list and sequence number when replicas disagree.

Two commands interfere only if their execution order matters (running A then B differs from B then A), so for most workloads conflicting dependencies are rare and commands can largely be committed independently.
Not all Paxos quorums need to be majorities; safety only requires the first-phase (leader-election) quorum and the second-phase (accept) quorum to intersect, i.e., Q1 + Q2 > N (Flexible Paxos).

Flexible Paxos trades availability for latency: because the accept phase is more frequent, Q2 can be shrunk toward N/2 if Q1 is enlarged correspondingly, and the system then tolerates up to N−Q2 failures as long as the leader is stable.
Raft makes the leader a first-class citizen and separates leader election, log replication, and safety, deliberately trading some generality for being easier to understand and implement than Paxos.

In Raft, time is divided into monotonically numbered terms with at most one leader per term, and on conflict the higher-numbered term always wins, with a node updating its term only when it starts an election or learns its term is stale.

A Raft leader can be elected only from nodes holding all committed entries (a vote is denied if the follower's log is more up-to-date), so committed log entries flow only from leader to follower and never the reverse.

Raft commits an entry by appending it to the leader's log, replicating it to a majority, committing it locally, then replicating the commit; committing an entry implicitly commits all entries preceding it.
Raft resolves split votes with randomized election timers so one candidate starts the next round earlier and wins, speeding up election without extra coordination.

Raft recovers after a leader change by finding the highest log entry the new leader and a follower agree on, ordering the follower to discard all entries after it, and overwriting them from the leader's log — while the leader only ever appends to its own log.

Raft guarantees one leader per term, an append-only leader log, that committed entries survive into all subsequent leaders and cannot be reverted, and that every entry is uniquely identified by message and term IDs.

Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus is required where nodes are untrusted or adversarial (or subject to bugs and corruption) and typically costs N² messages per step because every node must cross-validate the others' responses rather than trust a leader.

PBFT tolerates f compromised nodes only with at least n = 3f + 1 total nodes, because it must outvote f faulty plus f possibly-unresponsive nodes, and a client accepts a result only after f + 1 replicas return the same value.

PBFT proceeds through pre-prepare, prepare (advancing only on 2f matching messages from different backups), and commit (advancing on 2f + 1 matching messages), using signed collision-resistant digests to shrink and authenticate messages.

PBFT encrypts all inter-node communication and has replicas know one another's public keys to prevent message forging, and can serve read-only operations in a single round-trip after collecting 2f + 1 matching responses.

Recovering Byzantine replicas must verify received state with a state digest, otherwise recovery becomes an attack vector; PBFT bounds the log with periodic stable checkpoints proven by 2f + 1 responses, after which earlier messages can be discarded.

The storage engine and node-local read/write path most affect a database's performance (local request speed), while the cluster-communication subsystem most affects its scalability (maximum cluster size), so the two must be designed holistically rather than optimized in isolation.

The generalized solution to consensus models Paxos as write-once registers (states unwritten, value, or nil) with per-quorum states (Any, Maybe v, None, Decided v), reasoning from the last known state rather than from remote-actor interactions to remove ambiguity.

Multi-Paxos can be understood as an append-only log of strictly ordered, immutable values, whereas single-decree Paxos is a write-once register — a framing that clarifies why already-decided values cannot be modified.
The core classes of distributed algorithms a database relies on are failure detection, leader election, dissemination, anti-entropy, distributed transactions, and consensus.

EPaxos sequence numbers combine an epoch (cluster-configuration identifier), a node-local counter, and a replica ID, and a replica negatively acknowledges any proposal whose sequence number is lower than one it has already seen.

Creating effective indexes requires reviewing the query workload in detail, understanding the involved data types and operators, and then creating one or more indexes of the right type on the right columns.
Indexing can make a significant difference to the performance of an application's query workload.
Creating the right indexes can often improve query performance by 10x or even 100x.
Too many indexes slow down write performance.
Although the eBook focuses on Postgres, some indexing concepts are universal and apply to other relational databases as well.
An index is a redundant data structure that provides an alternate, faster way of finding specific rows stored in a Postgres table.
Besides improving lookup performance, indexes have other use cases such as enforcing uniqueness in a table.
Running CREATE INDEX on a table for a set of columns without specifying an index type makes Postgres default to a B-tree index.
Indexes can be more complex than single-column: they may span multiple columns, use expressions, or restrict indexed rows to a subset of the table (a partial index).
Every existing index must be kept up to date on each write, so inserts, updates, and deletes update the index and write a record to the Postgres WAL.
A predicate is a condition such as column = value, and multiple predicates can be combined in a WHERE clause using AND or OR.
During planning, Postgres evaluates the applicable indexes for a query and uses table statistics and index size to estimate the cost of scanning with each usable index.
The table or index scan method with the lowest estimated cost is the one Postgres chooses.
EXPLAIN typically shows one of four main table-scan types: Sequential Scan, Index Scan, Index Only Scan, or Bitmap Index Scan combined with Bitmap Heap Scan.
A Sequential Scan reads the source table row by row without using any index, and is always available for a table.
An Index Scan finds matching rows via an index and then retrieves them from the table, potentially filtering columns that are not contained in the index.
An Index Only Scan returns the query result directly from the index and avoids accessing the table.
exception: except when verifying visibility information for recently changed rows

statement: A Bitmap Index Scan plus Bitmap Heap Scan uses an index to build a bitmap of table sections likely to contain matches, then reads those table rows via the bitmap.
Bitmap scans are particularly useful for combining several indexes, each producing a bitmap, to implement AND and OR conditions in a query.
Optimizing query performance with indexes typically means turning a Sequential Scan into an index-based scan, or improving how existing indexes are used.
A single multi-column index is often more performant than satisfying a multi-column filter with several indexes combined via a Bitmap Index/Heap Scan.
Consolidating indexes reduces write overhead and increases the chance an index stays in cache rather than on disk.
When Postgres analyzes a query it determines the data types and operators involved.
The combination of the data type and the operator determines which index types are most effective for a query.
For an equality predicate on a 4-byte integer, a B-tree index is the best fit in most situations.
condition: the predicate is an equality comparison on a common scalar type

statement: B-tree indexes support equality and range comparisons and work with all commonly used data types.
The JSONB key-exists operator (?) is not supported by B-tree indexes because the B-tree structure cannot index lookups on arbitrary keys within a JSONB value.
A GIN index can support the JSONB key-exists operator (?) so that EXPLAIN shows the index being used for such a query.
Postgres uses operator classes to map a specific operator on a data type to its implementation, and groups operator classes into operator families for similar data types and operators.
Equality comparisons on text data types are not supported by the GIN index type by default.
For text, B-tree and Hash provide two operator classes: the default text_ops and text_pattern_ops.
The text_pattern_ops operator class is useful for indexing the LIKE operator when the database uses a non-C locale such as en_US.UTF-8.
condition: the database uses a non-C locale and you need to index pattern (LIKE) matching

statement: A special operator class can be specified at index creation, for example CREATE INDEX ON table (column text_pattern_ops).
The B-tree index is the most commonly used Postgres index type.
Many query workloads require only B-tree indexes for optimal performance.
A B-tree index is a balanced tree in which every leaf page is the same distance from the root, usually through one or more levels of internal pages.
Most pages in a B-tree index are leaf pages, and they hold the pointers to where the rows for a key live in the table.
The role of internal pages is to allow efficient traversal of the tree without scanning large numbers of unnecessary leaf pages.
A B-tree lookup locates a table row in a fixed number of steps instead of scanning the whole table.
Postgres B-tree indexes are more advanced than textbook B-trees because visibility rules and the need to respond to table modifications complicate their on-disk structure.
B-tree indexes implement the most commonly used operators—equality (=) and range comparison (<, <=, >=, >)—for all built-in Postgres data types.
When a query uses equality or range operators, a B-tree index is the right choice about 99% of the time.
condition: the query uses equality or range operators

statement: B-tree indexes can produce sorted output because their leaf pages are presorted, which avoids an extra Sort step in a query.
Sorted index output is especially valuable with LIMIT, because only the rows up to the limit must be retrieved instead of fetching all rows, sorting them, then applying the limit.
condition: the query uses LIMIT and can consume the index's sort order

statement: The sorted-output property of B-tree indexes is very useful for implementing keyset-based pagination in an application.
Hash indexes fit use cases similar to B-tree indexes but are focused solely on the equality operator and support no other operators.
Hash indexes build on Postgres hash functions that hash almost all data types to a 4-byte integer, and map those hash values to a fixed number of buckets that each hold one or more index entries.
For workloads that need only the equality operator and no advanced B-tree features, a hash index can yield a small but visible performance benefit over a B-tree.
condition: the workload requires only equality and no other B-tree capabilities

statement: Hash indexes should only be used on Postgres 10 or newer, because hash indexes were not crash-safe before Postgres 10.
exception: Postgres versions older than 10, where hash indexes are not crash-safe

statement: BRIN stands for Block Range Index and indexes a particular range of blocks, where a Block is a section of a table that is typically 8 kB in size.
A BRIN index is usually very small and imprecise because it points to a section of the table for a value rather than to a specific row.
Finding the matching rows through a BRIN index requires a Bitmap Heap Scan that filters out the rows that do not actually match.
A BRIN index produces a very slow scan when many block ranges have a min/max that includes the searched value, because Postgres then effectively has to look at the whole table.
condition: many block ranges' min/max bounds include the searched value

statement: BRIN indexes are best used with append-only tables whose indexed values increase linearly as rows are added at the end, with no deletes or updates.
condition: the table is append-only and indexed values increase linearly with physical row order

statement: Many updates and deletions can significantly degrade BRIN performance because the physical location of the data becomes non-linear relative to the indexed value.
condition: the table receives many updates or deletions

statement: BRIN indexes help specifically when the table's physical layout correlates with the value range, that is, when similar values are physically close on disk; in those cases they are very efficient due to their small size.
condition: the physical order of table rows correlates with the indexed value

statement: Postgres provides generic index-type infrastructure (GIN, GIST, SP-GIST) that makes it easier to implement custom indexes reusable for domain-specific applications.
GIN is an inverted data structure whose entries are commonly composite values, supporting queries that search for one of the elements of the composite value.
GIST implements a balanced, tree-structured index that is versatile, fitting structures such as B-trees and R-trees.
SP-GIST implements a non-balanced structure that repeatedly divides the search space into partitions of different sizes, usable for quad-trees, k-d trees, and radix trees.
Common practical uses are GIN for JSONB, GIN or GIST for full text search, and GIST for geospatial data, ltree, and range types.
The optional btree_gin and btree_gist modules give B-tree-like behaviour inside a GIN or GIST index, useful for combining a typical B-tree operator/type with one better suited to GIN/GIST.
btree_gist supports the not-equal operator (<>), which enables exclusion constraints.
The chosen index type defines which operators and data types the index can support and what its underlying data structure is.
Indexing multiple columns within one index is supported for the B-tree, GIST, GIN, and BRIN index types, and its exact behaviour depends on the index type.

In a multi-column B-tree index, column ordering matters: columns near the beginning should be used by all queries and only later columns by a subset, because a rarely queried leading column is read every time deeper columns are searched, wasting I/O.
condition: the index is a multi-column B-tree shared across several queries

statement: Before Postgres 13 it helped to put high-cardinality columns first in a multi-column index, but this mostly no longer holds in Postgres 13 because of B-tree deduplication.
condition: the Postgres version is older than 13
exception: Postgres 13 and newer, where B-tree deduplication changes this guidance

statement: B-tree deduplication automatically avoids storing duplicate index entries.

The more columns an index covers the larger it becomes, making the planner less likely to pick it because scanning it is expensive; as a ballpark rule it rarely makes sense to create multi-column indexes with more than 3 columns.
The INCLUDE keyword adds non-key columns to a B-tree index to enable Index Only Scans (a covering index), and performs better than placing those columns directly in the index definition.
condition: you want the index to return all queried columns without touching the table

statement: When comparing one index on multiple columns against multiple single-column indexes, it is often preferable to rely on a single multi-column index.
Combining multiple indexes through a Bitmap Index/Heap Scan is only supported when those indexes are of the same index type.
exception: indexes of differing index types, which cannot be bitmap-combined

statement: An expression index indexes the result of a function or expression (for example lower(column)) and is needed because an index on the raw column cannot satisfy a query that first applies a function to that column.
condition: queries filter on a function or expression of a column rather than the bare column

statement: If you also query a column directly without the function used in an expression index, you need a second index to support those queries.
condition: the same column is queried both bare and wrapped in a function

statement: A partial index has a WHERE clause and only contains index entries for the rows matching that condition, which also makes the index smaller.
Partial indexes are effective when the query workload consistently filters on a particular predicate with the same constant values, such as always checking that deleted_at IS NULL.
condition: the workload consistently uses the same constant predicate

statement: Creating a separate partial index for every possible query can backfire, because having hundreds or thousands of partial indexes makes Postgres take longer to determine which index to use during planning.
condition: the application would generate hundreds or thousands of partial indexes

statement: A simpler index is often better than one that tries to do everything.
After making index changes you should always verify whether the new indexes actually get used, for example by running EXPLAIN on your queries.

Effective index design starts by evaluating the data types and the operators required by the application workload, which then leads to picking the right index type and deciding whether an advanced index such as a multi-column or partial index fits.
When optimizing indexes you should stay close to what Postgres actually does, checking with EXPLAIN or the auto_explain extension which indexes are actually picked for a slow query invocation.
Database performance is a primary determinant of overall application performance.
Many applications and their ORMs are unaware of the actual SQL being executed, because the SQL is hidden behind ORM method calls.
A single, simple-looking ORM call can generate complex multi-join SQL that intermittently exhibits high latency.
condition: when the ORM resolves associations into joined queries

statement: Missing indexes are the single most common database performance problem.
Most development teams do not verify all of the new SQL that runs when they ship a feature change.
When ORMs are involved, it is difficult to know exactly which SQL statements execute while reviewing a pull request that adds functionality.
condition: when an ORM abstracts query generation

statement: You only learn what truly changed on the database side once a feature is tested with realistic data on staging, or its concurrent effects are observed on production.
condition: only after testing with realistic data on staging or observing concurrent production queries

statement: The most common mistake causing database performance issues is developers forgetting to add an index.
A missing index can go unnoticed for weeks or months, until the feature gains enough usage or data volume to become a performance bottleneck.
Use the pg_stat_statements extension to review query performance and identify slow or expensive queries in PostgreSQL.
pg_stat_statements is bundled in the PostgreSQL contrib package and can be installed easily on a database server.
pg_stat_statements may already be enabled on managed database-as-a-service offerings such as Heroku Postgres.
condition: when using a managed database-as-a-service

statement: To find the most expensive queries, query pg_stat_statements selecting queryid, calls and mean_time, ordering by total_time descending and limiting the results.
pg_stat_statements accumulates its statistics from when the extension was installed, or from the last time statistics were reset.
Reset pg_stat_statements counters with the pg_stat_statements_reset() function.
condition: when not using a dedicated monitoring product such as pganalyze

statement: pg_stat_statements stores an aggregated, normalized form of each query rather than a specific invocation, grouping similar queries by queryid and replacing literal values with placeholders such as $1.
Because pg_stat_statements normalizes query text and strips literal values, you cannot run EXPLAIN directly on the stored query text.
PostgreSQL execution plans depend on the specific values being queried, so the concrete bind parameter values are needed to run EXPLAIN.
EXPLAIN determines a query's execution plan by showing how PostgreSQL executes it, including whether it uses an Index Scan or a Sequential Scan.
An Index Scan is typically a good sign in a plan, whereas a Sequential Scan is often slow.
exception: except on very small tables, where a sequential scan is acceptable

statement: pg_stat_activity exposes the currently running queries and can be used to recover full query text and parameter values.
condition: works when the application sends all values inline in the query text and the table is sampled frequently

statement: Use the PostgreSQL logging system as a generic way to capture full query text and bind parameter values, covering both parameters used by pg_stat_statements and those sent separately by the application.
The slow-query log output is controlled by the log_min_duration_statement configuration setting.
Prefer log_min_duration_statement over log_statement = all for capturing slow query text on production systems.
Setting log_statement = all very rarely makes sense in production because the logging overhead on very fast queries can take down the production system.
condition: on production systems

statement: Set log_min_duration_statement to a threshold so any query running longer than it has its full text logged; start around 1000 ms and lower it as needed.
The goal of the slow-query threshold is to log only outlier queries, not every query that runs.
Use the auto_explain extension to gather EXPLAIN plans automatically and systematically, rather than running EXPLAIN manually.
auto_explain is bundled with PostgreSQL in the contrib package and must be enabled on the database before use.
The auto_explain.log_min_duration setting determines which queries get their execution plan logged; start at 1000 ms and lower as needed.
Reviewing log files a day or two after a slow query can yield a different execution plan than the one that actually occurred at the time of the slow query.
condition: when the plan is reconstructed later rather than captured at execution time

statement: When reading an EXPLAIN plan, focus attention on the most expensive part of the plan.
Run EXPLAIN with the ANALYZE and BUFFERS options to get full details of query execution, including actual timing and buffer activity.
A Sequential Scan reads through the table data sequentially without using any index.
A large 'Rows Removed by Filter' value indicates that PostgreSQL is discarding many rows during a scan, signalling inefficient access.
The amount of data loaded from disk can be estimated from the Buffers information by multiplying the number of buffers read by the default 8 KB block size.
A sequential scan on a filtered column occurs when no index exists on that column, even if the table has a primary-key index.
Use the psql \d command on a table to inspect its columns and existing indexes.
Creating an index on the filtered column changed the plan from a Sequential Scan to a Bitmap Index Scan and improved query performance about 2x in the worked example.
Including the selected column in the index (a covering index) enabled an Index Only Scan, yielding a further ~1.5x speedup and reducing data loaded from disk by roughly 500x versus the original plan.
Add a non-key payload column to an index using the INCLUDE keyword on PostgreSQL 11 or newer, or via a multicolumn index on older versions, to enable Index Only Scans.
condition: INCLUDE requires PostgreSQL 11 or newer; older versions must use a multicolumn index

statement: An Index Only Scan with Heap Fetches of 0 means the query was satisfied entirely from the index without reading the table heap.
Just-in-Time (JIT) compilation is available on PostgreSQL 11 or newer and activates for queries that are expensive and process many rows.
condition: on PostgreSQL 11 or newer

statement: Reducing the amount of data loaded from disk lowers stress on the disk and frees I/O bandwidth for other queries to use.
Optimizing query performance pays off, but manually running these diagnostic queries and working through the data for every query is labour-intensive.
Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY to build an index on a busy table without blocking concurrent writes.
A database index is a separate, redundant on-disk structure that holds a sorted copy of the indexed column values plus row pointers; it consumes its own space and does not alter the table data.
An index combines two structures whose interplay explains most index performance: a doubly linked list of leaf nodes (logical order) and a balanced search tree (the B-tree) for fast lookup.
Table data is stored unordered in a heap; each index entry references its row by a physical row pointer (ROWID/RID).
A B-tree is a balanced tree (equal depth at every leaf), not a binary tree.
Index tree depth grows logarithmically with the number of entries, so real-world indexes over millions of rows have a depth of only four or five and rarely six.
The B-tree tree-traversal is highly efficient and runs almost instantly even on huge data sets, because of tree balance and logarithmic depth.

An index lookup has three steps: tree traversal, following the leaf-node chain, and table access by row pointer; only the tree traversal has an upper bound (index depth), while the other two can touch many blocks and cause slowness.
The 'degenerated/broken index' is a myth: a slow index lookup is caused by a wide scanned range plus per-row table access, not an unbalanced tree, so rebuilding the index is not the remedy.

Oracle exposes three basic index operations: INDEX UNIQUE SCAN (tree traversal only, guaranteed at most one match), INDEX RANGE SCAN (traversal plus leaf-node chain), and TABLE ACCESS BY INDEX ROWID (fetch one row per matched entry).
An INDEX RANGE SCAN can read a large part of the index, and with one table access per matched row a query can be slow even though it uses an index.
A carelessly phrased where clause is the first ingredient of a slow query because it makes the database scan a large part of the index.
The database automatically creates an index for a primary key.
An INDEX UNIQUE SCAN cannot trigger more than one table access, so the two ingredients of a slow query are absent for it.
A primary key may be backed by a non-unique index (yielding an INDEX RANGE SCAN), for example to support deferrable constraints needed when inserting into tables with circular dependencies.
condition: when constraints are deferrable or circular insert dependencies exist

statement: The column order of a concatenated (multi-column) index has a great impact on its usability and must be chosen deliberately.

A concatenated index sorts by its first column primarily and uses later columns only to break ties, so it cannot support a search on a non-leading column alone (like a phone book ordered by surname cannot be searched by first name).
A full table scan's execution time grows in proportion to table size, so it is often fast enough on small development data yet causes serious production problems.
A full table scan can be more efficient than an index lookup when a large fraction of the table is retrieved, because it uses multi-block reads and avoids index-lookup overhead.
condition: when retrieving a large part of the table

statement: A database can use a concatenated index when filtering on its leading (leftmost) columns: an N-column index serves searches on the first column, the first two columns, and so on up to all columns.
Choose a concatenated index's column order so it can be used by as many of the application's queries as possible — the single most important indexing decision.
Prefer one concatenated index over two single-column indexes: it saves storage and maintenance, and fewer indexes give better insert/delete/update performance.
Defining an optimal index requires knowing how the application queries the data (the where-clause column combinations), which is development knowledge that DBAs and external consultants usually lack.
Changing an index's column order can affect every query on the indexed table, not just the one being tuned.

A cost-based optimizer enumerates execution-plan variants, computes a cost for each from the operations and estimated row counts, and picks the lowest-cost plan; rule-based optimizers use a fixed rule set and are seldom used today.

The cost-based optimizer relies on statistics (table row/block counts; per-column distinct values, min/max, NULL count, histogram; per-index depth, leaf count, distinct keys, clustering factor) to estimate where-clause selectivity.
When statistics are missing the optimizer falls back to default values, producing poor row-count estimates and potentially a bad plan.
The efficiency of an INDEX RANGE SCAN varies over a wide range, especially when followed by a table access, so the mere use of an index does not mean a statement runs in the best way possible.
For a range-scan-plus-table-access plan, the response time depends on the number of rows the database must fetch and inspect, not on the size of the final result set.
Applying a function or expression to an indexed column (e.g. UPPER(last_name)) makes a plain column index unusable, because the optimizer treats the function as an opaque black box.
To support a query that filters on a function or expression, create a function-based index on that exact expression; the database uses it only when the identical expression appears in the statement.
condition: only when the exact indexed expression appears in the SQL statement

statement: Only deterministic functions (those that always return the same result for the same arguments) can be indexed; non-deterministic functions such as current-time, random, or environment-dependent functions cannot.
exception: non-deterministic functions (SYSDATE, random, environment-dependent) cannot be indexed

statement: PostgreSQL and Oracle require a function used in an index to be declared deterministic (DETERMINISTIC in Oracle, IMMUTABLE in PostgreSQL) and trust that declaration.
condition: when using a function in an index definition

statement: SQL Server has no function-based indexes but can index a computed column to the same effect, with no query rewrite needed; MySQL 5.6 also lacks function-based indexing.
Do not index everything: every index carries ongoing maintenance cost, and function-based indexes make it especially easy to create redundant indexes.
A single index cannot support both UPPER and LOWER case-folding, so use the same case-folding function consistently across the application to let one index suffice.
Unify the access path so that one index can serve several queries.
Aim to index the original column data, which is usually the most useful information to store in an index.
Bind parameters are the single best defense against SQL injection.

Databases with an execution-plan cache (e.g. SQL Server, Oracle) can reuse a cached plan across executions, but only when the SQL text is exactly identical; literal values change the text and force re-optimization.
condition: only when the SQL statement text is exactly identical

statement: Writing a literal value instead of a bind parameter can yield a better plan when the affected data volume depends on that value, because the optimizer can use the column histogram for the specific value.
condition: when the affected data volume depends on the actual value (skewed distribution)

statement: Column histograms are most useful when the column's values are not uniformly distributed; for uniform columns, distinct-values divided by row count suffices and works with bind parameters.
condition: when column values are non-uniformly distributed

statement: Use bind parameters by default and supply literal values only for the few values that should deliberately influence the execution plan (e.g. skewed status codes, partitioning keys, LIKE patterns).
exception: values that should deliberately steer the plan: skewed predicates, partitioning keys, LIKE wildcards

statement: Bind parameters cannot change the structure of an SQL statement (e.g. table or column names); use dynamic SQL when the structure must change at runtime.
condition: structural elements like table/column names

statement: Oracle CURSOR_SHARING and SQL Server forced parameterization auto-replace literals with bind parameters as a workaround for applications that do not use binds, but they prevent intentional use of literals.
Inequality operators (<, >, BETWEEN) and LIKE can use indexes like equality, but they constrain the viable column order of a multi-column index and can rule out an optimal order.
The golden rule of indexing is to keep the scanned index range as small as possible; check it by asking where an index scan starts and stops.
Access predicates are the start/stop conditions that define and narrow the scanned index range; index filter predicates are applied during the leaf-node traversal and do not narrow it.

For a query combining an equality and a range condition, put the equality column first: it limits the first index column to a single value so the range column then narrows the scan; a leading range column leaves the equality unusable for narrowing.
condition: when a query combines equality and range predicates

statement: The rule of thumb is to index for equality first, then for ranges.
The belief that the most selective column should be at the leftmost index position is a myth; the equality-versus-range role of columns matters more than per-column selectivity.
BETWEEN is inclusive of both boundary values, equivalent to combining >= and <=.
In a LIKE pattern only the part before the first wildcard acts as an access predicate; characters after the first wildcard are filter predicates that do not narrow the scanned range.
A more selective prefix before the first LIKE wildcard yields a smaller scanned index range and a faster lookup.
Avoid LIKE patterns with a leading wildcard ('%term'): they cannot serve as an access predicate and force a full table scan when no other access predicate is available.
condition: absent another access predicate in the query

statement: For full-text search, use the database's dedicated full-text index (MySQL match/against, Oracle/SQL Server contains, PostgreSQL @@) rather than a LIKE filter.
For a single where clause, one multi-column index is usually better than one index per column.
Because a B-tree index is a single ordered chain, it can support only one range condition as an access predicate; two independent range conditions cannot both narrow the scan.

When two independent range conditions are unavoidable, accept a filter predicate on a multi-column index and place the more selective column first so it serves as the access predicate — the only situation where 'most selective first' holds.
condition: when a filter predicate cannot be avoided

statement: One index scan is faster than combining two indexes, because index-merge adds a second tree traversal plus memory and CPU to combine the intermediate results.

Bitmap indexes combine easily and give decent performance when each column is indexed individually (useful for data-warehouse ad-hoc queries), but their insert/update/delete scalability is so poor that they are almost unusable for OLTP.
condition: OLTP vs. data-warehouse workload

statement: A tailored multi-column B-tree index is still faster than combining several bitmap indexes when the query is known in advance.
condition: when the query column combination is known in advance

statement: Partial (PostgreSQL) or filtered (SQL Server) indexes restrict which rows are indexed via a where clause, shrinking the index both vertically (fewer rows) and sometimes horizontally (a constant predicate column can be dropped).
A partial index is well suited to common queries on constant values (e.g. a status flag in a queue), and can keep the index size effectively constant even as the table grows without bound.
condition: commonly used predicates on constant values

statement: A partial index's where clause may be arbitrarily complex but may use only deterministic functions; SQL Server further forbids functions and the OR operator in index predicates.
condition: deterministic functions only; SQL Server forbids functions and OR

statement: Oracle treats an empty string as NULL and cannot store an empty string in a VARCHAR2 column, unlike other databases.
Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL rather than = NULL to test for NULL.
Oracle does not index a row when all of its indexed columns are NULL, so every Oracle index behaves like a partial index and a single-column index cannot satisfy an IS NULL query.
A row is included in a concatenated index when at least one of its indexed columns is non-NULL.
condition: at least one indexed column is non-NULL

statement: To make an Oracle index usable for an IS NULL query, place the nullable column first and add a column that can never be NULL (a NOT NULL column or a constant expression) so the index contains every row.

Indexing an IS NULL condition requires the database to be certain no NULL can occur, which needs a NOT NULL constraint (or a constant / a NOT-NULL virtual column); removing the constraint renders the index unusable for that query.
condition: the column must be provably non-NULL (NOT NULL constraint)

statement: Obfuscated conditions are where clauses phrased so that the optimizer cannot use an index; they are anti-patterns developers should recognize and avoid.
Applying TRUNC or any function to a date column disables an index on that column (the function is a black box); fix it with a function-based index or, portably, an explicit range condition.
Write queries for continuous time periods as an explicit range condition (column >= start AND column < end), even for a single day, so a plain index on the column can be used across all databases.
When a comparison would otherwise wrap the indexed column in a conversion, convert the search term instead of the table column to preserve index usability (and convert the input only once).
Bind parameters support all data types (e.g. a date object), avoiding string-conversion obfuscations on date columns.

Storing numbers in text columns and then comparing against a numeric literal forces an implicit conversion of the column (TO_NUMBER), which disables the index, changes match semantics, and risks conversion errors on invalid data.
Store numbers in numeric column types rather than text columns.
Comparing a numeric column to a string literal is safe because the database converts the literal, not the indexed column; manually wrapping the column in TO_CHAR re-introduces the problem.
condition: numeric column compared to a string literal

statement: Combining columns in a predicate (e.g. ADDTIME(date,time)) prevents proper use of a concatenated index because the search is on derived data; prefer a single combined column, or add a redundant range condition on the most significant column to regain an access predicate.
