You can deliberately obfuscate a condition (e.g. appending an empty string to a column) to stop the optimizer from using an index, but only as a last resort when you know the index is harmful (such as an always-leading-wildcard LIKE).
condition: only when the index is known to be harmful

statement: The 'smart logic' pattern of optional filters (col = :p OR :p IS NULL) is one of the worst performance anti-patterns: with bind parameters the database builds a generic plan for the worst case and does a full table scan even when an index exists on every column.
The full table scan under smart logic results from generic bind-parameter plan caching, not from the database being unable to resolve the logic.
Use dynamic SQL for dynamic where clauses — build a statement with only the filters needed right now — and still use bind parameters within that dynamic SQL.

Databases are optimized for dynamic SQL; avoiding it in favor of static catch-all SQL because of the 'dynamic SQL is slow' myth does more harm than good with a shared plan cache (DB2, Oracle, SQL Server).
The most reliable way to obtain the best execution plan is to avoid unnecessary filters in the statement.

Oracle bind peeking and SQL Server parameter sniffing use the first execution's bind values when building the cached plan, giving nondeterministic behavior because that plan then governs all later executions and can change on restart or cache expiry.
Arithmetic on an indexed column in a predicate (e.g. col - 1000 > ? or 3*a = b) disables the index because the database has no equation solver.
An arithmetic predicate can be indexed with a function-based index if rewritten so the table references are on one side and the constants on the other, then indexing that expression.
condition: when the database supports function-based indexes

statement: Scalability describes the dependency of performance on environmental factors such as data volume and system load, not merely the addition of hardware.

A single performance measurement is just one point on a scalability curve, so a query that is fast under test conditions may not be fast in production — especially when the dev environment holds only a fraction of production data.

An index whose conditions are all access predicates scales with the number of selected rows, whereas a filter predicate makes response time grow with the number of rows in the scanned range — the dominant cause of poor scaling.
The predicate information is essential: an execution plan without it is incomplete, and it is where access-versus-filter predicates — the real cause of scaling differences — are revealed.
Inefficient filter predicates are amplified under concurrent load; the same query can run dozens of times slower with many concurrent queries than with none.
The optimizer chooses an index because it beats a full table scan, not because it is the optimal index, so a used index is not necessarily the best index.
Careful execution-plan inspection yields more confidence than superficial benchmarks, though a full stress test remains worthwhile.
Bigger or more hardware mainly raises throughput (it can handle more load) but does not make a single query faster — like a wider highway rather than a faster car.
Horizontal scaling adds throughput but does not improve the response time of a single query; an efficient search tree is still required, even in non-relational systems like CouchDB or MongoDB.
Proper indexing is the best way to reduce query response time, in relational SQL databases and in non-relational systems alike.
More hardware cannot compensate for sloppy indexing and can even make a system slower, because complex production infrastructure accumulates latencies absent from a simple dev environment.
Response time has two dimensions — latency (response time) and bandwidth (throughput) — and the number of database round trips affects response time more than the volume of data transferred.

Disk seek latency (a few milliseconds on spinning disks) is incurred once per B-tree level, and a single statement — especially a join — can trigger thousands of seeks; caching and SSDs reduce but do not eliminate this.
Databases cache frequently accessed data such as index root nodes in memory, so a lookup on a fully cached index can trigger no disk seek at all.
Join algorithms process only two tables at a time, so an N-table query is executed as a pipeline of pairwise joins through intermediate results rather than materializing them.

Join order does not change the result but does affect performance; the optimizer evaluates permutations (factorial growth), so optimizing a many-table statement can itself be costly — mitigated by bind parameters.
The more complex the statement, the more important bind parameters become.
A nested loops join runs a driving query and, for each of its rows, a lookup into the other table; it performs well when the driving query returns few rows.
condition: when the driving query returns a small result set

statement: The N+1 selects problem occurs when an ORM emits one query per driving row instead of a join (N+1 statements for N rows); a single SQL join is more efficient because it avoids the round-trip latency, even when it transfers more data.
Execute joins in the database rather than emulating them with per-row nested selects.
Enable SQL logging during development and review the SQL that the ORM actually generates.
Eager fetching helps only when the child records are always needed; a static eager configuration is not a solution, so control join/fetch behavior at runtime.
condition: only when child records are needed every time the parent is accessed

statement: Index a nested loops join like the underlying selects: a function-based index on the driving table's filter plus a concatenated index on the inner table's join predicates.
For a hash join, indexing the join predicates does not help; only indexes on the independent where predicates (those applied during a single table access) improve it.
Indexing a hash join is symmetric — independent of join order — unlike a nested loops join.
Hash-join performance improves by minimizing the in-memory hash table so it fits in memory; the optimizer uses the smaller side, and you can shrink it by adding filtering conditions.
condition: an optimal hash join requires the hash table to fit in memory

statement: Selecting fewer columns reduces a hash table's memory footprint (here by about 97%) and improves hash-join performance; the relevant factor is memory footprint, not row count.

A sort-merge join needs the same indexes as a hash join (index the independent predicates, not the join predicates) and is fully symmetric in join order, which makes it well suited to full outer joins; but it is rarely used because sorting both sides is expensive unless the inputs are already sorted.
condition: advantageous mainly when both inputs are already sorted

statement: An index clusters rows with similar values together because leaf nodes store the indexed columns in order; this clustering capability is a distinct benefit of indexing.
Index filter predicates can be used intentionally to keep consecutively accessed rows clustered and to discard non-matching rows during the index scan, reducing the number of table-access fetches.

Table-access cost depends on the physical clustering of the accessed rows: rows in one block need one read, rows scattered across many blocks need many; the index clustering factor measures this correlation between index order and table order.
To exploit an index filter predicate, extend an existing index to cover the where-clause columns rather than creating a new index, keeping maintenance low.

Do not blindly index every where-clause column; column order determines which conditions become access predicates and matters more, and added columns enlarge the index, so use index filter predicates intentionally to cut data volume in an earlier step.

An index-only scan (covering index) satisfies a query entirely from the index, avoiding table access; to cover a query the index must contain every column the statement references, including select-clause columns.
'Covering index' is a misleading term because the index-only scan is an execution-plan operation, not a fixed property of the index.

The benefit of an index-only scan depends on the number of accessed rows and the index clustering factor, and it is an aggressive strategy — do not add select-clause columns on suspicion because it wastes memory and increases update maintenance; index the where clause first and extend only if needed.
condition: benefit scales with rows accessed and clustering factor

statement: Extending a query's where clause with a column not in the index can make it slower despite selecting fewer rows, because the database must then access the table; what matters is how many rows the database must inspect, not how many it returns — always check the execution plan before extending a query.

Aggregating queries that read many rows but few columns are good index-only-scan candidates because a slim index suffices; this is another reason to select only the columns you actually need and avoid SELECT *.

Databases impose limits on the number of columns per index and the total key length (e.g. SQL Server 900 bytes/16 columns, Oracle ~6398 bytes/32 columns, PostgreSQL 2713 bytes/32 columns, MySQL InnoDB 767 bytes/column), so you cannot index arbitrarily many or arbitrarily long columns.

SQL Server INCLUDE columns and similar features let you add long non-key columns to an index purely to enable an index-only scan; such columns are stored only in leaf nodes and cannot be access predicates.

An index-organized table (clustered index) stores the whole table inside a B-tree, saving the heap and making every access an index-only scan, but a secondary index on it stores the clustering key (not a row pointer) and so requires a second full tree traversal per row — making secondary-index access to an IOT very inefficient.

Tables with a single index are best implemented as clustered indexes / index-organized tables, while tables with several indexes often benefit from a heap table (still usable with index-only scans) to avoid slowing the secondary indexes.
condition: single-index vs. multi-index tables

statement: A secondary index cannot store a physical row pointer for an index-organized table because rows move to maintain index order, whereas heap-table rows never move once written.
Sorting is resource-intensive and cannot be pipelined — it must read the entire input before producing the first row — which is a problem for large data sets.

Because an index stores data pre-sorted, a query's order by can be satisfied without an explicit sort when the same index used for the where clause also covers the order by, enabling a pipelined order by.
It suffices that the scanned index range is ordered per the order by clause for the sort to be omitted, so an equality predicate on a leading column can let a sort by a later column be pipelined.
condition: when the scanned index range is already ordered by the order-by columns

statement: If the database uses an explicit sort despite an order by, either the sort plan had a lower cost or the scanned index range does not match the order by; using the full index definition in the order by clause distinguishes the two cases.
Databases can read an index in both directions, so a pipelined order by is possible even when the requested order is the exact reverse of the index order.

When an order by mixes ASC and DESC, the index must be declared with matching ASC/DESC modifiers to allow a pipelined order by; this does not affect the index's usability for the where clause (MySQL ignores index ASC/DESC modifiers).
condition: when order by mixes ASC and DESC directions

statement: The sort/group group-by algorithm can use an index to avoid its sort and run pipelined (delivering the first group before reading all input), with the same prerequisites as a pipelined order by but without ASC/DESC sensitivity; the hash group-by algorithm needs less memory but is not pipelined.

Top-N queries that limit the result to the first rows must rank via a pipelined order by for efficiency, and the database can only optimize for a partial result if it is told from the start that not all rows are needed (LIMIT/FETCH FIRST/TOP/ROWNUM).

A pipelined top-N query's response time is essentially independent of table size (it grows only with the number of rows fetched), whereas without a pipelined order by the database must read and sort the whole table.
The offset method for paging makes the database count and discard all rows before the requested page, so its response time grows the deeper you page and pages drift when rows are inserted.

The seek (keyset) method pages by filtering on the values after the last row of the previous page, letting the database skip prior pages via an index access; it gives stable results under inserts and constant deep-page performance, at the cost of not supporting arbitrary page jumps and harder backward paging.

Paging requires a deterministic sort order, so developers must extend the order by clause (and the index) with enough unique columns to make the row sequence deterministic, otherwise parallel execution can return rows in different orders.

The SQL row-values syntax (e.g. (a,b) < (?,?)) expresses keyset 'comes after' logic cleanly, but support is uneven — PostgreSQL uses it for index access while SQL Server, Oracle, and MySQL cannot use it as an index access predicate, so an approximated form with a redundant leading-column condition is needed.
Indexes negatively affect the performance of insert, delete, and update because every such write must also maintain each index that holds a copy of the affected data.

The number of indexes on a table is the dominant factor in insert performance, because the insert has no where clause to benefit from and must add the new entry to every index (with tree-balancing and possible node splits); the first index makes the greatest difference.
Keep the number of indexes small and avoid redundant indexes to protect insert, delete, and update performance; for large bulk loads it can pay to temporarily drop indexes not needed meanwhile.

A delete uses its where clause (and indexes) like a select followed by row removal, so deleting without any index forces a full table scan to find the rows; the truncate-table command deletes all rows fast but does an implicit commit (except PostgreSQL) and fires no triggers.
Under PostgreSQL's MVCC, a delete only flags the row and physical removal plus index maintenance happen during VACUUM, so PostgreSQL delete performance does not depend on the number of indexes.

The execution plan is the first place to look when diagnosing a slow statement, because the optimizer compiles the SQL into this step-by-step plan.

All four major databases distinguish three predicate roles — access predicate (start/stop of leaf traversal), index filter predicate (applied during traversal, does not narrow the range), and table-level filter predicate (needs a row fetch) — but label them differently in their plans.
Oracle's EXPLAIN PLAN FOR may produce a different plan than actually executing the statement, so the explained plan is not guaranteed to match runtime.
In an Oracle plan, if a condition is shown as a filter predicate it is a filter predicate even when it is also listed as an access predicate, so it does not narrow the scanned range.
PostgreSQL cannot EXPLAIN a statement that uses bind parameters directly; it must be PREPAREd first, and since 9.2 plan creation is deferred to execution so actual values are considered.
PostgreSQL EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the statement — including insert, update, and delete — so wrap it in a transaction and roll back to avoid modifying data.

PostgreSQL plans do not separate index access predicates from index filter predicates — both appear as 'Index Cond' — so the plan must be compared against the index definition to tell them apart; a 'Filter' is always a table-level filter predicate even under an Index Scan.

SQL Server's graphical plan hides predicate information in a hover tooltip and is hard to share, whereas the tabular plan (SET STATISTICS PROFILE ON) shows everything and is copyable; 'Seek Predicates' are access predicates and 'Predicates'/WHERE are filter predicates.

MySQL's EXPLAIN gives a false sense of safety: a used index (even TYPE=index) does not mean efficient indexing, and the key_len value reveals how many leading columns actually serve as access predicates.

MySQL's Extra column encodes index usage: 'Using index' means an index-only scan, 'Using index condition' (5.6+) means an index filter predicate, 'Using where' means a table-level filter, and 'using filesort' means an explicit non-pipelined sort.
